column12: Affordable housing is housing whose cost is restricted, subsidized, or otherwise structured to remain within reach of households at specified income levels. Market-rate housing is generally offered without income restrictions or ongoing public subsidy, with its price determined by prevailing market conditions.  The identity of the builder or property manager does not, by itself, determine whether housing is affordable or market-rate. Private developers can build income-restricted housing, and publicly supported projects can include market-rate units. The most important distinctions are who can afford the housing, whether eligibility or rent restrictions apply, and whether those restrictions remain in place over time.

column23: I support creating more housing and allowing a broader range of housing types, but I do not support a blanket policy legalizing apartment buildings of any scale on every residential lot in the District. I also support incremental increases in housing capacity within residential neighborhoods, including allowing an additional home on many lots. That approach can create more housing choices without automatically authorizing six-unit apartment buildings in every location. The District should pursue substantial housing growth while still making thoughtful distinctions among different areas and development types.

The failure to consistently deliver basic public services and maintain public infrastructure, particularly in areas experiencing chronic illegal dumping, overflowing trash, deteriorating alleys, drainage problems, and neglected public space. Residents should not have to repeatedly report the same conditions while agencies debate responsibility. These problems affect public health, pedestrian access, neighborhood safety, and residents’ confidence in District government.

If elected, I would: Continue documenting conditions, organizing residents, introducing ANC resolutions, conducting site visits, and pressing the responsible agencies for specific actions and deadlines. When a problem crosses agency boundaries, I would bring those agencies together and insist on coordinated short-term mitigation while permanent solutions are designed and funded. I would publicly track commitments and escalate unresolved cases rather than allowing them to disappear into separate agency systems.
column36: I would make decisions by combining resident input with evidence, applicable law, professional expertise, and the broader interests of the approximately 2,000 people I represent. Public testimony is important, but the people who attend meetings or send emails do not necessarily represent everyone affected by a decision.  I would actively seek input beyond the residents who contact me first. That includes communicating through multiple channels, speaking directly with affected neighbors, sharing understandable information before important votes, and making a particular effort to hear from renters, families, older residents, people with disabilities, and others who may not regularly participate in ANC meetings.  I would also examine who benefits, who bears the costs, and whether a decision advances the long-term interests of both the neighborhood and the District. I would not treat the loudest or most organized voices as an automatic majority.  Finally, I would explain my decisions publicly. Residents may not always agree with my vote, but they should be able to understand the facts I considered, the competing interests involved, and why I reached my conclusion. Good representation requires listening carefully, exercising independent judgment, and being accountable for the result.
column37: I have demonstrated that I will do the detailed, persistent work required of an effective commissioner. I regularly connect residents with District agencies, document problems, organize site visits, press for clear timelines, and continue following up when an issue is not resolved after the first request.  My work has included advocating for safer pedestrian crossings, improved streets and alleys, better stormwater management, stronger enforcement against illegal dumping, and coordinated responses to problems that involve multiple agencies. I understand both the limits of an ANC’s formal authority and the influence a commissioner can exercise through careful research, organized residents, public resolutions, and sustained follow-through.  I am accessible, direct, and willing to hold agencies accountable. I also understand that effective advocacy requires building working relationships with agency staff and approaching decisions with facts, preparation, and respect for differing views.
column38: My positions reflect a practical approach to growth, affordability, transportation, and land use. The District needs more housing, including substantially more income-restricted and family-sized housing. The strongest opportunities for significant new development are near transit, along major corridors, and on vacant or underused properties. I also support incremental additions within residential neighborhoods, including allowing one additional home on appropriate lots.  I do not believe supporting housing production requires treating every neighborhood, lot, or development proposal identically. Infrastructure capacity, transit access, affordability, displacement, design, and community needs should all be considered. The District must also ensure that public infrastructure and services keep pace with growth.  On transportation, I support dedicated bus lanes, protected bicycle infrastructure, safer pedestrian facilities, and congestion pricing. These policies can reduce injuries, improve mobility, and make it easier for residents to choose alternatives to driving. Implementation should include meaningful public engagement, clear safety and mobility objectives, and careful attention to accessibility and the needs of residents who depend on vehicles.  As a commissioner, I would approach these issues with a willingness to support change, an insistence on competent implementation, and a commitment to making decisions based on evidence rather than slogans.

The biggest issue facing my neighborhood is how we manage growth and change while protecting Georgetown’s historic character and everyday livability. I support thoughtful growth, including new housing where appropriate, but development cannot be considered in isolation. We need coordinated planning that accounts for transportation, parking, pedestrian safety and accessibility, public infrastructure, historic preservation, and the cumulative impact of development on residents and the public realm. As micromobility use continues to grow, DC should require street-level, geofenced parking areas for shared scooters and e-bikes so these devices are kept off sidewalks and pedestrian routes, improving both accessibility and safety.

If elected, I would: I would use the ANC’s advisory role aggressively and constructively: engage residents early, scrutinize major development and transportation proposals, bring the appropriate District agencies and community stakeholders to the table, and advocate for infrastructure and transportation planning alongside growth—not after problems emerge. I would push for better coordination among DDOT, the Office of Planning, preservation agencies and other District agencies; insist that cumulative neighborhood impacts be considered; and work to identify practical solutions before taking positions. My goal would be thoughtful, evidence-based advocacy that allows Georgetown to evolve while protecting the historic resources, public spaces and quality of life.

I would listen to differing perspectives, look carefully at the facts, and use common sense and practical judgment. Not every issue requires an ideological answer; often the best solution is the one that reasonably balances competing interests and actually works for the community.  I also believe in transparency. Residents should know what is being considered, have a meaningful opportunity to weigh in, and understand why I ultimately take a particular position.  My decisions would be guided by constituent input, reliable information, common sense, and what I believe will best serve Georgetown over the long term.

I am collaborative but independent, and I am willing to ask questions, do the research, and challenge assumptions. I also bring a practical, common-sense approach: listen to people, understand the facts, bring the right people together, and focus on solutions that can actually be implemented. column38: I believe housing, transportation, land use, and historic preservation should be considered together rather than as separate policy questions. I support creating additional housing opportunities, including affordable housing, but I also believe growth must be accompanied by thoughtful planning and investment in the infrastructure needed to support it.  Georgetown is a dense, historic neighborhood that is already absorbing several significant multifamily developments. As we add housing, we must also address transportation, parking, pedestrian accessibility, public space, infrastructure, and the cumulative effects of development. Historic preservation should not be viewed simply as an obstacle to housing; preserving and adaptively reusing existing buildings can itself be an important part of a thoughtful housing strategy.  I also support transportation alternatives that make it easier to live without relying exclusively on a car. At the same time, those systems need to work for everyone. For example, shared scooters and e-bikes should have designated street-level, geofenced parking rather than obstructing sidewalks and creating accessibility barriers.  I do not believe good urban policy requires choosing between housing and preservation, pedestrians and drivers, or growth and neighborhood quality of life. These interests can coexist when decisions are based on evidence, common sense, community input, and careful planning. My approach is to look at the whole system, understand the tradeoffs, and pursue practical solutions.

column12: Market-rate housing is housing whose rent or sale price is generally determined by the private market. A landlord can charge whatever rent the market will bear.   Affordable housing, in the policy and land-use sense, generally refers to housing where the cost is deliberately restricted so that it is affordable to households at specified income levels. The biggest issue is the shortage of housing and the limited range of housing options available to people at different incomes and stages of life. Too many residents must choose between an apartment that no longer meets their household’s needs and leaving the neighborhood altogether. We need more homes overall, including deeply affordable housing, family-sized apartments, accessible homes for seniors and people with disabilities, starter homes, accessory dwelling units, and smaller multifamily buildings. Brookland should be a community where renters, first-time homebuyers, families with children, and longtime residents can all find a suitable home.

If elected, I would: I would continue using the ANC and its Development, Zoning, and Land Use Committee to support projects that meaningfully increase the number and variety of homes, especially near Metro, along major corridors, and on underused sites. I would advocate for zoning changes that allow accessory units, duplexes, triplexes, small apartment buildings, and additional family-sized homes throughout the neighborhood. I would also push for deeper and longer-term affordability, accessible design, anti-displacement protections, and a more predictable approval process so needed housing is not delayed by unnecessary procedural barriers.
column36: An ANC commissioner is a representative, not simply a vote counter. Public comments and meeting turnout matter, but they are not a scientific sample of roughly 2,000 constituents. Renters, young people, immigrants, parents, shift workers, people with disabilities, and residents who do not follow ANC proceedings are often underrepresented, while people with more time and familiarity with government are more likely to participate.  I will therefore use several inputs: direct outreach beyond ANC meetings; the experiences of people most affected; reliable data and agency analysis; applicable law and adopted citywide plans; equity and accessibility impacts; and the long-term interests of both current and future residents.   On major issues, I will explain the choices, tradeoffs, and limits of ANC authority before a vote. I will seek practical changes that address legitimate concerns without using endless process as a substitute for a decision.   My goal is not unanimity. It is a fair, transparent process and a decision grounded in evidence, consistent principles, and the interests of 5B03 and District.
column37: I am seeking another term with both a record and a clearer understanding of how to make the ANC effective. As chair of ANC 5B’s Development, Zoning, and Land Use Committee, I have led a public forum for detailed review of zoning cases and worked to move the conversation beyond a reflexive “yes” or “no.” During this term, ANC 5B supported the 901 Monroe PUD, greater flexibility in RA-1 zoning, and a stronger Ward 5 bikeway network.  My work co-founding LightHouse DC also keeps housing policy grounded in the experiences of residents who are unhoused, transitioning from homelessness, or living on very low incomes. I understand that producing more homes and ensuring deeply affordable housing are related but distinct responsibilities.  I bring preparation, follow-through, and a willingness to make decisions. I listen respectfully, ask detailed questions, explain my reasoning, and keep working after a resolution passes. I want another term to turn more of our plans into completed housing, safer streets, stronger neighborhood businesses, and a more accessible ANC.
column38: I reject the idea that DC must choose between housing abundance and housing affordability. Market-rate construction expands the overall supply, can strengthen the tax base, and can produce inclusionary units; it does not, by itself, create enough homes for residents with the lowest incomes. Public investment, income restrictions, tenant protections, preservation, and social housing are also necessary. The 15% planning-area affordability target should be a floor, not a ceiling. We should pursue both supply and subsidy while avoiding rules or discretionary processes that make every kind of housing slower and more expensive.  I favor predictable zoning that legalizes substantially more housing by right, including apartments and family-sized missing-middle homes throughout the District, with the greatest scale near transit and major corridors. Clear citywide affordability and design standards are preferable to negotiating whether each individual project should be allowed to exist. When a PUD is necessary, negotiations should focus on durable public benefits—especially deeper affordability and larger affordable units—not one-time payments or delay for its own sake.  Historic preservation should protect genuinely significant buildings and places, not operate as a second zoning process controlling height and density. Transportation policy should prioritize safety, accessibility, and moving people efficiently over preserving every travel or parking lane.

The biggest issue facing facing ANC 2C03 (historic Penn Quarter and the National Mall) is downtown's office vacancy and the slow pace of converting empty office buildings into housing. Ground-floor retail here depends more on residential foot traffic, not office workers who no longer commute five days a week. Every building sitting vacant instead of converting is lost housing and a dead loss for small businesses.  My position: the District should keep cutting friction from conversions, i.e. faster permitting, tax abatements, and code flexibility like single-stair reform. Conversion economics are fragile, and a multi-year approval timeline kills deals before they start.

If elected, I would: An ANC commissioner doesn't control zoning or permits. But I can use ANC 2C's "great weight" at BZA and HPRB to support conversion-related relief rather than obstruct it, write letters backing pending conversion incentives at DMPED and the Zoning Commission, be a pro-conversation and housing voice at Comp Plan and zoning hearings, and use my real estate background to connect owners and brokers with the right city programs so that buildings do not sit empty for years.

I try to get input through multiple sources, i.e. through direct outreach to affected parties, written comment periods, and conversations with people who I know disagree with me before I take a position. When neighborhood disputes arise, I've made it a point of talking to both the protesting residents and the applicant's side. With off-hour construction permits, I try to find solutions that address neighborhood concerns without impeding tight worl schedules. And when I make a call that a vocal group disagrees with, I will always try to clearly explain why.

column12: Affordable housing is where the rent or purchase price is kept within reach of households at certain income levels, usually based on Area Median Income (AMI). It can be publicly or privately owned, built, and managed.  The central tenet is that enforceable affordability requirements are adopted the length of time those requirements stay in place. These protections can take the form of affordability covenants, deed restrictions, land trusts, or public ownership designed to keep housing affordable over the long term. It also also for mixed income buildings which many are calling for and are adopted in Montgomery County, MD.  In general, affordable-housing IS based on a foundation that households should not have to spend much more than about 30 to 35% of their income on housing. In contrast, market-rate housing is priced mainly by what the market will bear, rather than by income-based affordability rules. As noted above, a development can include both market-rate and affordable units or a mixed-income building.  It is not about who owns, builds, or manages the housing. It is whether the rent or purchase price is based on enforceable affordability requirements tied to household income.

column12: Affordable housing is housing that is available to people at all income levels so that they are not paying more than 30% of their income toward housing and utility costs. Typically it is subsidized by local or federal government. Market rate housing is available at rents that the market can support without taking into account income levels. Most often, we consider affordable housing to be housing that is available at below-market rents and therefore is occupied by folks with incomes below the average or median AMI. It is important to focus on this population because they have less disposable income to spend on housing costs so it is harder for them to support themselves and their families if they are spending more than 30% of their income on housing and utilities. Affordable housing can be subsidized or not and it can also be built with government support or not, though it generally includes government subsidies of some kind in the capital stack, which helps to offer sub-market rents. Affordable housing can also mean subsidized rents through vouchers or project-based assistance. Market-rate housing can include some subsidized units but typically only a small percentage of the overall units in a building.

column12: As a society we've attributed certain characteristics to a basic need like housing based upon the financial and other characteristics of a person. This is unfortunate but given the inequities in society the notion of “affordable housing” is required to ensure that everyone has a roof over their heads (a goal we’re not able to meet). Affordable housing is generally funded by the government. These subsidized homes or apartments are often income-restricted and means tested. Market-rate housing typically is built by developers/private industry, costs what the market will bear. It  has no income restrictions or limits. There are many cases where the government also subsidizes, in part, market-rate housing in exchange for affordable rate units and there are other agreements like land swaps and tax giveaways that make many projects both public and private. Given the shortage of affordable housing, I would venture to say that the private entities have benefitted more often than the public from these deals.

column23: We certainly need more affordable housing in the District and I fully support the proposal to go beyond the projections of the DC 2050 Plan. It concerns me that we allowed developers to build mostly luxury or market-rate housing on our largest land tracts: the Wharf, NOMA, Navy Yard, etc. And now, the only way to meet much needed affordable housing goals is to usurp the community voice, and compromise on character by upzoning with no controls. This zero sum game, especially concerns me because developers will have a field day once these zoning regulations are lifted. While residents won’t be required to add additional units in newly upzoned areas, the pressure from developers will be unrelenting and we can predict who will be targeted: seniors and financially strapped individuals. We will need safeguards to protect us from both legitimate developers and scammers. I believe we can have both: more affordable housing - even in communities zoned for single family homes AND attend to the character of a neighborhood and protection of residents. This has been achieved in many communities across DC with guardrails for developers. It is what attracted me and countless others to the city and each neighborhood has a different expression of this balance. As an ANC, I would structure a democratic conversation that considers both needs with an emphasis on: increasing units of affordable housing, reducing traffic congestion, increasing walkability and protecting neighborhood assets and character.

One issue that has affected many is safety on the streets with car traffic not stopping completely at four way stops, cars making illegal right turns on red, and drivers speeding down residential roads. In fact, both my husband and I had near hits crossing Piney Branch on two separate occasions. These actions have caused several accidents across the SMD. Despite the fact that our ANC has issued more speed bumps, and increased no right turn on red signs, there has been little change. One problem is that the traffic is not limited to this neighborhood. Given our proximity to Maryland, there are several thoroughfares in and out of the District: Blair Rd. North Capitol, Piney Branch, Georgia, etc. I believe we might need even more restrictive measures such as, stop lights where there are only signs in high traffic areas; more speed bumps, and larger signage. This is also where car reduction methods are useful as we decrease the incentives to driving and increase the number of protected bike and bus lanes. I also think that education in the form of signage about the impact of speeding or the large signs that measure a particular car speed might also be helpful. I believe there has been significant discussion about street and road safety in the ANC and there has been incremental success but we must do more.

If elected, I would: I’m very concerned about the impact that federal cuts to Medicaid and SNAP, layoffs of Federal workers - our friends and neighbors and Federal occupation is having on our community. I’d work to assess the well-being among our most vulnerable residents using data and information by agencies, engage in community walks and canvass the neighborhood. Given the limited purview as ANC, I would work to engage city agencies to understand the needs of 4B01 residents. For instance, a year after the federal occupation there’s still an element of over policing across the District with check-points led by the MPD (not ICE) on Georgia Ave. As a Commissioner I would work with the ANC, local organizations and residents to hold the MPD accountable for these actions that continue to promote fear and frustration in the neighborhood. Regarding reductions in the social safety net, the ANC can’t replace job loss but we can work more closely with every agency to ensure that the District resources are made available to those struggling with childcare loss, homelessness, food insecurity, domestic violence, immigration matters and other issues that are on the rise. Finally, rodent abatement is a concern that many have especially in the alleyways and easements. I’d work with other ANC and community members to assess the extent and locations of the problem and then execute a plan that would involve various agencies.

column14: At a minimum, two bedrooms—but realistically, cities need three-plus-bedroom homes. Family-sized housing should give families the space to grow in place rather than forcing them to leave the city as their household grows. Cities should be home to everyone: twenty-somethings starting careers, retirees aging in place, and families with one, two, or more children. Yet major U.S. cities are rapidly losing families with young children, and high housing costs are an important reason. When large parts of DC allow only detached homes (prohibiting the rowhouses that make DC so iconic), or when small-scale apartments are banned in many neighborhoods in the urban core, multifamily construction gets concentrated on a relatively limited supply of expensive sites. On those sites, studios and one-bedrooms often generate more rent per square foot, creating a strong incentive to prioritize smaller units. Historic preservation rules can create additional barriers to growing in place. Many people don’t realize this but roughly one in five homes are in historic districts. In Truxton Circle, I know neighbors who are growing—or want to grow—their families. But HPRB generally will not approve a street-visible roof addition to a rowhouse, even when that extra story is permitted by zoning. For a family in a two-bedroom rowhouse, a second child can therefore mean sharing bedrooms or moving away. We should make it easier for families to add space and remain in the neighborhoods they already call home.

column26: For context, I represent a neighborhood composed largely of two- and three-story row houses, many of which are individually owned and some of which are subdivided into condos or apartments. The eastern boundary of 5E01, however, is North Capitol Street—an area that nearly everyone wishes were better developed, had more retail amenities, and was more walkable. Put simply, additional residential growth and development along North Capitol is essential to creating a more vibrant and accessible corridor and I will always welcome new construction along the corridor.  I also want to highlight two vacant historic schools, known as the Langston and Slater Schools. In 2021, DMPED selected an affordable-housing development team to adaptively reuse the buildings and convert them into more than 50 mixed-income homes. When I became an ANC commissioner last year, I was excited about the opportunity this development represented, but also curious why no progress had been made in nearly five years. As I understood it, the next step was for the D.C. Council to approve the disposition of the property, allowing it to move from District ownership to the developer. This February, I sponsored an ANC resolution calling on the Council to “expeditiously” pass the legislation necessary to advance the project (https://resolutions.anc.dc.gov/AttachmentsFiles/25/ANC_5E_Resolution_2026_001_Langston_Slater_Redevelopment_Sale_2026_TM_20260217091826PM.pdf). Following the resolution’s passage, two Council committees took up and approved the bill, the full Council ultimately passed it, and the Mayor signed it this summer. I genuinely do not know whether our ANC’s resolution helped get this unblocked—there may well have been many things moving in the background that I was unaware of—but I am proud of my small contribution toward making these homes a reality while preserving two buildings with an important history in the neighborhood. Outside SMD 5E01, ANC 5E also includes the Reservoir District (formerly McMillan Park), one of the most important remaining infill development sites in D.C. Believe it or not, the PUD is still undergoing very meaningful potential revisions, and in the coming years it will be critical to continue pushing both the District and the developers for dense housing and much-needed retail amenities. I say this often, but I feel very fortunate to have found a home in Truxton Circle. Yet in ZIP code 20001, median rents have more-than doubled since 2010 and home prices have grown nearly 75%. That largely reflects more people wanting to live here than there are homes available. The simple fact is that keeping Truxton Circle accessible to families of different incomes and backgrounds means building more homes in and across ANC 5E. I want neighbors who have called this place home for decades to be able to afford to keep living here, and I want people who want to come here to be able to afford to make the move!

Again, I don’t like picking one (see my final answer for more thoughts) but I think street safety for neighbors remains of the utmost importance. Just this past week, there were two tragic crashes just in the small area I represent. In one, a teenager was hit by a car (and fortunately experienced non-life-threatening injuries) while biking at the intersection of New Jersey and N St. NW. In the other, a 29-year-old woman was killed while walking in the crosswalk on New York Avenue NW at the intersection with North Capitol Street. Anyone who has walked that intersection to NoMa knows how constantly dangerous it is. Truxton Circle is a small neighborhood, but it borders major arterial roadways and as a consequence commuters constantly speed down our roads as they try to get someplace else. I am a passionate advocate for street interventions to slow drivers down and ensure that pedestrians, bicyclists, wheelchair users, and other non-car road users both are and can feel safe wherever they walk in the neighborhood. And, perhaps surprisingly, this is an area where a single Commissioner can have a big impact.

If elected, I would: Almost immediately after becoming an ANC commissioner, WMATA announced, as part of the Better Bus Network, a new bus route down 3rd Street, a road that drivers regularly speed down to bypass traffic on New Jersey Ave. Neighbors had understandable concerns, so I gathered their suggestions and worked them into an ANC resolution responding to DDOT’s NOI. Within months, DDOT repaired multiple speed humps and added flex-posts to daylight the crosswalk at Bates and 3rd Street—improvements the agency had not originally planned. In another example, through DDOT’s Safe Routes to Schools program I learned about planned safety improvements around Dunbar High School. I got DDOT to incorporate lane hardening between O and N Streets into the plan, which as far as I can tell has completely stopped drivers from illegally driving into the opposing lane to bypass southbound congestion. Finally, I’m working with Mundo Verde PCS to get DDOT to prioritize a raised crosswalk at the school’s P Street entrance (https://resolutions.anc.dc.gov/AttachmentsFiles/25/2026_003_ANC_5E_Resolution_Mundo_Verde_Traffic_Safety_Improvements_FINAL_TM_20260317102945PM.pdf). I hope this resolution reflects the approach I try to bring to this work every day: methodical, detailed, and outcome-oriented. These are the types of improvements that genuinely give me the most pride as an ANC because every time I see them, I really believe I’ve helped make this neighborhood safer and more walkable for residents and visitors.
column36: There's pretty good research at this point showing how local representatives are highly responsive to non-representative negative feedback (Neighborhood Defenders is a great book on this). I have been attending community meetings for years, and have always striven to be a voice for those who cannot attend such meetings--parents with young children, shift workers who can't skip work, renters, and even future neighbors--the folks who might want to live in an area but cannot afford to or do not have the opportunity to due to the high cost of homes. It's not easy, but I think it's as straightforward as the prompt suggests: being an ANC representative means caring about the District as a whole and that can mean taking tough votes. It doesn't mean ignoring the folks who are willing and able to show up, but it does require having an intentionality about remembering that those voices aren't always representative. Ultimately, I try to understand who will actually be affected, proactively seek out people I am not hearing from, look at the facts and broader policy implications, listen closely to the people who do take the time to participate, and then exercise my own judgment rather than treating a public meeting or an email as a referendum. I’ll also add that, even when I may not vote the way a specific constituent wants me to vote, I always work to make sure neighbors know about important issues as soon as I am aware of them, and I strive to attend every possible civic association or building association meeting in 5E01. While the ANC plays an important role in formal matters with the District, I think a lot of the true community building and neighbor-to-neighbor relations in 5E01 are due to the work and care of the Bates Area Civic Association and Hanover Area Civic Association!
column37: I stand by everything I said about this in 2024 (https://ggwash.org/files/2024_5E01_Gardiner.pdf, Q24). When the Dunbar Aquatic Facility mysteriously failed to open last fall, I wrote an ANC resolution, gave testimony to Council, and hounded agencies until it was re-opened (and, for the first time since 2019, has stayed open through the summer!). That’s what I think makes a good ANC commissioner: someone who shows up, follows through, and keeps pushing until the problem is fixed.

The biggest issue in Park View is that too many residents feel they are not getting the government they deserve. Basic services, like public safety, are inconsistent, 311 and agencies can be difficult to navigate or broken, and people often feel they have to fight City Hall just to get problems acknowledged.  That is a problem in its own right, but it also threatens our ability to build the more abundant, growing neighborhood I want. It is difficult to ask residents to embrace more housing and greater density when they do not believe the city can adequately serve the people who already live here. If residents are asking, “The city cannot handle things now — what happens when we add another 210 homes?” we need a credible answer. My position is not to stop growth. It is to demand that government improve alongside it.

If elected, I would: I would keep using the ANC as an accountability tool: documenting problems, gathering evidence, bringing agencies before residents, filing formal complaints when necessary, passing resolutions, testifying before the Council, and following up until there is a result. That approach has already helped us win action on repeated Pepco outages, trash collection, street safety, public safety, and protections for condo owners.  That commitment to transparency and accountability starts with me. I have posted this questionnaire and all of my responses on my campaign website so residents can see exactly where I stand and hold me accountable for the commitments I make.  But I also want to make the ANC itself much more accessible. I would make a concerted effort to ensure residents understand what ANCs do, how we can help them, and how they can participate directly in decisions affecting their neighborhood.  I have already passed a resolution authorizing a district-wide mailer inviting residents to join ANC 1E committees because I believe those committees are where some of the most valuable neighbor-to-neighbor relationships are built. They give residents a place to learn about issues, work through disagreements, develop solutions, and have a real hand in shaping their community.  That matters for housing, too. People are more willing to accept change when they believe they have a voice in how that change happens and some control over the future of their neighborhood. Better government and stronger civic participation are not alternatives to growth; they are part of how we build durable support for it.
column36: I start by doing my homework. I read the available data and research, look for credible arguments on both sides, and study how other jurisdictions have approached the same issue. Most importantly, I try to separate theory from practice. A proposal may sound great in principle, but that means very little if it cannot be implemented, administered, enforced, or funded. I want to know: Who is responsible for carrying it out? What will it cost? What happened when another city tried it? What could go wrong?  Research alone is not enough. I talk directly with the people who will be affected and try to understand not only what they want, but what is driving their concerns. I ask questions and hear them out. I also invite residents to participate in committee meetings, which are often less intimidating and allow for a more substantive conversation than the limited public-comment period at a full Commission meeting.  I rely heavily on my fellow commissioners, too. ANC 1E includes people with very different backgrounds, life experiences, and areas of expertise. It is a commission with an enormous amount of experience, and I have learned a great deal from my colleagues’ mentorship over the past two years. Honest conversations with them frequently expose a complication, consequence, or perspective that I had not considered.  Ultimately, however, I accept responsibility for making the decision. My vote must align with my values, my conscience, the commitments I made to voters, and what I believe is in the long-term interest of both our neighborhood and the District. We are not separate from the future of this city; we are all invested in it together.  And I never consider a position permanent simply because I have taken it before. If new evidence, experience, or governing and economic realities show that an assumption was wrong or that a policy is not working as intended, I will reevaluate it. Changing my mind in response to better information is not inconsistency. It is part of doing the job responsibly.
column37: I think I’m the right choice for 1E01 because I’ve shown that I can make the ANC useful. I don’t see this job as simply attending meetings and casting votes. My job is to identify problems, bring the right people to the table, and keep pushing until residents get results.  I bring nearly two decades of experience in government—from City Hall, to the Obama Administration, to Congress—including constituent services, communications, and grassroots mobilization. I know how to press an agency, and when necessary, how to take an issue public and build enough attention to get the response our neighborhood deserves.  And when we fix one problem, I don’t stop there. When a condo association in my district spent years believing it could be on the hook for hundreds of thousands of dollars because the city had lost track of a required security warranty, I pressed the agency until it found it. Then we kept going: pushing for process reviews, reforms, and commitments to provide clearer guidance to every ANC so another association doesn’t get trapped by the same preventable clerical failure.  That’s how I approach this job: solve the immediate problem, figure out why it happened, and force the system to work better for the next resident too. I live here, I own my home here, and I’m running again because there is more work to do—and because I’ve shown that I know how to get it done.
column38: A few clarifications on my responses:  Question 16 — Parking minimums: I oppose mandatory parking minimums for new developments. Housing providers should determine actual parking needs rather than be forced to build parking that increases costs and can make housing harder to produce.  Questions 27 and 28 — Dedicated bus and protected bike lanes: I support dedicated bus and protected bike lanes, even when they require reallocating space from cars.  On Georgia Avenue, I think implementation should be thoughtful and tied to the corridor’s growth. As more housing, residents, and foot traffic come online, we should continue reducing the amount of space devoted to cars while protecting the corridor’s economic vitality. I also want designs that prioritize safe pedestrian crossings, accessibility, and a connected bike network that actually gets people where they need to go.  Question 29 — Congestion pricing: I support downtown congestion pricing with protections for low-income drivers. I also support measures that discourage unnecessary out-of-District vehicle traffic, particularly during major events.  I would generally support a Sunday morning exemption from certain pricing requirements. Many longtime Washingtonians who were displaced from the District still return to attend churches and other places of worship that have anchored their communities for generations. We should not penalize them for maintaining those ties.  Questions 12 and 21 — Historic preservation: While researching this issue, I learned of a pending 2021 application for a Park View Historic District. After reviewing it, I do not believe the application makes a strong case or that designation is in the best interest of Park View.  Park View’s history is important, but broad neighborhood-wide restrictions can also limit housing and redevelopment without adequately weighing those consequences. In September, I intend to introduce a committee resolution opposing the application and requesting its withdrawal.  I also want to raise an issue the questionnaire did not address. I think we in the pro-housing community should do more to ensure existing residents directly benefit from housing growth.  D.C. should make it easier for longtime homeowners and seniors to add housing through pre-approved plans, clearer guidance, and accessible financing. Missing-middle housing can create homes while helping residents build wealth or generate retirement income. We should also do more to help renters become homeowners, help condo associations protect themselves when developers fail to meet their obligations, and help residents understand how to advocate effectively through ANCs and the Council. Doing these things might help make existing homeowners less resistant to pro-density reforms.  For me, abundance is not just about unit counts. It is about creating more housing while giving residents more opportunity to build wealth, stay in their communities, and shape their neighborhoods.

They stay if they feel they can walk safely to school, take their children to a well-maintained playground, play with their dog in a renovated park, spend time in a welcoming civic plaza, and shop at a wide range of businesses that meet their daily needs. column23: My answer is not opposition to apartments or more housing generally. It is opposition to a blanket allowance that replaces comprehensive planning that can be matched with smart zoning reform. Columbia Heights is among the densest neighborhoods in the District and one of its proudest examples of apartment living, combining rowhouses, flats, mid-rises, and large multifamily buildings side by side, many within a 10-minute walk to our Metrorail station or a major bus line. I live in and represent one of the most apartment-rich SMDs in the city, and I want more of the District to look like it. But I want all districts, communities, neighborhoods, and the District to grow smartly. I believe that must be done through the iterative planning process we are in right now with the Comprehensive Plan rewrite, and matched with the development of smart zoning reforms that ensure we can actually implement those proposed zoning changes.  So, my position is not less upzoning or no growth where we know it’s needed most. My position on upzoning will be reflected in my ANC’s comments on the Comprehensive Plan and the Future Land Use Map – which I think need to be informed by my constituents' views, irrespective of how I feel – and that process is underway now, which is why my view is not a punt or a delay tactic. In my own neighborhood, I want the FLUM to be generous, but I also want to give residents a voice in saying where that growth can be absorbed best and where they feel it can’t be – and where all housing types are preferred. So, taking a position that supports one housing type everywhere seems contrary to my role as their SMD representative and as chair of my commission’s planning committee. But let me be clear: I support and will advocate for transit-oriented development, which is where the bulk of our new housing supply needs to be to deliver the most good for working families. Columbia Heights absorbed the growth it did because planners and residents in 1997 could see the logic: density paired with transit, public-realm investment, and affordability. I believe we can and must build similar consensus now in other neighborhoods. As an ANC, my job is to help the District get upzoning right if that is what my constituents see in the draft Comprehensive Plan and say they want. And I take that responsibility seriously: not to block more homes, but to make sure each project and map change delivers the diverse housing types we need, creates the affordability and rent drops we all want, maintains the affordable homes we have, and improves city services to support the added density that we will be creating. We can have it all if we work together, and I know Columbia Heights will deliver on that belief and promise; I deeply believe that the rest of the District will do the same.

Public life, and the stewardship of a thriving, albeit disordered, public realm. Columbia Heights deserves a public realm worthy of its residents and a quality of life that ensures every family that wants to live here thrives. After many years living here, I've watched a progressive deterioration in nearly every facet of the public realm, which impacts almost everything else in a neighborhood like ours. Our civic core, centered on 14th Street and the Metro, is the gateway to nearby communities and our main commercial corridor. But that welcoming mat for our "city within a city" is often the biggest reason a visitor doesn't return or a resident moves away. That cannot be our future — and won't be if I am re-elected. The Civic Plaza should be our greatest community asset, but deferred maintenance and a lack of accountability have left it neglected — alongside storefront vacancies on a corridor that should thrive, public safety challenges residents face daily, and city services that underperform for the density they serve. Columbia Heights turned 145 this year and deserves the stronger future residents are counting on.

If elected, I would: If re-elected, I will continue revitalizing our public realm, championing implementation of the CHMP Public Life Study, transforming Civic Plaza, implementing my recently adopted neighborhood cleanup strategy, ensuring every park and community facility serves its purpose, and leading the charge for the service delivery improvements my constituents deserve.
column36: I know from firsthand experience that it can be tough to reach all 2,000 of my neighbors, but it's not impossible – and not every decision I make will impact all 2,000 of my constituents. So, I start from the premise that I can and must reach as many of them as I can for the issues that affect them most on their blocks, and go even further to reach them all when it's far-reaching, like the Comprehensive Plan rewrite. I don't wait to be contacted. During my time in office, I have made a point of writing to my constituents before, not after, about all officially noticed government actions on and around their blocks. I've ensured I’m engaging on social media platforms to amplify that engagement (and regularly checking the pulse of the larger neighborhood on issues generally), in the off chance I can reach more of them that way. And I’ve made sure my phone number and email are readily available to anyone who needs to get in touch with me, no matter the issue. I believe that every resident deserves to know a decision is coming while they can still shape it. That’s why I’ve regularly pushed for outreach and engagement formats that lower the barrier to participation and have the greatest chance of getting as much feedback as possible from as many people as possible. For example, on the Comprehensive Plan, I’ve focused on housing walks where neighbors can stand on blocks of interest and talk through where new homes fit; for the Public Life Study, I walked to every home and apartment building in central Columbia Heights to drop off flyers for open houses and workshops. When the people most affected aren't in the room, my job is to find them and invite them into the conversation, period. Every decision I’ve made as Commissioner – and will continue to make if re-elected – is fully grounded in my constituents’ views because I regularly talk to them about any number of issues. Whether at the dog park, passing through Civic Plaza, during the farmers’ market, at the grocery store, or at a neighborhood event, I am always engaging my constituents where I can – and they know they can do the same for me. And many do when they see me walking the district with my dog, or when I’m walking around the district to spot-check or follow up on issues. I also have an official website that I’ve shared with my constituents, and they know they can keep up with my work and check my votes on every single issue that has come before the ANC. So, even when I haven’t been able to reach every resident before a particular debate and vote on an issue, they can see how I came down on it without having to comb through meeting minutes – and if re-elected, I am committed to posting more of my full statements from the dais so residents can understand the full rationale for that vote. Constituents deserve to have transparency in how I do my job, and I will always give them the information and access they need to do just that.
column37: I am the right person for my SMD because I show up for the neighbors of 1A06, not only when it counts or when people are watching – and that won't change. That commitment is why I've been able to listen deeply to constituents and turn their concerns into results, and I have a record to show for it. When the neighborhood needed a serious public safety strategy, I wrote one — and paired it with real engagement with neighborhood partners for a new community safety initiative. As our commercial corridors have struggled, I've met directly with key agencies to demand that Columbia Heights receive greater focus and investment, not a patchwork of failing programs or unmet needs – again, identifying solutions with a plan. I've singularly championed service delivery improvement through new planning and accountability models to ensure my residents get the basics and more for their tax dollars. I've championed improvements to the ANCs overall so we can all succeed in this role and truly deliver for all the residents we serve. And most importantly, I have made my residents the center of every single one of my decisions, writing to them before every major decision about a liquor license, a transportation project, or a community planning effort. I am the best representative for my neighbors because I go out of my way to make sure they know what I'm doing, why I'm doing it, and how their views guide my vote, and I will keep doing that as I fight for a stronger future for Columbia Heights.
column38: Columbia Heights should be the proof that urbanism works. That conviction fuels the fire in me to fight for the best for my neighborhood, and all that is yet due to it — and it carries an obligation the District has not yet met: to invest in the public realm it asks a growing neighborhood to share. Because of that, I will continue to fight relentlessly for smart growth, service delivery improvements, and a government that works – all necessary elements that will make our collective desire for increasing housing supply, maintaining affordable and deeply affordable housing, building a better multimodal transportation network, and making better use of our limited land. As the chair of my ANC’s neighborhood planning committee, I am intimately aware of the value of having conversations about what has been, where we are now, and what can be. I’ve devoted countless hours to pouring over research, plans, and studies, and I’ve made a point of seeking out a range of opinions about all of it. Why? Because I care deeply about what’s still possible for Columbia Heights. We’ve made the bet GGWash and others ask of other neighborhoods. We welcomed apartments, density, and transit-oriented growth, and our Mid-City planning area has exceeded its production target, with a substantial share of affordable units. The returns are real: enviable walkability, record-breaking Metro ridership, unmatched diversity, and a genuine urban center that has the potential to rival downtown DC. And yet, there is still more that we can do to absorb growth smartly in so many areas, which I am committed to championing as 1A06 Commissioner and at the helm of a key ANC committee. My record on housing, transportation, and land use is clear: I say yes where it makes sense, serves as many residents as possible, is affordable, and where residents and families can live, grow, and thrive in a safe, walkable, and welcoming neighborhood. So, again, let me be straight with you: I support ambitious upzoning delivered through the Comprehensive Plan rewrite and the Future Land Use Map, matched with smart zoning reforms, not a uniform by-right entitlement applied District-wide without regard to on-the-ground context. Our city blocks differ in infrastructure, displacement risk, and capacity to absorb growth, and the planning process exists to weigh exactly that – which too can be reformed to be nimbler without sacrificing outcomes. So, I will use the ANC's great weight not to block housing, but to secure more housing types, including family-sized units and deeper affordability, matched with increased service delivery improvements that arrive with added density rather than after. I will keep fighting for bus priority on our crosstown and major corridors, protected bike lanes and better bikeway planning, automated curbside management, parking alternatives to get more cars out of public space where possible, and improvements to our overall multimodal transportation system. You have my word on all this.

In ANC 4B05, for example, we have a mix of single-family detached houses, duplexes, and apartments. Some residents invested their life savings to buy a house in the neighborhood; others have chosen to rent on a long-term basis. Allowing developers to demolish 100-year-old detached houses or duplexes and replace them with four-story apartments, as recently proposed by the D.C. Office of Planning, would radically change the character of our neighborhood in ways not envisioned by current residents. It also would threaten to displace residents, some 80 percent of whom are Black or Latino. Moreover, it's not necessary to encroach on well-established residential neighborhoods to expand apartment construction. New developments, such as those at the McMillan Reservoir, the nearby Walter Reed campus, and the RFK stadium site, are examples of how new apartments can be built at scale. Other appropriate sites are the central business district (including conversion of office buildings), near Metro stations, on commercial corridors, and at re-imagined former industrial zones. Housing affordability should be addressed holistically by streamlining the permit process, expanding the District's Home Purchase Assistance Program (HPAP) for first-time home-buyers, and even embracing vocational education in the building trades to address the shortage of skilled workers that drives up the cost of construction. (Question 6 of this questionnaire wrongly assumes that achieving more housing and preserving the character of existing neighborhoods are mutually exclusive goals. They are not, and neither is "more important" than the other.)

column12: Affordability is a relationship between what a home costs and what a household earns. It is not a building type, an architectural style, or a developer's tax status. A home is affordable if a household is not spending more than about 30 percent of its income to live in it.  "Affordable housing" as a term of art in DC usually means income-restricted units produced through inclusionary zoning, the Housing Production Trust Fund, vouchers, or public ownership. Those tools are essential and I fight for them in every project that comes before ANC 2G, because the market on its own will not produce a home for a family earning 30 percent of MFI.  Where the distinction gets misused is when it is deployed to argue that market-rate housing does not help. It does. A market-rate unit built on 9th Street is a unit whose occupant is not outbidding a longtime neighbor for an older, cheaper apartment two blocks away. The most naturally affordable housing in my SMD is old, small, and unsubsidized — units in buildings that were legal to build a century ago and have since aged into affordability. We stopped allowing that kind of building, and then acted surprised when the pipeline dried up.  So I treat them as complements, not substitutes. I push for the maximum number of income-restricted units in every project, and for the maximum number of units, period.

column26: 210 homes in 2G04 is not a stretch. I can point at the land today.  Start with the surface parking lots. Naylor Court and the blocks around it still give over land to at-grade parking in one of the most transit-rich places in the country — four blocks from Mount Vernon Square and Shaw-Howard University Metro, on the D40 down 7th Street. Those lots are the largest supply of buildable land in my SMD and every one should be housing. Built to the scale of what stands around them, they get most of the way to 210 on their own.  The clearest large-scale site is the surface lot on the northeast corner of 10th and L Street NW. It sits across from the Marriott Marquis, one of the largest hotels in the District, and shares its block with two apartment buildings and two condo buildings that are already seven-plus stories and north of 100 units each. There is no neighborhood-character argument available on that corner: the context is high-rise residential and convention-center hotel, Metro is a short walk, and a tall building there would look like its neighbors. One project on that lot could deliver at least 100 homes by itself.  Next, 1300 Naylor Court. The Council restored funding for the new archives facility at UDC, which means the District will soon hold a publicly owned building in the middle of my SMD, four blocks from two Metro stations, with no program in it. It should not sit vacant for a decade. It should be housing, with a substantial share of income-restricted and family-sized units, and because the District already owns the land it is one of the strongest social housing sites in Ward 2. It's a former stable; its street-facing fabric is worth keeping, and a facade has never been a reason to leave a site empty.  Then the 9th Street NW corridor. We approved a 40-unit building at 1322 9th Street during my first term, and projects at 1515 9th Street and 1200 5th Street have moved forward. 9th Street can absorb considerably more — it has the width, the transit, the retail, and the demand.  Then the alleys. Blagden Alley and Naylor Court have carriage houses and outbuildings that already demonstrate the form works at a scale nobody needs to be alarmed by. Legalizing and encouraging alley dwellings and small multi-unit conversions across our alley blocks adds homes while putting eyes on alleys I have spent two terms working to make not just safer, but genuinely usable as public space — places families, neighbors, and community actually get to enjoy.  And conversion: Mount Vernon Square and the blocks toward downtown hold offices that are not coming back as offices. Converting them is faster than building new and puts residents where the infrastructure already is.  The constraint is not land or demand. It is that too much of the above runs through a discretionary process a housing provider can rationally decide isn't worth the wait. Fix that and 210 is a floor, not a target.

Pedestrian and traffic safety in our alleys and at our intersections. Blagden Alley and Naylor Court are not service corridors: they are where people live, where children play, and where thousands of visitors walk every week. Shepherd Court does carry real loading and garage traffic for the big buildings on its block, which is exactly why design and speed matter there: an alley can serve a loading dock and still be a place a kid walks safely. For years these alleys were treated as free-flowing shortcuts by drivers and rideshare vehicles, at speeds no residential alley should see. My position is that our alleys are pedestrian spaces first, and that every design, enforcement, and curb decision should follow from that.

If elected, I would: Keep doing what has already worked and finish what's unfinished. In my terms we geofenced Blagden Alley against rideshare pickups, relocated the 9th Street loading zone, won DDOT safety improvements at 10th and Massachusetts, and got sidewalks replaced. What's left: daylighting every alley entrance in 2G04, physical traffic calming rather than signage, a permanent trash compactor so collection vehicles aren't idling in the alley, and sustained enforcement instead of one-off responses. A commissioner's authority is limited to great-weight advice, testimony, and relentless follow-up with agencies — so that is exactly what I use, meeting after meeting, until the work is scheduled and built.
column36: Most of the job is going to find people rather than waiting to be found. The neighbors who make it to an ANC meeting on a weeknight are a small slice of 2,000 — older, longer-tenured, more likely to own, and more likely to be there because they're against something. That's not a knock on them; it's a description of who can spare a Tuesday evening. So I knock doors, I stand in the alley, I run community days that bring out 100-plus neighbors, and I answer every email.  When what I hear conflicts, I try to separate a preference from a harm. Pushing loading into an alley that kids walk through is a harm. So is a curb, an entrance, or a construction staging plan that leaves a neighbor using a wheelchair unable to get down their own sidewalk — that one comes up more than people realize, and it rarely gets fixed unless someone keeps calling the agency. Those I work until they're resolved. A building casting a shadow on a patio is not in that category, and neither is the neighborhood feeling different with more people in it. I'll hear those out, but I'm not voting against homes on that basis, and I'd rather say so in the meeting than nod along and disappoint someone later.  I also count the people who aren't in the room. A vote on housing is partly a vote for people who don't live here yet and can't email me. A vote on a bus lane affects riders passing through who will never attend an ANC 2G meeting. Representing 2,000 constituents in a city of 700,000 means some decisions are correctly made on behalf of the wider city, and being straight with my neighbors when that's what I'm doing instead of pretending a consensus exists.  What I owe my neighbors is being reachable, prepared, and honest about my reasoning — not producing whatever answer the room wants on a given night. When I've disagreed with a group, I've told them why in advance, in person, and kept working with them on everything else. That's how I've chaired ANC 2G and how I'd keep doing it.
column37: Because I have a record and it is specific.  In two terms I've voted to approve 94-plus homes in my own single-member district alone, including a 40-unit building at 1322 9th Street, and hundreds more across ANC 2G as a whole. I geofenced Blagden Alley against rideshare traffic, relocated the 9th Street loading zone, got DDOT to deliver safety improvements at 10th and Massachusetts, restored trash service after a DPW error, got sidewalks replaced, and worked to keep our historic alleys cleaner and clearer for public accessibility. I've brought 100-plus neighbors out to a Blagden Alley Community Day, and I've served as Chair of ANC 2G.  None of that is glamorous and all of it required the same thing: showing up to every meeting, knowing the agency process better than the person on the other end of the email, and refusing to let an item die quietly between meetings. That's the actual skill this job requires.  I also want the density. I'm not a commissioner who tolerates new housing as the price of a public benefit package. I want the parking lots on Naylor Court built on, I want the vacant District-owned Archives building turned into homes, and I want more people living on 9th Street. I said that in 2024 and I've voted that way since.  Shaw and Mount Vernon Square should be a place where more people get to live, and where getting around safely on foot doesn't require luck and a prayer. I've spent four years working on both.
column38: Three things.  On by-right development: I answered that I'd prefer by-right, and I want to be clear that this is not a retreat from negotiating. It's a recognition that the PUD process has become slow enough that developers avoid it, which means the ANC's leverage increasingly exists in theory rather than in practice — and a benefit package that never gets built benefits nobody. Predictable zoning that permits substantially more housing produces more homes and more income-restricted homes than a discretionary process most projects route around. Where a PUD is proposed in 2G, I will still negotiate hard, and my priorities remain deeper income restrictions, more subsidized units, and multi-bedroom units before anything cosmetic.  On historic preservation: I represent Blagden Alley–Naylor Court, and I don't want to see the fabric of those alleys damaged. But I've watched height and mass review become the mechanism by which a design conversation turns into a delay and then into a smaller building. HPRB should govern materials, rhythm, detail, and how a building meets the street. It should not be the venue for deciding whether a fourth floor exists. Those are separable, and treating them as separable is how a historic neighborhood grows instead of freezing.  On social housing: 1300 Naylor Court is publicly owned, sits four blocks from two Metro stations, and is in one of the most expensive submarkets in the city. With the new archives facility at UDC funded, the District is about to have that building on its hands with nothing in it. If the District is serious about social housing, that is the site to prove it on, and I intend to spend my next term making sure the disposition conversation starts before the building goes dark rather than years after.  Finally: I'd rather be judged on whether the things I said I'd do got done. Two years ago I told GGWash I wanted to see the parking lots near Naylor Court become housing and the alleys made safe for people on foot. The alley work is largely done or scheduled. The housing is the unfinished half, and it's why I'm running again.

I feel that traffic safety is the biggest issue in my neighborhood. Specifically, drivers’ excessive speeding down Michigan Avenue, Taylor Street, 10th, 12th, and 13th Streets, drivers not stopping at stop signs and pedestrian crossings, inadequate timing/sequencing of stoplights on Michigan Ave between Taylor St and 13th St which causes drivers to drive erratically seeking alternate routes down side streets and alleys, and a dangerous intersection at 12th St & Upshur St. These traffic safety issues should be addressed for the safety of pedestrians, cyclists, and other motorists who rely on safe travel lanes while sharing the road with drivers. If elected, I would: DC faces big issues that are outside the scope of the ANC—like our Trump-induced recession and occupation by the National Guard. Safety for me means everything from tackling crime to road safety. DC experienced a surge in crime post-COVID, and while 2026 so far is very promising, safety concerns rightfully linger. Just last month there were multiple shootings just outside Bruce Monroe Elementary school. As an ANC commissioner I will build a relationship with the 4th District MPD, convene residents around specific areas of concern, and look for grant opportunities to address safety needs.  But safety to move through the city without risking life and limb is equally important. I support common sense road safety measures including the Grant Circle redesign, putting in traffic lights at dangerous intersections like NH Ave and Quincy, putting in more speed tables so drivers don't speed through residential streets, and including pedestrian safety as part of larger projects like the Georgia Ave Bus Priority Project. It should feel safe for kids to walk themselves to school  At the same time, too many businesses in 4C have been forced to close. I will work with new businesses and the Mayor’s office to reduce the time it takes to open so that businesses don’t run out of runway before they have a chance to turn a profit.

If elected, I would: If elected, I would use my position to ensure that the residents most impacted by housing and development decisions have a meaningful seat at the table. I would proactively engage renters, lower-income residents, young people, families, seniors, and longtime residents before major development and housing decisions come before the ANC—not after decisions have already been shaped.  I would hold community conversations, bring developers and District agencies directly before residents, advocate for affordable and family-sized housing, and push for commitments that allow people of different incomes to remain in Southwest. I would also make housing information and resources easier to access and consistently follow up with agencies when residents face housing concerns.  I understand that an ANC Commissioner cannot build housing or set housing policy alone. But a Commissioner can organize, advocate, ask difficult questions, build coalitions, and use the ANC’s advisory voice to influence decisions. I would use that authority to make sure decisions about our neighborhood are made with the people who live here, not simply for them
column36: I believe representation means more than listening to the loudest voices or the people who attend every meeting. If elected, I will make decisions by actively seeking input from across my single-member district, especially from residents who have historically been less represented in neighborhood decision-making.  I will use multiple ways to hear from constituents—community meetings, conversations in our buildings and public spaces, surveys, digital outreach, and direct engagement with renters, homeowners, seniors, young people, families, and lower-income residents. I also recognize that the people who contact me on an issue may not represent the views of all 2,000 residents.  When making decisions, I will weigh constituent input alongside available data, the impact on those most directly affected, expert and agency information, and what I believe serves the long-term interests of the entire community. I will not make decisions based simply on who speaks the loudest or has the most access.  There will be times when everyone will not agree with my decision. In those moments, I will be transparent about how and why I reached it. My responsibility is to represent the many, not the few, while making sure those whose voices are too often overlooked have a meaningful seat at the table.

column12: It's important to remember that "affordable housing" isn't about quality or who lives there — it's about how a unit's price is set. Affordable housing has its rent or sale price tied to a percentage of Area Median Income, is typically achieved through subsidy, inclusionary zoning set-asides, or public financing, and is allocated through an application or lottery process. Market-rate housing has its price set by supply and demand in the private market. Critically, these two categories are not in competition — every home added to the market-rate supply reduces upward pressure on rents throughout the submarket, including for existing affordable units, because it takes pressure off older, naturally-occurring affordable housing stock. An ANC that only fights for subsidized units while opposing market-rate density is effectively fighting with one hand tied behind its back. I support an "all of the above" approach: more subsidized affordable housing as well as more market-rate supply, because DC’s affordability crisis is fundamentally a supply crisis at every income level.

column12: On an abstract level, I don’t think there is necessarily a distinction between the terms “affordable housing” and “market-rate housing,” as the end goal of any rational land-use framework is to work toward making market-rate housing affordable. Of course, the law uses the terms in specific ways: “affordable housing,” in the inclusionary zoning world, is used to describe the units set aside for households meeting some sort of pre-determined income threshold, and is contrasted with the market-rate housing units in the same development. I think inclusionary zoning is one of the many policy tools that can be leveraged to increase the supply of units accessible to families with lower incomes, but should not employed to detract from the effort to increase the supply of housing such that even units priced on the market can be within reach to families of different incomes.

column36: Being an elected representative - even one as relatively insignificant as an unpaid, advisory one - has to be a balance between the desires of the constituents and the individual representative’s prudent determination about what’s best for the community, in all the different ways that “community” can be defined. That can, at times, be the people who are showing up to meetings, but more often that is going to include the interests of constituents that are not able to show up to meetings (or an even broader community beyond the SMD) that could be impacted by changes within the ANC’s boundaries. There has to be a recognition that, whatever effect ANC decisions actually have, they are going to impact more than just the people who show up at meetings or respond to newsletters. There is no doubt that housing or urban planning issues can be the subject of heated debate and disagreement between good-faith actors; I’ve been on plenty of neighborhood listservs, attended ANC meetings, and other forums where I have seen that dynamic firsthand. What is important is engaging in those conversations in a constructive manner and doing affirmative outreach when you are not sure you are getting the fullest picture of neighborhood perspectives.

It’s not what I feel, but what the community feels, and the biggest issue in our neighborhood is the lack of attention to our community. I’ve held listening sessions and a simple survey via my website (darrensheets.com) and this was the consistent issue being raised.   There is a lack of street infrastructure that accommodates safety for pedestrians and cyclists, and residents have expressed interest in more bike lanes, priority bus lanes, and the modification of street corners to prevent traffic from running red lights.  There is a perceived lack of support for local business due to many empty store fronts (retail, restaurant, and commercial). Some have been empty for years.  The cost of housing continues to rise and is especially prohibitive among younger generations.  There is an unhoused community that needs professional support to meet their needs.   Many in the community are distrustful of the crime statistics being reported from MPD, and don’t feel MPD’s statistics match resident experiences.

If elected, I would: I will be an unwavering, impartial ANC Commissioner committed to listening to residents and representing the community. I’ll be an articulate, objective voice for our community. It’s not enough to raise an issue one or twice during a meeting, it has to be persistent and I’m committed to getting results for our community. I want to be an ANC representative to provide a voice to the residents and collaborate with local DC government to work on these issues I described above.

Neighbors frequently bring up rats and poor service delivery from District government. Sometimes this is in reference to responsiveness to 311 requests. Sometimes this is a children's pool or splash pad that is closed without any public announcement.   I have become immensely frustrated with the state of public facing tools and processes from the District government. To prove the benefits of urbanism, we must provide good government service. If the public only experiences a sclerotic government, they reduce their expectations, and the District becomes worse as a result.

If elected, I would: If elected, I would: I have already built many tools that residents, and the government, can use for better service and to better understand proposals from the government. These can all be found on districtjosh.com. I think it's helpful to go through some examples so I'll provide them here: - rats.districtjosh.com - I used this to show the differences in rodent abatement treatment timelines across the city. It turned out Ward 5 was taking ~3x longer than other Wards. I notified Councilmember Parker who then worked with the Dept of Health to reduce this timeline. - dc2050.org - This allows the public to propose their own changes (such as sixplexes everywhere) so they can see the impact on potential housing stock. - dcbudget.com - understanding the budget shouldn't take scrolling through 700+ page PDFs, so I built a website that makes it easier to view. I also found a $2 million mistake in the budget for Paid Family Leave.  - pools.districtjosh.com - a place where neighbors can report whether or not a children's pool or splash pad is actually open. My neighbor built a better 311 app (Snap311.app) that can submit requests 3x faster and provides a much better user experience, and I've been advocating for OUC to adopt this tool.
