column12: It is important to distinguish between affordable housing and market\-rate housing because they serve different roles in a healthy housing ecosystem\. **Affordable housing** is typically income\-restricted and designed to ensure that households at specific income levels—often very low, low, or moderate income—do not pay more than a set percentage of their income on rent or mortgage costs\. It is often supported through public subsidies, tax credits, or regulatory requirements, and is essential for preventing displacement and ensuring that long\-term residents, essential workers, and vulnerable populations can remain in the city\.  **Market\-rate housing**, by contrast, is priced according to prevailing market conditions without income restrictions\. While it is not directly subsidized, it plays a critical role in increasing overall housing supply, which can help moderate price pressures over time\. Market\-rate development can also generate resources through taxes and fees that support public services and affordable housing programs.

It also means looking beyond bedroom count. Family-sized housing should provide adequate living and storage space and, where possible, access to schools, childcare, parks, recreation, transportation, grocery stores and other neighborhood services families depend on.  Affordability is especially important. A three-bedroom unit is not truly serving a working family if its rent or purchase price is beyond that family’s means. DC should therefore encourage both market-rate and income-restricted family-sized units while expanding pathways to homeownership.  As we address the housing shortage, we should not measure success only by the total number of units constructed. We should ask whether we are building the right mix of housing for residents at different stages of life. I support building new housing in my SMD and ANC, but I favor a balanced, community-based approach. We should first identify underutilized and vacant properties, appropriate commercial and transportation corridors, publicly owned land suitable for housing, areas near transit, and locations where existing zoning and infrastructure can reasonably support additional residents. They could be distributed throughout the ANC through a combination of apartments, condominiums, townhomes, duplexes, accessory dwelling units, and family-sized housing. Smaller developments strategically located throughout a community may sometimes achieve the housing goal while fitting better within established neighborhoods.  We should also examine what type of housing is being produced. I would want a meaningful mix of affordable, workforce and market-rate housing, with particular attention to family-sized units, senior housing, homeownership opportunities, and housing that allows longtime DC residents to remain in their communities.  Infrastructure must be part of the discussion. Before significantly increasing density, we should consider transportation, parking, schools, utilities, public safety, recreation, green space, and access to neighborhood services.  Most importantly, residents and ANCs should have a meaningful role in identifying appropriate locations and understanding the tradeoffs involved. Community participation should help us determine how and where we grow, rather than being viewed as either an automatic veto or an afterthought.  I support an ambitious citywide housing goal, but a numerical target should not replace good planning. The objective should not simply be to put 210 units somewhere in an ANC. It should be to identify multiple appropriate locations and create housing that strengthens the community, expands affordability and homeownership, and accommodates growth without sacrificing neighborhood integrity.

Biggest issue is proper utilization of government  facilities and assets

If elected, I would: Given the limited authority of an ANC commissioner, my most realistic and effective role would be to advocate for transparency and accountability in how public assets are identified and used, ensure residents are informed early in the planning process, and work with city agencies to prioritize underutilized government property for community benefit\. I would also push for data\-driven assessments of public facilities so that decisions are based on actual usage, needs, and long\-term community impact\.  I support an ambitious citywide housing goal, but a numerical target should not replace good planning\. The objective should not simply be to place 210 units somewhere in an ANC\. It should be to strategically use public and private assets to create housing and community resources that strengthen the neighborhood, expand affordability and homeownership, and make better use of the public investments already within our community\.
column36: My approach would begin with ensuring that residents are **informed early and consistently** about issues affecting public land, facilities, and development decisions\. Too often, communities are brought into the process too late, when options are already limited\. I would prioritize proactive communication, well\-advertised and accessible community meetings, and strict adherence to notification requirements so that all residents—not just a small subset—have a fair opportunity to participate\.  At the same time, I recognize that community input must be balanced with objective information\. I would advocate for **data\-driven assessments of public facilities and assets**, including actual usage rates, infrastructure capacity, and long\-term community needs\. This helps ensure that decisions are not based solely on perception, but on how spaces are truly being used and how they can best serve the public\.  When making decisions as an ANC commissioner, I would weigh three key factors:  1. **Community input at scale** – not just individual opinions, but patterns of feedback gathered through meetings, surveys, and outreach\. 2. **Data and technical analysis** – including agency reports, facility utilization, zoning constraints, and infrastructure capacity\. 3. **Long\-term community benefit** – how a decision affects housing affordability, access to services, neighborhood character, and equitable use of public resources\.  Importantly, I would also recognize that ANC commissioners are stewards of public assets, not just representatives of immediate preferences\. That means advocating for **transparency and accountability in how government property is identified, evaluated, and used**, and pushing city agencies to prioritize underutilized public land for community benefit whenever appropriate\.  Ultimately, my role is to ensure that decisions are not made in isolation from the community, but also not delayed or distorted by incomplete participation\. By combining early engagement, strong data, and a focus on long\-term outcomes, I would aim to make decisions that reflect both the voices of residents and the broader needs of the entire ANC\.
column37: I believe I am the right person to serve as an ANC commissioner for my SMD because I bring a balanced, thoughtful approach that combines community engagement, data-driven decision-making, and a focus on long-term neighborhood outcomes.  I recognize that no single resident or small group can fully represent an SMD of roughly 2,000 people. For that reason, effective representation requires listening broadly, identifying patterns in community feedback, and ensuring that quieter voices are not overshadowed by the most vocal participants. My goal would be to ensure all residents have meaningful opportunities to be heard through early notice, accessible meetings, and consistent outreach. Ultimately, I am well-suited for this role because I approach issues with balance, discipline, and a commitment to representing the full range of residents—not just the loudest voices—while working toward thoughtful, evidence-based decisions that strengthen the community over the long term.
column38: I believe housing, transportation, and land use decisions in DC require a consistent balance between growth, livability, and accountability to the people who are directly affected\. My approach is rooted in the idea that we can and should expand housing opportunities, improve affordability, and invest in better transportation options, but we must do so in a way that is transparent, data\-informed, and responsive to community input\.  On housing and affordable housing, I support increasing supply across income levels, including deeply affordable, workforce, and market\-rate housing\. However, I also believe we have a responsibility to ensure that new development is appropriately sited, supported by infrastructure, and integrated thoughtfully into existing neighborhoods\. I am particularly interested in solutions that expand housing without displacing long\-term residents and that include a meaningful mix of unit types, including family\-sized housing and homeownership opportunities\. Accountability matters here: we should track whether housing goals are actually being met in terms of affordability, not just unit counts\.  On transportation, I support investments that improve safety, reliability, and access for all users—especially pedestrians, cyclists, transit riders, and people with disabilities\. At the same time, transportation decisions must be evaluated based on real\-world usage patterns and neighborhood impacts\. We should prioritize projects that reduce congestion, improve connectivity, and make it easier for residents to access jobs, schools, and services without overburdening local streets\.  On land use, I believe we should make better use of underutilized land, including vacant lots, transit\-adjacent sites, and publicly owned property, before considering more disruptive changes to fully built\-out residential blocks\. Land use decisions should be guided by clear criteria: infrastructure capacity, environmental impact, community needs, and long\-term sustainability\. Importantly, these decisions should not be made in isolation but in coordination with residents, ANCs, and relevant agencies\.  Across all of these areas, I believe accountability is essential\. That means clear communication about what is being proposed, why it is being proposed, and what tradeoffs are involved\. It also means following through on commitments, evaluating outcomes after decisions are made, and being willing to adjust course when policies are not achieving their intended results\.  Ultimately, I support a DC that grows responsibly and equitably\. My goal as an ANC commissioner would be to ensure that housing, transportation, and land use decisions are not driven by extremes on either side, but by a balanced process that respects community input, relies on evidence, and produces fair and sustainable outcomes for current and future residents.

While a close second would be that I’m concerned about the recent uptick in the number of empty storefronts on some of our important business corridors, I’m going to stick with the same issue I highlighted when I answered this question two years ago: persistent problems with the lack of pick-up/drop-off (PUDO) zones in Navy Yard, and just a general – seemingly growing – problem with chaotic traffic patterns around apartment buildings and restaurants, which we have plenty of here in my neighborhood. We consistently see problems with traffic lanes being blocked due to delivery drivers leaving their cars in travel lanes to pick up food, and large trucks parking on top of flexposts and into bike lanes to unload packages. This can lead to very dangerous situations where blindspots are created and frustrated drivers try to quickly swerve around stopped traffic, which is going to lead to pedestrians or bicyclists getting hit.

If elected, I would: I want to encourage District agencies to do a few things to help tackle this [chaotic traffic; see below] problem: 1) remove a fair number of long-term curbside parking spots and replace them with either daylighting zones or PUDO zones (or “short-term parking” spots, as DDOT tells us that they’ll soon be called) to give small-to-medium-sized trucks a better place to stop for 20-30 minutes, 2) offer ANC support to programs such as the MicroFreight Pilot which will take some of these trucks off the road altogether and replace them with smaller vehicles that can deliver packages and travel in the bike lanes, and 3) insist upon more aggressive ticketing for those who park illegally or those who leave their cars in short-term spots over the allowable limit.
column36: As I come to the end of my fourth year as an ANC commissioner, I am acutely aware that the loudest voices are not necessarily representative of a majority view of my constituents. Sometimes, the loudest voices aren’t even constituents- we’ve certainly seen residents with an axe to grind travel across town to attend our public meetings to complain about a broad issue, without any particular connection to a local project here in Navy Yard. I will say that in all honestly, I have been somewhat lucky in that I haven’t had to encounter all that many controversial (within the neighborhood) topics as a commissioner. I’d say there is fairly broad agreement about the issues here in Navy Yard: traffic is bad and fairly chaotic, particularly during game days and concerts, as out-of-town cars conflict with delivery drivers. Our slow recovery from the pandemic-era’s elevated crime rates in 2022-2023 was unsettling. It’s not good to see businesses closing up shop along N St. I think there is fairly broad agreement on the positives too: Navy Yard is a very dense, walkable neighborhood with plenty of fantastic amenities that we all enjoy. The topic where there is probably the most disagreement amongst constituents (and also the commissioners!) is that of curbside management and bike lanes. As is probably obvious from this questionnaire, I’ve got my own beliefs which are generally pro-bike lane and not particularly parking-sympathetic, but I do try to gain my constituents’ feedback on each individual project on a case-by-case basis. I also like to try to be pragmatic when dealing with somewhat-contentious issues; I do like to try to find compromise if at all possible.

column26: Columbia Heights, and by extension much of ANC1D06, which is split between a section of northern Columbia Heights and northern Mt. Pleasant, has some of the highest population densities in Washington, DC. While development of housing should be equitably spread through all 8 wards there is still room for appropriate and additional growth in this area to meet the District’s ongoing housing shortage. I feel that this is particularly true for neighborhoods like Columbia Heights and Mt. Pleasant which have great access to a variety of essential services and facilities like schools, grocery stores, and pharmacies, as well as a wealth of transit and micro-mobility options including the Metro, major bus routes on 16th, 14th, Columbia and Irving, and a growing network of bike lanes and rideshare options. While much of the land in this area has been developed ANC1D06 has a large stretch of church owned parking lots and an undeveloped space on the 1400/1500 block of Meridian Pl NW that has previously been identified as a prime development opportunity. Efforts to develop this land have had broad community support in the past, but have stalled due to a number of hurdles facing the church, including partial ownership of some of the land by the DC government. The current Commissioner, Angela Allison, worked in close coordination with church leadership and community members to identify ways to streamline the sale of the land, and while progress has stalled in the last few years, if elected I would reinitiate conversations with the church and neighbors, and based on their feedback, use all the options at my disposal as an ANC to work towards making this land available for new and preferably affordable housing development. After knocking on many doors around the SMD to collect signatures to appear on the ballot and hearing from neighbors on the issues that matter to them most I feel that one of the biggest issues currently facing the area is the intersecting problems of litter and rats. This issue is not unique to ANC1D06, but it is compounded by several factors including a lack of street cleaning in much of the area, proximity to concentrations of businesses along nearby commercial corridors like 14th and Mt Pleasant Street, and the limited number of public waste cans on residential streets. Beyond the direct impact on the neighborhood I have also seen firsthand the impact of litter and pests like rats on places like the Piney Branch section of Rock Creek Park where I have worked with the Rock Creek Conservancy and the National Park Service to organize and host volunteer litter clean-up events. From these experiences I have learned that there are low barrier and easy to implement solutions that can make an immediate and direct impact on this issue.

If elected, I would: If I elected, I would serve as an advocate for my neighbors in ANC1D06 and work towards a multi-pronged approach to make progress towards mitigating the persistent issue of litter and rats. First, I would leverage the outreach of the ANC (email lists, public meetings) to work with neighbors on streets without street sweeping to see if they would be open to submitting a formal request for street sweeping services. This would be combined with regular outreach to DPW to ensure ad-hoc street and alley cleanings are being performed to keep litter (and the food it provides for rats) at bay. Second, I would also work with neighbors on each street in the ANC to organize coordinated rat abatement by the city using the abatement.home-rule.org petition program so that pest management is carried out holistically instead of focusing on a single property at a time. Third, utilizing my experience organizing events in Rock Creek Park, I would follow the model of ANC1D07 and Mt Pleasant Street and setup a schedule of regular community lead volunteer litter clean-up events. This would not only supplement city services, but could serve as an opportunity to educate community members on the harms of litter and strategies to keep rats and other pests at bay. I believe that combined these approaches can make a dent in the prolific litter on our streets and the ever-increasing presence of rats and other unwanted pests.

column26: I would love to work on bringing multifamily housing to the block bounded by Kilbourne, Lamont, Mt. Pleasant and 17th streets. This is square 2601  - the site of the former Best World supermarket and Don Juan restaurant. The block is punching below its weight; it contains no housing, four of five parcels are vacant and is smack in the center of a vibrant and accessible corridor. The D72 bus stops directly in front of Don Juan on the corner of Lamont and Mt. Pleasant Street. The 16th Street buses are one block away. The Columbia Heights Metro station is four blocks away. The Capital Bikeshare station is across the street. Although it is five separate parcels, the whole block is owned by a single entity, which obviously makes site assemblage and control easier. Moreover, the block is nicely configured for multifamily; the shallow footprint means you wouldn’t have challenges getting natural light into units. A significant challenge is that the MU-4 zoning only allows a Floor Area Ratio of 3 and a height limit of 50 feet. Rough math - The land area is 12,211 across the five lots. 75% lot occupancy means 3 floors of 9,150 square feet per floor (above the first floor retail). After common areas, we are talking roughly 7,750 square feet per floor. If you average 850 square feet per unit - ideally it would be more since this is a great neighborhood for family-sized units - that’s 9 units per floor and a total of 27 units in the building. To me, that feels like the site would still be punching below its weight when it comes to housing. As a first step at allowing for more ambition on the site, I would introduce an ANC resolution requesting that DC 2050 Comprehensive Plan up-designate Square 2601 and the Mt. Pleasant Street corridor and testify in support when the plan reaches the city council. (I’m aware that even if zoning were to change, the Historic Preservation Review Board could still scale back any project on the site unless its review powers were amended).  I am glad that, after a long delay, 1701 Park Road is changing hands and that Monument Realty seems eager to finish the renovation while preserving the original vision. This is a gorgeous building whose boarded up windows are currently an eyesore. Bringing it back to life will both enliven the street and provide more affordable units in the neighborhood.  I have toured the Henderson building on 16th street. I watched the discussions about the project at the Historic Preservation Review Board. Converting the historic building at 3224 16th Street is no small feat as it is currently laid out for classrooms. The additions provide much needed new housing, but if I was King-for-a-Day I would push for more ambition. I don’t think we need to constrain the massing by reference to the art deco building directly to the south.

column36: Representing roughly 2,000 constituents means decisions get made without hearing from most people — and the input I do receive tends to skew toward those with the time or motivation to reach out. My approach is to widen that input as much as possible, then apply a consistent, transparent framework when the picture is still incomplete. I'll hold regular posted office hours, walk the neighborhood, partner with civic associations (e.g. Brookland Neighborhood Civic Association), and use short targeted surveys for specific decisions. I'll also track who isn't showing up — renters vs. homeowners, different blocks — and reach out directly to fill those gaps rather than assume silence means agreement. We have at least two major projects of note in our SMD - the Taylor Street Bike Lane and the Brookland Lanes redevelopment. Both issues have strong advocates on both sides of the issue. In cases like that, I weigh input by who's most directly affected, check it against available information and any existing corridor or transportation plans, and distinguish reversible decisions — where I can act and adjust — from harder-to-reverse ones, where I slow down and push for broader outreach first. My campaign priorities give me a starting lens, but they don't replace listening when new issues surface. Since most constituents won't weigh in directly, I think it's just as important to explain decisions after the fact. I'll report back through ANC recaps and direct follow-up to people who wrote in — what I heard, what I weighed, and why I landed where I did — so even residents who didn't participate can see the reasoning and raise concerns before the next decision. My job isn't to average the loudest voices in my inbox — it's to make sound decisions for everyone in the SMD, including the people I never hear from. Expanding who I hear from, applying a consistent framework when input is thin, and staying transparent about my reasoning are how I intend to do that.

column12: Market-rate housing prices are set by market values, and supply and demand dynamics.  Thus, subsidies or government assistance have little role. Market-rate housing rents can vary based on location, demand, amenities, size, etc. Features of the property or neighborhood that are considered undesirable may affect the prices, pushing them downward or upward. Market-rate formulas may be based on the America Median Income (AMI) for the area’s residential population, but average area rent prices can also be used. Market-rate housing has no income restrictions for tenants, and property owners have leeway in setting rents, increasing them, and choosing tenants based on broader criteria. Affordable housing has regulated or government-subsidized rent and purchase prices capped for low- to moderate-income households. Rent prices are below market rate, which is determined by the income level of residents. AMI is also relevant for affordable housing schemes in that eligibility is determined by the AMI, with the goal of keeping housing expenses under 30% of a household's monthly income. Affordable housing is also supported by government subsidies and non-profits. Rents are locked in and do not rise based on supply-demand dynamics. Properties may get tax credits to offset lower rental income.  As housing costs have risen dramatically in the District—reflect nationwide trends —access to adequate, affordable housing is increasingly important in creating opportunities for residents to succeed.

I have long been a strong advocate for affordable housing, both in Washington, DC, and through my work as an international development professional. As a community leader and former president of the Luray Warder Neighborhood Association, I helped build community support for the Park Morton and Bruce Monroe projects from their inception. If elected, I would: If elected, I’ll continue consistent involvement in all phases of the Park Morton development process, closely monitoring construction, timelines, and compliance with expectations and specifications. I’ve worked with development partners to keep residents informed and facilitate engagement with the broader community while ensuring that partners remain responsive to neighborhood needs. I make it a point to introduce myself to people as I walk through the neighborhood and visit cafés, eateries, and businesses. I intentionally walk throughout the neighborhood and introduce myself while walking my dog, for example. I let neighbors know that I’m their commissioner, explain what ANCs are, and make clear that I’m here to support them in addressing their concerns and priorities. This includes connecting them with agencies on their behalf and giving them the tools to advocate for themselves so they can feel invested in the outcome.  As needed, I canvass residents who may be affected by neighboring restaurants and bars with live music to gauge whether there are any disturbances. I also participate in local activities to engage with constituents, including monthly neighborhood cleanups and the Lower Georgia Avenue Main Streets Annual Chili Cook-Off.  I also create events that bring people together while giving me opportunities to meet neighbors, learn what issues matter to them, and understand what they want to see for Park View. column12: In practice the distinction is who the housing is priced for and what protects that price. Market-rate housing is priced at what the market will bear (unsubsidized, not income-restricted), and in a place like Park View that increasingly means priced beyond the families who have lived here for decades. Affordable housing is housing where a household pays no more than about 30% of its income, held there by something durable: income restriction, subsidy, or rent control, so affordability survives a hot market instead of evaporating in it. The label matters less to me than the guarantee behind it: "workforce" units that no longer pencil as affordable for the people being displaced are affordable in name only. In a district changing this fast, the test I care about is whether a longtime resident, a renter on Sherman Avenue or a fixed-income homeowner near Otis Place, can still afford to stay. That line is where the two actually part in my casework.

Staying affordable for the people who already live here. Park View, Pleasant Plains, and the blocks around Howard are changing fast, and in my casework the change isn't abstract: it's a fixed-income homeowner near Otis Place watching costs climb, a longtime renter on Sherman Avenue unsure how much longer they can stay. My position is that growth and affordability aren't opposites. I'm a yes on more homes, especially along the Georgia Avenue corridor where the transit and the zoning already are. But "more homes" has to mean homes reachable by the neighbors already here, not only market-rate units that speed displacement up. The test I hold new development to is simple: does it help a family that's here stay here?

If elected, I would: Be honest about the tools (an ANC advises, it doesn't set housing policy), but use the levers we do have deliberately. When a project comes before us seeking flexibility (Wonder Plaza, the Howard-area sites, any PUD), I'd use the ANC's "great weight" to push for income-restricted and family-sized units and real community benefits, not the minimum. I'd back District policy that moves the needle, like 15% affordable housing in every planning area. And I'd do the unglamorous work that keeps people in place now: making sure residents actually hear about rent changes, tenant-purchase rights, rent-control protections, and senior and disabled property-tax relief in time to use them, because the people most at risk of displacement are the ones a notice failure reaches last.
column36: I try to decide from evidence and process, not volume. The residents I hear from are real and they matter, but they aren't automatically the majority of the roughly 2,000 people I represent, so I treat what I hear as the start of the work, not the end of it. My habit is to go to the record. On the Otis Place parking case a constituent was upset, and I could have simply amplified that. Instead I read DDOT's own notice and found the agency's stated need was about 50 hours a week while the remedy it imposed ran 168. So the fair ask wasn't "do nothing" or "give her everything"; it was to match the remedy to the documented need. It's slow, and I'd rather tell you it's unfinished than pretend one commissioner can make an agency move on command. I also try to keep my own opinions separate from my role. My job is to carry what residents ask me to carry: to represent their interests when they ask me to, and to move quickly to help a neighbor or a community project go forward, not to attach my personal preferences to a matter coming before the commission. When I take a position to an agency, it's usually because a constituent asked me to represent theirs, not because I decided to make it my cause. And I weight the residents who never email, the ones a notice failure leaves out entirely. That's why so much of my work is making sure people actually get told before a decision lands on their block. Good representation, to me, is being reachable, doing the homework, carrying what residents ask me to carry, and being honest about the limits of what one commissioner can change.

I think this is particularly true for younger residents starting careers here who are getting pushed further away from their places of work and community, Black residents who grew up in the District and are getting priced out, and young families who can’t find a place to raise kids affordably.   4C06 and our segment of Petworth is unique in that it has somewhat more family sized houses and units than other areas of the city, and has a residential feel while still being accessible to bike lanes and transit options that connect it to the rest of the city.   I think our ANC, and the city government more broadly, has a responsibility to tackle the lack of affordable housing and do so through several policy interventions, as there is no silver bullet to the housing crisis. Speaking broadly, I believe those include:  1 - Increasing the stock of available housing by breaking down legal barriers blocking developers from building efficiently and densely  2 - Mandating a certain amount of that private housing stock provides for low income renters   3 - Protecting tenants from unjust rent hikes/evictions/harassment  4 - Publicly providing low income housing housing through voucher systems and eventually a public developer

If elected, I would: 1 - By advocating for tenants undergoing unfair treatment by their landlord in district, and connecting them to city resources like the Office of the Tenant Advocate and the Landlord and Tenant Legal Assistance Network  2 - By working with developers abiding by the city’s zoning laws (including inclusionary zoning and building electrification rules) to garner community support for new developments and oppose unnecessary hurdles towards construction  3 - By connecting constituents looking to rent a spare room or expand the number of units on their property to the appropriate city resources  Nonetheless ANC commissioners are obviously limited in tackling a citywide (national even!) housing crisis, so I’d use the office to symbolically advocate for legislation in City Council that:   1 - Ensures more denser zoning of much of the District under the new Comprehensive Plan that allows for more housing, more quickly built.   2 - Improve our inclusionary zoning program so it is better able to track and more quickly fill vacancies, and certify tenants’ income  3 - Re-expands TOPA and/or expands rent stabilization to buildings constructed after 1975 to give power to tenants hoping to own their own building or have a say in its purchase  4 - Creates a citywide social housing developer to create multi-income public housing with its own revenue stream.

column12: Market-rate housing means that the price/cost of housing is set at the intersection of what the owner/developer is willing to accept and what the purchaser/renter is willing to pay.  The market rate in DC is high because it is a desirable place to live with a large population, limited land, and restrictive zoning requirements that limit apartment construction.  Market rate housing is generally built by private developers, but it doesn’t have to be.  Affordable housing is housing that costs 30 percent or less of a household’s income according to HUD, but it could also have other features listed under this question (e.g. rent-controlled, means/income-restricted, built by the government, subsidized).  It does not have to be any or all of those things to be affordable housing in my opinion.  DC has not set a specific definition for what qualifies generally as “affordable housing” but has defined "affordable housing unit."  In addition, affordable housing can take a number of different forms, depending upon who’s renting. ANCs have the opportunity to put their stamp on affordability in developing PUDs for developers seeking to enter the market in their particular commission area.  The public benefit derived by negotiating a PUD with a developer can take many forms including levels of affordability, size of units (particularly family sized units), workforce housing set asides, and percentages of income required.

column12: I view affordable housing and market-rate housing as complementary but distinct parts of the housing ecosystem. Market-rate housing is typically priced based on prevailing market conditions and consumer demand, without income-based eligibility requirements or public subsidies. Affordable housing, by contrast, is designed to remain accessible to households with low or moderate incomes, often through income restrictions, subsidies, or other affordability programs. In my view, the key distinction is not whether a unit is relatively expensive or inexpensive, but whether housing costs are reasonably aligned with a household's income. A market-rate unit may be affordable for one household and out of reach for another. Effective affordable housing policies should therefore be grounded in the actual incomes and housing needs of DC residents. I also believe the District needs both. Expanding housing supply, including market-rate development, can help address overall demand and improve housing availability. At the same time, preserving and increasing income-restricted affordable housing is essential to ensure that lower-income residents, seniors, and working families have access to stable housing opportunities in the city.

column23: I do not believe apartments should automatically be legal in every part of every District neighborhood. While I support increasing the housing supply and expanding housing options throughout DC, I also believe land-use decisions should account for the unique characteristics, infrastructure, and needs of different neighborhoods. In many areas, particularly near Metro stations, major transit corridors, commercial centers, and employment hubs, additional apartment development can help meet housing demand and make efficient use of existing infrastructure. However, a uniform citywide approach may not adequately account for differences in neighborhood scale, transportation capacity, public services, environmental considerations, and existing development patterns. I favor a balanced approach that allows substantially more housing, including apartments, in appropriate locations while maintaining reasonable standards related to building scale, setbacks, open space, stormwater management, and infrastructure capacity. I also believe residents should have meaningful opportunities to participate in planning decisions, while recognizing that community input should not be used solely to block needed housing. In short, I support making it easier to build apartments in many parts of the District, especially where increased density can be accommodated effectively. However, I do not believe a one-size-fits-all policy is the best way to plan for the District's long-term housing and neighborhood needs.

I would also favor a mix of housing types rather than relying solely on large apartment buildings. New homes could be created through a combination of apartment buildings, mixed-use development, townhomes, accessory dwelling units, and appropriately scaled infill projects. A diverse housing strategy can increase supply while allowing neighborhoods to evolve gradually and accommodate residents with different needs and incomes. I would place particular emphasis on family-sized housing and housing that is attainable for low-, moderate-, and middle-income households. Meeting housing goals is not only about the number of units produced, but also about ensuring that residents at different stages of life can find housing that meets their needs. At the same time, housing growth should be accompanied by investments in the infrastructure and services that support a growing population, including transit, sidewalks, schools, parks, utilities, and stormwater management. I believe one of the biggest issues facing my neighborhood is managing growth in a way that expands housing opportunities while preserving and improving the infrastructure and services that residents rely on every day. As the District continues to grow, neighborhoods need more housing, but they also need transportation improvements, safe pedestrian infrastructure, adequate public space, schools, utilities, and other services that support a growing population. As stated in my campaign slogan from when I first ran for office several years ago, I want to ensure that “Progress fits the Neighborhood." My position is that growth and quality of life are not competing goals if development is planned thoughtfully. I support additional housing and responsible development, particularly in areas that are well served by transit and neighborhood amenities. At the same time, I believe the District and developers should be accountable for ensuring that infrastructure, public services, and community needs keep pace with new development. I also believe residents deserve a meaningful voice in planning decisions. Community engagement should help improve projects and identify potential issues, while recognizing that change and growth are a necessary part of meeting the District's long-term housing and economic needs.

If elected, I would: My experience as ANC commissioner has shown me that many neighborhood issues require persistent follow-up with agencies and elected officials rather than a single meeting or request. If reelected, I would continue to focus on being an accessible, responsive, and effective advocate for the neighborhood while recognizing the limited authority of an ANC commissioner. I would continue to maintain regular communication with residents, identify recurring concerns, and work directly with District agencies, developers, and elected officials to address issues affecting the community. I would use my pre-existing knowledge of the role and the ANC's advisory role in zoning, development, transportation, public space, and licensing matters to ensure that residents' concerns are heard and that proposed projects are evaluated thoughtfully and transparently. I would also continue to  work to hold agencies and applicants accountable for commitments they make to the community. Many neighborhood issues require persistent follow-up rather than new legislation. Where the ANC lacks direct authority, I would help residents navigate the appropriate agencies, monitor progress, and advocate for timely responses. My goal would be to provide clear communication, practical problem-solving, and consistent follow-through on behalf of residents.
column36: As the current ANC commissioner, I have learned that the residents who contact the ANC most frequently are not always representative of the entire SMD, which is why I believe it is important to seek input from a broad cross-section of the community. I would continue to approach decisions by balancing constituent input, objective information, and the broader interests of the community. Hearing from residents is essential, but I would not assume that the number of emails received or the number of people attending an ANC meeting necessarily reflects the views of the entire SMD. I would make a deliberate effort to hear from a broad cross-section of residents, including people who may not regularly attend meetings or participate in neighborhood discussions. For significant issues, I would use multiple methods to gather feedback, including community meetings, surveys, email, and direct conversations with constituents. I would also seek out differing viewpoints and make a genuine effort to understand the concerns and priorities of people on all sides of an issue. In addition to constituent input, I would consider objective information and the likely consequences of different courses of action. Depending on the issue, that may include District policies, agency recommendations, zoning and planning considerations, transportation and infrastructure impacts, budget implications, and other relevant facts. I would distinguish between concerns that affect the broader community and requests that primarily advance a narrow individual interest. Ultimately, I believe an elected representative's responsibility is to listen carefully, evaluate the available information, exercise independent judgment, and explain the reasoning behind a decision. I would not simply base my vote on whichever viewpoint was expressed most loudly or most recently. Instead, I would strive to make decisions that are fair, practical, and consistent with the long-term interests of the neighborhood. My goal would be to represent the entire SMD, including residents who disagree with me or choose not to participate in the ANC process, while remaining transparent, accessible, and open to reconsidering my position when new information warrants it.

These properties can contribute to illegal dumping, pests, crime and safety concerns, and a general sense of neglect. I believe every resident deserves to live in a neighborhood that is clean, safe, well-maintained, and beautiful.  My position is that vacant and blighted properties should not be allowed to remain community eyesores indefinitely. I support bringing these properties back into productive use through rehabilitation, responsible redevelopment, or enforcement when owners fail to maintain their properties.  As an ANC Commissioner, I understand that I cannot personally compel an owner to renovate a property or make city agencies take action. What I can do is use the authority and relationships of the ANC to organize residents, document problem properties, work with DC agencies and Council offices, track complaints and enforcement, and advocate for timely action.  I would also make neighborhood beautification a priority by organizing community cleanups, encouraging landscaping and tree planting, supporting well-maintained public spaces, and partnering with residents, businesses, churches, and civic organizations.

column38: My approach to housing, affordable housing, transportation, and land use is grounded in one principle: growth should improve the quality of life for both existing and future residents. I also believe affordable housing should be distributed throughout the District so that residents at different income levels have meaningful opportunities to live in every neighborhood.  At the same time, I want to make sure housing growth is accompanied by the infrastructure and services necessary to support it. That includes safe sidewalks, reliable public transportation, pedestrian safety, parks, sanitation, parking management, and other neighborhood services.  My greatest concern in ANC 5D05 is the condition of vacant and blighted properties. I believe these properties represent both a challenge and an opportunity. Rather than allowing vacant properties to deteriorate, we should pursue rehabilitation, responsible redevelopment, and productive reuse that can add housing while improving the appearance and safety of the neighborhood.  Neighborhood beautification is also a priority for me. Clean streets, maintained properties, trees, landscaping, attractive public spaces, and well-maintained sidewalks contribute to residents’ quality of life and neighborhood pride.  I support thoughtful transportation investments, including improved transit and protected bicycle infrastructure, but decisions about reallocating street space should consider the needs of residents, businesses, pedestrians, people with disabilities, emergency services, and those who depend on automobiles.  Ultimately, I am pro-housing and pro-community. I want 5D05 to welcome new residents and new investment while ensuring that existing residents are not forgotten or displaced. Development should create opportunity, strengthen neighborhoods, and leave the community better than it found it.

column12: At its core, the difference between market-rate and affordable housing comes down to how prices are set and who they serve. Both are critical to D.C.'s economic diversity.  Market-rate housing prices are dictated by the open market—supply and demand—without government price restrictions. In DC, these prices are often out of reach for working-class residents. However, building adequate market-rate housing is essential.  Affordable housing is explicitly income-restricted and often subsidized, and ensures housing costs do not exceed 30% of a household's gross income. While market-rate housing absorbs growth and generates our tax base, dedicated affordable housing is the intentional safety net that guarantees our neighborhoods remain inclusive. As an ANC Commissioner, I will champion an all-of-the-above approach: increasing overall supply to stabilize market rates, while fiercely advocating for deeply affordable, income-restricted units. This it is rooted in my belief that everyone deserves access to a safe, stable home, which is a fundamental right and the foundation of a thriving, equitable community.

column26: Meeting the 210-unit housing goal in my ANC requires a strategic approach that makes the best use of underutilized public and institutional land. While the goal should not necessarily be to put all 210 units into a single location, our most viable path forward involves identifying appropriate sites where new homes can be integrated alongside the services, parks, libraries, and community spaces that residents rely on.  In our neighborhood, the clearest opportunity to add substantial housing is at the Chevy Chase Civic Core. DMPED is currently leading a project here to bring affordable housing alongside a new library, community center, and upgraded outdoor amenities. The current proposal by Rift Valley Partners contemplates 177 new apartments on this publicly owned site. Importantly, recent project revisions have boosted affordability to 80 units alongside 97 market-rate units.  Maximizing this site is not just good policy; it is a practical necessity. Given our current market conditions—characterized by tough financing environments and high construction costs—purely private development has slowed significantly. Leveraging District-owned land is arguably the only way we will secure a substantial, near-term housing win. This project has strong community support, would bring new energy to upper Connecticut Avenue, and provides housing opportunities to a greater diversity of residents. As Commissioner, I am personally committed to unapologetically championing this project, shepherding the land disposition agreement through, and fiercely defending its housing components.  To achieve the remainder of our housing goals and ensure sustainable, distributed growth, I also support the proposed project at Ingleside at Rock Creek. There is significant demand for additional housing in this senior living community. Supporting this helps our older residents comfortably age in place.  Ultimately, every ward must contribute to meeting the city’s housing needs. By aggressively supporting the Civic Core and exploring institutional land opportunities, we can deliver an early, impactful win for housing equity in upper Northwest D.C.

column34: Meeting the District’s goal to be carbon-free by 2045 requires us to rethink our daily routines, and as an ANC Commissioner, I believe in leading by example. I commit to taking transit for my local trips along the Connecticut Avenue corridor—whether I am heading to the pharmacy, running errands, or going out for lunch or dinner.  For our specific neighborhood, particularly in my SMD (3/4G01), choosing transit is more critical now than ever. We suffered for years from the loss of our E6 bus route, which cut off many residents from essential services and isolated our community. Thankfully, with the WMATA Better Bus Network redesign, the implementation of the new C83 bus has finally restored our access to Connecticut Avenue. The most pressing issue in our neighborhood is pedestrian safety, exacerbated by failing sidewalk infrastructure and dangerous vehicular traffic patterns. Through my recent community survey, residents overwhelmingly highlighted their daily anxieties navigating our streets.  We see this danger acutely at Pinehurst Circle, where confusing configurations and poor visibility regularly lead to drivers going the wrong way and near-miss accidents. We also see it in the ongoing neighborhood battles for safe passage, such as the Utah Avenue sidewalk project and the urgent concerns neighbors have recently raised regarding the lack of safe pedestrian access along 32nd Street.  My position is simple: our infrastructure should not prioritize vehicle speed over human lives. When residents cannot walk their dogs, push a stroller, or safely reach our local bus routes because of crumbling sidewalks and dangerous intersections, it degrades our community's foundational quality of life. We must rapidly repair our failing infrastructure and implement physical traffic calming to protect our most vulnerable road users.

If elected, I would: While ANC Commissioners don’t have the authority to pour concrete or physically install traffic cameras, we do possess the statutory power of "great weight" and the platform to relentlessly organize our community. Realistically, my approach will center on persistent, data-driven advocacy to hold the District Department of Transportation (DDOT) accountable. If elected, I will leverage the hard data from our community survey—which documents the exact locations of near-misses and resident safety priorities—to draft targeted ANC resolutions and calls for action. Additionally, I will serve as a fierce liaison between our neighbors and District agencies
column36: Serving as an ANC Commissioner requires a balanced, intentional approach grounded in active listening and mutual respect. My role is to actively seek community feedback, recognizing that residents bring different lived experiences and valid concerns to the table.  The loudest voices in a room rarely represent the entirety of our 2,000-person Single Member District. While it is easy to govern when there is an overwhelming majority, most local issues are complex and lack a single consensus. I strongly rebuke the idea that "majority rules" should be the absolute deciding factor in neighborhood politics. Relying solely on who speaks the loudest means the needs and voices of quieter, less organized groups are completely overridden. A few Commissioners argue for this blunt approach, but I believe they are fundamentally wrong.  How we govern is just as important as the policies we support; we must conduct ANC business with compassion, civility, and respect. Disagreements on neighborhood issues—whether about housing, historic preservation, or infrastructure—should never be an excuse to weaponize the process, stall progress arbitrarily, or alienate neighbors or fellow Commissioners.  It is no secret that our current ANC has struggled with deep dysfunction. Over the past term, we have witnessed a breakdown in basic decorum, where differing opinions are met with isolation rather than curiosity, and where unacceptable rhetoric—such as telling a colleague they must serve the ANC as their "master"—has poisoned the well of local governance. When our meetings devolve into hostility, the neighborhood loses out. Local government should be a tool for community problem-solving, not a theater for personal grievances. We desperately need a reset. My focus will be on returning our commission to a place of constructive dialogue where every resident and Commissioner is treated with baseline dignity.  Knowing I will not hear from every constituent organically, my decision-making process will rely on proactive outreach, utilizing tools like the community surveys I have already deployed, door-knocking, and meeting people where they are. I will combine these qualitative stories with hard data to ensure my votes align with both neighborhood well-being and citywide goals. When I cast a vote, I will clearly communicate the "why" behind it, especially to those who may disagree. Ultimately, my goal is to make decisions that secure the best future for our community while ensuring everyone feels heard and respected.
column37: I am the right person to serve as ANC Commissioner because I bring a proactive, data-driven approach to local governance, paired with an unapologetic commitment to making our neighborhood more inclusive, accessible, and safe.Too often, local politics are dictated by the loudest voices in the room, leading to stalled progress. My leadership is rooted in proactive outreach—such as the community surveys I have already deployed—to ensure I represent the entire district, not just the most vocal faction. I believe in listening to all sides and leading with civility, but I will not shy away from making tough decisions that align with our broader citywide equity goals.  Our district is at a pivotal moment. We have a rare opportunity to bring desperately needed mixed-income housing to the Chevy Chase Civic Core, and we face urgent infrastructure crises, from dangerous traffic at Pinehurst Circle to failing sidewalks across the neighborhood. I have the organizational skills to hold agencies like DDOT and DMPED accountable and aggressively champion the transit lifelines our residents rely on. I am running because I believe in an "all-of-the-above" housing strategy, transit/pedestrian first infrastructure and empowering our community, and I am ready to deliver tangible, progressive wins for our community from day one.

I want GGWash and my neighbors to know that my progressive policy positions are inseparable from my commitment to good governance.  Right now, we must turn the civility in our Commission and our neighborhood around. In recent years, local debates over land use and housing have become increasingly toxic. By rooting our public discourse in empathy, active listening, and factual data rather than animosity, I know we can move past the division and build a more equitable, vibrant neighborhood together.

column12: I believe the distinction between affordable housing and market-rate housing is fundamentally about who can afford to live there—not simply the price of a unit.  Market-rate housing is priced according to what the private market will bear. Affordable housing is intentionally structured so that lower- and moderate-income households can afford to live in their communities without sacrificing other basic needs. That distinction matters because housing costs have risen faster than wages for too many DC residents.  Affordable housing should not mean lower-quality housing. It should mean quality homes accessible to people across a range of incomes, including working families, seniors, service workers, and others who contribute to our city.  We need to do more than add units labeled “affordable.” We must preserve existing affordable housing, prevent displacement, expand deeply affordable options, and ensure new development creates meaningful housing opportunities at different income levels.  Market-rate development can help increase overall housing supply, but it cannot, by itself, solve the affordability crisis. DC needs a housing strategy that supports new development while making affordability, stability, and inclusion central to how we grow.

Instead, I would look to major corridors, underutilized sites, surface parking lots, redevelopment opportunities, and appropriate infill—particularly in areas well served by Metro and other transit.  Most importantly, new housing should expand affordability and not come at the expense of existing residents. I would prioritize projects that include meaningful affordable housing, preserve existing affordable homes, and minimize displacement of residents and small businesses. Publicly owned and underutilized land should receive particular consideration for deeply affordable housing.  I also believe ANC review should focus on outcomes, not simply unit counts. We should ask: Who can afford these homes? Will existing residents be displaced? What community benefits are provided? Can infrastructure support the additional density? One of the biggest issues facing my neighborhood is affordability and its impact on the people who make our community work. In Foggy Bottom and across Ward 2, rising housing costs, commercial rents, and everyday expenses are making it harder for longtime residents, seniors, working families, students, and small businesses to remain in our community.  I believe a neighborhood is strongest when the people who live, work, and contribute to it can afford to stay. Development should strengthen—not displace—the communities already here. I support preserving affordable housing, protecting renters, responsible development, and a neighborhood economy that includes locally owned businesses and working people.

If elected, I would: My responsibility is to use the authority and platform of the ANC effectively. I would make affordability a consistent consideration in ANC decisions, particularly around zoning, development, public space, and commercial activity. I would use the ANC’s formal recommendations to advocate for meaningful community benefits and push back when proposals would unnecessarily displace residents or small businesses.  I would also bring residents together with developers, District agencies, Councilmembers, and community organizations to identify practical solutions and build support for them. Most importantly, I would use the position to organize—not simply react.  The ANC has limited formal authority, but it has a meaningful voice. I would use that voice consistently, transparently, and in partnership with residents to protect the diversity, affordability, and long-term vitality of our neighborhood.
column36: I believe an ANC Commissioner must be responsive to constituents without being reactive to the loudest voices. Representing roughly 2,000 people means recognizing that the residents who attend meetings, send emails, or contact me directly are important voices, but they do not necessarily represent the views of the entire community.  My approach would be to listen broadly, seek out perspectives that may not otherwise reach the ANC, and then use my independent judgment to make decisions in the best interest of the community.  I would also consider the facts, the law, District policies, and the short- and long-term consequences of a decision. When appropriate, I would seek information from District agencies, subject-matter experts, and community partners rather than relying solely on individual opinions or the volume of feedback I receive.  Most importantly, I would not treat the absence of constituent feedback as consent, nor would I assume that the largest number of emails or speakers represents a majority view. My responsibility as an elected representative is to weigh the perspectives I hear, understand who may be missing from the conversation, consider the broader community impact, and exercise sound judgment.  I will not always make a decision that everyone agrees with. But I believe constituents deserve a Commissioner who will listen respectfully, explain the reasoning behind decisions, remain accessible and accountable, and lead when leadership is required. My goal would be to represent the whole community—not simply the people who speak the loudest.
column37: I believe I am the right person to serve as ANC Commissioner because I bring lived experience, a proven record of service, and a deep commitment to my community. As a fourth-term ANC Commissioner representing SMD 2A03, I understand that effective representation requires being accessible, accountable, and willing to do the work.  My approach is rooted in listening, advocacy, and results. As a worker organizer and advocate for economic justice, I have spent my career bringing people together, navigating complex systems, and turning community concerns into action. I bring that same approach to ANC service: listening to residents, asking hard questions, working collaboratively with District agencies and community partners, and using the ANC's voice effectively.  I also recognize that an ANC Commissioner represents the entire community—not just those who attend meetings or speak the loudest. I work to engage renters, seniors, workers, small businesses, and both longtime and newer residents, ensuring diverse perspectives inform my decisions.  Most importantly, I view ANC service as a responsibility, not a title. I would continue to bring experience, independence, and a commitment to practical results to representing SMD 2A03.
column38: I believe housing, transportation, and land use decisions should be guided by a simple principle: DC must remain a city where people at different income levels can afford to live, work, and build a future.  As an ANC Commissioner, I have seen how development can create opportunities for new housing and investment while also raising legitimate concerns about affordability, displacement, public space, infrastructure, and neighborhood character. I support building more housing—including affordable housing—but growth must be intentional and equitable. New development should provide meaningful community benefits and not treat existing residents and small businesses as an afterthought.  Affordability also means more than increasing the number of units. We must preserve existing and naturally occurring affordable housing, prevent displacement, expand deeply affordable housing, and ensure public investments do not inadvertently make neighborhoods unaffordable to the people who already live there. I support additional housing density, particularly near Metro and other high-capacity transit, where infrastructure can support growth.  Transportation and land use are inseparable from affordability. A household's cost of living includes not only rent or a mortgage, but also the time and expense of getting to work, school, and essential services. DC should continue investing in reliable public transportation, safe pedestrian and bicycle infrastructure, and transit-oriented development while ensuring that infrastructure keeps pace with growth.  Finally, ANC engagement should be meaningful, transparent, and focused on outcomes—not simply a procedural requirement. Residents deserve a voice, but that voice must be balanced with the District's responsibility to address its housing and affordability crisis. My approach is to bring residents, developers, agencies, and community organizations together to find practical solutions and advocate for growth that is equitable, sustainable, and strengthens our neighborhoods.

column26: Columbia Heights is already one of DC’s densest and most transit-rich neighborhoods, but there is absolutely room for additional homes here. In my own SMD, I would especially look to 14th Street between Monroe and Spring, where lower-density properties could accommodate significantly more housing, including affordable and mixed-income homes. I’ve been advocating for this exact upzoning to OP as part of DC 2050. As you move away from 14th Street into our residential blocks, I also support more opportunities for “missing middle” housing like duplexes, triplexes, and other smaller-scale multifamily housing. Across ANC 1A, there are several larger opportunities. Columbia Heights Village and the low-density properties along the 2800 block of 14th Street could accommodate substantially more housing while preserving or expanding affordable units. I also continue to think the Giant property on Park Road is an enormous missed opportunity. We have a grocery store in the heart of a dense, Metro-accessible neighborhood with a parking garage above it rather than housing. Furthermore, Columbia Heights has many vacant properties or underutilized sites, and those should become housing rather than remain empty. I’ve been a huge proponent of the Vacant to Vibrant law that passed in 2025, which reforms how DC deals with vacant properties and creates stronger tools to get more properties back into productive use. I don’t think every block needs to look the same. Columbia Heights’ mix of apartment buildings, rowhouses and smaller homes is part of what makes it special. While I’m firmly pro-housing, I also believe in the importance of single-family homes and gradual density transitions. But particularly areas near Metro stations and along our major corridors, we should be ambitious about adding housing.

column35:
One of the biggest challenges facing Columbia Heights is that our public spaces and commercial corridors have not received the level of sustained investment and management they need. The Civic Plaza, the 14th Street core, and other shared spaces should be clean, safe, welcoming and active. That is tied directly to our neighborhood’s economic health. When public spaces struggle, small businesses and residents feel the impact too. Columbia Heights has enormous potential, but we need to reinvest in it.

If elected, I would: Build on the momentum I’ve helped create the past four years. That includes seeing the Columbia Heights & Mount Pleasant Public Realm recommendations through implementation; advocating for a well-funded Neighborhood Management Authority that can provide ongoing cleaning, programming, public-space management and business support; pushing DDOT and other agencies to deliver planned street and pedestrian improvements; and continuing to organize neighbors through cleanups and community events.  I’m also excited about the opportunity to work with a new Mayor and Ward 1 Councilmember to bring fresh energy, attention, and investment to Columbia Heights and to the needs of my SMD. We have spent years identifying the challenges, advancing plans, and making the case for resources. The next step is making sure Columbia Heights is a priority for the next administration and Council, and turning that groundwork into tangible results neighbors can actually see and feel. An ANC can’t deliver all of that on its own, but we can educate neighbors, pass resolutions, advocate for funding, testify, and keep pressure on agencies and elected officials until things move.
column36: One of the biggest lessons I’ve learned as a Commissioner is that the people who come to an ANC meeting or send an email are important, but they are not necessarily representative of the 2,000+ people I serve. I try hard to think about the voices that are not in the room. Columbia Heights includes longtime homeowners and renters, young families, immigrants, Spanish-speaking residents, people in subsidized housing, small business owners, seniors, and many others who engage with local government in very different ways. That means I don’t view an inbox tally as a referendum. I listen carefully to the people who contact me, but I also seek people out through neighborhood events, business visits, cleanups, one-on-one conversations, community meetings, and regular newsletters. On major issues, I try to explain what is being proposed early on so that people can actually weigh in. Ultimately, I make decisions based on the information available, what I hear across the community, the likely impact on my SMD and the broader District, and what I believe will make Columbia Heights better over the long term. Sometimes that means making a decision that some of the loudest voices disagree with. When that happens, I think I owe neighbors an explanation of how I reached the decision. More broadly, I think nuance has disappeared from too much of our politics, and I reject that. Very few issues are truly black and white. I always try to find a reasonable path forward that takes seriously the many different voices and perspectives of the people I represent. That does not mean avoiding hard decisions or trying to make everyone happy. It means being willing to wrestle with tradeoffs, listen to competing concerns, and make a judgment based on what I believe is best for the community as a whole. I also think representation requires a willingness to learn and change your mind. My job isn't simply to arrive with a predetermined answer. It's to do the work, listen, ask questions, and then make the best decision I can.
column37: I’ve spent nearly four years showing neighbors how I approach this job: I communicate proactively and transparently, I build effective relationships, and I keep pushing hard to move things forward. I’ve helped turn vacant-property reform from an ANC resolution into DC law; led efforts to secure greater investment and dedicated neighborhood management for Columbia Heights; advocated before the Council and District agencies on everything from small businesses and street vendors to trash, rats and public spaces; advanced pedestrian-safety improvements and secured a long-needed crosswalk; and organized cleanups and community events that bring neighbors together. Just as importantly, I’ve tried to make local government accessible. I send regular newsletters, respond to constituent issues, connect neighbors with agencies and resources, and tell people what is happening even when the answer isn't simple or the news isn't good. I’ve learned how the ANC and DC government work, I’ve built relationships across our neighborhood and city government, and I still have the same basic approach I brought to the job: don’t just talk about problems, educate people, find a path forward, and keep pushing. I want to continue doing this work to make my SMD and Columbia Heights a better place to live, work, visit, and thrive.
column38: I’m very supportive of building more housing and making it easier to live in DC without relying on a car. I also think the details of implementation matter. Columbia Heights is already one of DC’s densest, most transit-rich and most diverse neighborhoods. We should continue adding housing, especially affordable and mixed-income housing, near Metro station, on 14th Street and other major corridors, while also allowing more small-scale multifamily housing within residential areas. At the same time, we need to preserve existing affordable housing and ensure longtime residents can remain in the neighborhood as it grows. On transportation, I support bus priority, protected bike infrastructure, safer crossings and reducing dependence on cars. But good projects also require good execution. DDOT should work with residents and small businesses early, plan for loading and accessibility, communicate clearly, and avoid treating legitimate implementation questions as opposition to safer streets. More broadly, land-use policy cannot be separated from what happens at street level. Adding housing and transit investment should go hand-in-hand with stronger public spaces, active storefronts, cleaner streets and neighborhood amenities. My goal is not growth for growth’s sake, it is a Columbia Heights that becomes more vibrant, affordable, connected, and welcoming as it grows.

column12: IMO, “affordable” is an outcome we strive for, while “market rate” is about a process to create housing. Often government can require a building to have what it terms “affordable housing” that may be subsidized and/or means-tested along with a requirement that it meet a certain income threshold (30 percent), but when residents say they desire “affordable housing” that is not the limit of their vision, nor should it be ours. It is possible for market rate housing to become more affordable if there are sufficient housing options relative to the number of people who want to live in a place. At the same time, government intervention shapes the marketplace both directly (e.g., requiring a number of affordable units, subsidizing down payments/rent, direct investment in new/refurbished buildings) and indirectly (e.g., loosening parking requirements for new buildings, zoning to support increased numbers of housing units), and government must take an active role to support affordable housing, full stop.

I support the need for diverse housing and opportunity for the full spectrum of community members, new and old.

If elected, I would: DC 2050 is critical in addressing the city’s housing shortage, so first and foremost I would work with the rest of the 4B ANC to ensure the plan reflects an appropriate vision for the city. This effort would extend to the Ward 4 Councilmember as the plan comes up for a vote and, especially, as the plan moves towards implementation. To the maximum extent possible I would use the ANC’s “great weight” to lobby the Office of Zoning (and, as relevant, the Office of Planning, DDOT/Public Space Committee, and the Office of Building) to support increased density and increased development for projects in 4B and neighboring ANCs. I would also work with Upper Georgia Ave Main Street and local businesses to ensure the ANC is doing what it can to support investment in the community because having destinations in a community supports increased development as well as the other way around. Additionally, ensuring that DDOT is providing adequate transportation services and traffic mitigation to support additional non-car development of the city is a primary avenue to increasing density, which is ultimately the only way the city will move to being more affordable, and that makes traffic safety/road design a critical part of the equation, something which itself is a principle issue of concern for myself as well.
column36: Facilitating a breadth of access is critical. I plan on having a virtual suggestion box along with QR codes around the SMD to encourage anyone walking around to reach out to me with any concerns/issues as a way to facilitate communication with those in the neighborhood who may not have the time or capacity to attend our ANC meetings. This also serves as a connection point and reminder for folks to express their input. I would also, like many ANC commissioners, aim to have monthly in-person office hours and a regular newsletter, both of which would include any relevant NOIs or other local information for which the ANC may weigh in or which I, as commissioner, could help facilitate feedback for residents with the DC govt. My goal as ANC is to be the conduit to relevant offices—residents may know what they want done but not who is responsible, so anything I can do to create more point-to-point interactions and connections can aid that.
column37: First and foremost, I have the time and resources to devote to being available to constituents, in addition to the desire to make an impact. I have attended ANC meetings over the past few years and have been looking for opportunities to be involved, including participating in ANC 4B’s Vision Zero committee—the current political has deepened that desire. I have a scientific background and am by nature someone who likes to dig in on an issue—this has allowed me to excel at understanding complicated regulatory issues and get up to speed quickly on new topics. I want to now put that skillset to work at a local level for my community and believe I can be effective at digging into the minutiae so the residents in my SMD don’t have to. I also already have experience when it comes to transportation issues—my day job is explicitly focused on reducing pollution and improving the efficiency of our transportation system, and (as noted) I was engaged with ANC 4B’s Vision Zero committee before its dissolution at the end of 2024. I am well prepared to build on that experience to target more localized solutions while also being able to identify some of those localized challenges in a broader context to better inform DDOT and DC government operation.
column38: In saying that I believe a family of four needs a car in the city today, I know that it is not literally true—more than a third of DC households are car-free, and presumably at least some of those are families of four. However, that does not make living car-free easy—the city does not currently support these families with sufficiently frequent transit services nor enough safe, protected bike lanes or, in some areas, sidewalks to facilitate family travel across the city in all areas. For too many families a car can still feel necessary, even if that is a financial burden that especially young families should not be tasked with. DC is not yet a city where the default option for a family of four is to go carless—but we should aspire to be. And I hope to push agencies like DDOT and WMATA to do what is possible to facilitate that.
