column12: In my opinion, affordable housing is designed to ensure that individuals and families can live in a home without spending more than approximately 30% of their household income on housing costs. It may be income restricted, subsidized, rent controlled, or supported through public programs, tax incentives, or partnerships with nonprofit and private developers. Affordable housing does not mean “cheap” or lower quality housing; it means housing priced in relation to residents’ incomes.  Market rate housing, I believe, is generally rented or sold at prices determined by current market conditions. It is typically not means tested, income restricted, subsidized, or rent controlled. However, “market-rate” does not automatically mean expensive, nor does it necessarily mean that a household will spend more than 30% of its income on housing.  Both are important. Income restricted affordable housing provides stability for residents whom the private market may not adequately serve, while additional market-rate housing expands the overall housing supply and creates more choices. The District needs a balanced approach that produces housing across income levels, prevents displacement, and allows residents to remain in their communities.

Family sized housing should also consider accessibility, so that grandparents, relatives with disabilities, or future changes in mobility can be accommodated.  Equally important, I believe family sized housing should be located near schools, parks, childcare, transit, and essential services. A true family sized home is not just about interior space it is about being in a neighborhood where families can thrive, stay connected, and build stability over time without being forced to move due to rising costs or lack of appropriate housing options.

One of the most significant issues facing ANC 6A02 is ensuring that our neighborhood remains affordable, safe, and accessible as it continues to grow. Too many residents face rising housing costs, limited housing choices, and the possibility of displacement. At the same time, vacant and underused properties prevent us from fully addressing the District’s housing shortage.  I support increasing the supply of both income restricted and market rate housing, including family sized homes, accessible units, rowhomes, and small apartment buildings. Greater density should be encouraged near transit and commercial corridors, but every neighborhood should contribute to meeting the District’s housing needs. Growth should be accompanied by strong affordability programs, tenant protections, infrastructure improvements, and opportunities for longtime residents to remain in their communities.

If elected, I would: If re-elected as ANC Commissioner for 6A02 I would use the ANC’s advisory role to influence decisions. Additionally, I would introduce and support pro-housing resolutions, provide testimony before the Zoning Commission and Council, and advocate for predictable by right development that increases housing choices.  I will continue to  review local development proposals promptly, communicate accurate information to residents, and convene community discussions focused on practical solutions. My work with the Office of Planning, Department of Buildings, housing agencies, Councilmember Charles Allen, and other partners would continue to identify underused sites, address unnecessary approval delays, and connect residents with rental, homeownership, and anti displacement resources. Finally, I would publicly track agency commitments and development matters so residents can hold both government and housing providers accountable.
column36: As an elected representative, I understand that the residents who attend meetings or contact the ANC may not reflect the full diversity of the approximately 2,000 people I represent. Public participation is essential, but I will not assume that the loudest, most frequent, or most organized voices automatically represent the majority.  I will continue to make decisions by combining meaningful public engagement with objective information, applicable laws, agency guidance, professional analysis, and consideration of the long-term public interest. I will continue to proactively seek input through in person and virtual meetings, surveys, community walks, newsletters, social media, direct outreach, and conversations with residents who may be less likely to attend traditional ANC meetings. This includes renters, homeowners, young people, seniors, families, people with disabilities, small-business owners, and residents with limited time or transportation.  When evaluating housing and land use matters, I will consider the needs of current residents as well as people who would like to live in our neighborhood but cannot find or afford a home. I will examine affordability, displacement risk, accessibility, transportation, environmental impact, public safety, infrastructure capacity, and consistency with the District’s housing and climate goals. I will distinguish between evidence based concerns and objections based primarily on resistance to change.  My responsibility is not simply to count the number of emails received or treat every decision as a popularity contest. It is to listen carefully, ask questions, review the facts, and exercise informed judgment on behalf of the entire community, including residents who are not present in the room and future neighbors who do not yet have a voice.  I will explain my decisions publicly, disclose the information and principles that informed them, and remain open to revisiting a position when credible new evidence becomes available. Even when residents disagree with my decision, they should be able to understand how and why it was made. My goal is to continue to provide transparent, equitable, and forward looking representation that serves the broader interests of ANC 6A02 and the District as a whole.
column37: I am the right person to continue serving ANC 6A02 because I combine proven public-service experience with responsive, hands-on community leadership. During my first four months as Commissioner, I have remained visible and accessible, responded to constituent concerns, organized a youth cleanup along the H Street corridor, helped businesses navigate licensing questions, and worked with District agencies on snow and ice removal, trash collection, alley cleanings, rodent abatement, and public-safety concerns.  I am committed to representing the entire SMD not only the residents who attend meetings or communicate most frequently. I will continue seeking diverse perspectives, making evidence based decisions, and clearly explaining my positions.  ANC 6A02 deserves a Commissioner who is responsive, prepared, collaborative, and willing to do the daily work of public service. I will continue advocating for safer and cleaner streets, abundant and affordable housing, responsible development, reliable transportation, thriving small businesses, and an improved quality of life for every resident.
column38: My positions are grounded in the belief that Washington, D.C. must remain a place where people of different incomes, ages, abilities, and household sizes can find a home and build a stable life. Addressing our housing shortage requires both income restricted affordable housing and substantially more market rate housing. These approaches are complementary, not competing.  I support allowing more homes and a wider variety of housing types throughout the District, including rowhomes, small apartment buildings, in-law suites, family sized units, accessible homes, and housing for seniors. I favor predictable by right development, gentle density increases across residential neighborhoods, and greater density near transit and commercial corridors. I also support converting vacant and underused properties into productive community assets.  Housing growth must be equitable. I support the goal of ensuring that at least 15% of homes in every planning area are affordable, along with strong tenant protections, homeownership opportunities, and anti-displacement resources. Family sized housing should include functional space and be located near schools, parks, childcare, transit, and essential services.  Transportation and land use policy must work together. I support dedicated bus lanes, parking flexibility, congestion pricing, safer pedestrian and bicycle infrastructure, and development patterns that reduce car dependence. These policies should be implemented with consideration for people with disabilities, seniors, caregivers, essential workers, small businesses, and residents who have limited transportation alternatives.  Meaningful community engagement is essential, but public participation should help shape growth rather than prevent needed housing. I will listen to residents while also considering objective evidence, District wide goals, and the needs of people who are not present at ANC meetings; including renters, future residents, and families currently priced out of our neighborhoods.  As Commissioner, I will continue to use the ANC’s advisory authority to support inclusive housing policies, reduce unnecessary barriers and delays, provide informed testimony, and hold agencies and developers accountable. My goal is a safer, more affordable, walkable, connected, and welcoming ANC 6A02 that provides room for both longtime residents and new neighbors.

One of the biggest issues in my neighborhood is ensuring we see equitable development across our SMD. During recent conversations with neighbors, several expressed concerns about the growth of development along Kennedy Street, fueled by investment from wealthy developers that can limit locals’ ability to invest in and grow their own businesses right at home. Additionally, neighbors do not feel they have an adequate say in weighing in on what businesses or housing types are being added to their neighborhood. I believe that development is only beneficial if it is co-created by the people who will be most impacted by it. The city needs to provide residents with grants or financing programs that can make starting businesses in our communities more accessible. When it comes to community involvement, ANCs need to have a more vocal presence in the neighborhood and communicate changes and opportunities for community input to neighbors in various ways, ensuring they have meaningful opportunities to voice their unique desires for change.

If elected, I would: If elected, I would support prioritizing local business development and advocate for our councilmember and the new mayor to conduct more analysis on the number of D.C. small-business owners by SMD and work with ANCs to provide more input on the programs, outreach, and training residents need to turn their ideas into tangible business opportunities. We should also help residents understand how to turn their existing networks into avenues for economic growth and ensure everyone understands how they can contribute to the neighborhood’s economic and overall well-being.
column36: Democracy on paper is a noun, but in reality, it is a verb. During my campaign, I have expanded my outreach beyond traditional media to meet neighbors where they are. This includes creating flyers, doing multiple rounds of door-knocking, providing a campaign phone number, and developing a website where neighbors can learn more about my work and ideas for Brightwood Park. In conversations with neighbors, I have reminded them that I take daily walks around the SMD and encourage folks to say hello or share ideas if they see me walking. If elected, I would continue to use online media, including social media, when possible, to share resources and ways folks can get involved. column38: As someone who rides the bus and metro every day, has walked all over the city, and occasionally been known to bike, I think that car-free or car-lite is one of the best ways to enjoy the city. We can also tie car registration to size or weight of vehicles, requiring vehicles that weigh more to pay more for road use.  I don’t think that government and private provision of housing are in conflict with one another. I know that frequently there is debate about if markets can provide enough housing at a low enough price point to house everyone, but I think that they can complement one another. Private housing induces affordability cascades that provide better units for lower rents in a neighborhood, not to mention the market has the capital DC does not to build enough housing to bring down rents. If Jubilee’s construction costs are standard, it would be almost $1 million per apartment built by the District. In 2025 there were almost 2,000 housing starts, a 15 year low,  which would mean DC needs to spend $2 billion a year, or one-sixth of its entire annual capital budget, just to match private housing starts in today’s post-DOGE, high interest-rate DC economy.  The District can provide counter-cyclical development during economic downturns that insure our housing is not at the whims of macroeconomic conditions. DHCD could also provide new-housing in low-investment areas that have difficulty attracting buyers. I do think that any District-owned housing should be revenue neutral or even positive. We have seen frequently with DHCD and DOB where buildings are allowed to fall into disrepair because they do not have the money to stay in good condition or because the political will to keep them up has dissipated. Allowing District-housing to be at the mercy of yearly budget debates, tax receipts, and voting cycles makes them vulnerable, they will need to be able to stand up on their own.

column12: Affordable housing and market-rate housing serve different purposes, and both have a place in a healthy community. Market-rate housing is priced according to current real estate conditions and what the private market will support. Affordable housing, however, is intentionally structured so that lower- and moderate-income residents are not forced to spend an unreasonable share of their income on rent or housing costs.  For me, affordability must be measured against what residents actually earn—not simply whether a unit is cheaper than another unit in the same development. Teachers, service workers, seniors, people with disabilities, working families, and longtime DC residents should be able to live in the communities they help sustain.  As an ANC Commissioner, I would support responsible development that includes a meaningful mix of housing options. New market-rate development can contribute to neighborhood growth, but it should not come at the expense of displacement. I would advocate for deeply affordable units, stronger tenant protections, preservation of existing affordable housing, homeownership opportunities, and development policies that allow residents of different income levels to remain part of our community.

column12: Affordable housing is housing where some form of subsidy, income restriction, or rent regulation keeps the cost below 30% of the household's income. Market-rate housing has no such support. However, it's important to provide a variety of housing forms and types (multi-family buildings, duplexes, triplexes, single-family homes, and so on) in DC, particularly in neighborhoods that have good access to transit. For example, in my SMD, a two-bedroom unit in a co-op may be “affordable” relative to the single-family homes that are on the market. A variety of housing types within a neighborhood have many benefits; they not only allow a greater diversity of residents, but they enable people to stay in a neighborhood they like as their needs change. A young couple can move to a larger home and start a family, an older empty-nest household can downsize to an apartment or a condo, and so on.  The comprehensive plan and zoning code should be updated to allow as many housing and building types as possible. What is built will depend on the market.  More market-rate supply eases the upward pressure on rents/costs across the board. That means fewer households need assistance in the first place, and the subsidy dollars DC does spend reach further.

column14: A housing unit with at least two bedrooms — ideally three or more — plus two full bathrooms and larger shared living space than a standard apartment layout provides. Family-sized housing can be provided in a variety of building types: single-family homes, duplexes, triplexes, small apartment buildings, and larger buildings. It should be flexible enough that a grandparent, in-law, or other extended family member can live there permanently or visit, and that the household can host holidays, family functions, and the other gatherings that are essential to family life. The real test is this: if you are fortunate enough to consider your own home "family housing," would you trade it for something new that is marketed as family housing? Too often the answer is no, and the reason isn't the bedroom count. It's storage, daylight, somewhere to put a stroller, a place to eat that isn't the couch. Affordable family housing shouldn't be merely acceptable, it should be as good as what people already have. That's a challenge to how we design and what the zoning code asks for, not an argument for building less.

The biggest issue in my SMD is one I think drives a lot of our other problems: vacant buildings and empty lots that have sat unused for years. This includes two large former residential complexes near Rhode Island Ave, along with smaller vacant lots scattered throughout the neighborhood and into neighboring SMDs.    These aren't just missed opportunities for housing. Empty buildings and lots become magnets for trash, unsafe conditions, and neglect, and of course, rats. Anyone who's lived here for a while knows exactly what these vacant spaces attract, and it's a problem that keeps coming up because the buildings just keep sitting there. That takes a toll on how safe people feel on their own block, and it wears down the pride people have in their neighborhood. The real problem is simple: we have buildings sitting empty instead of being put to use.

If elected, I would: I know an ANC commissioner can't rezone a property or force an owner to build. What I can realistically do is use the position to keep pressure on. That means working directly with property owners, the zoning commission, and DC agencies to push these sites toward actual redevelopment under the mayor's new housing initiative, showing up consistently at the meetings where these decisions get made, and making sure my neighbors' voices are part of that conversation. It won't fix everything overnight, but a commissioner who won't let these lots be forgotten is a start.
column36: Two thousand constituents is a real number, but it isn't an excuse to govern by guesswork. My approach starts with treating outreach as the job, not an afterthought to it.  This is a neighborhood position, and I don't think it should be run like a political campaign built around my own personal platform. The decisions that come before an ANC, alley closures, zoning cases, liquor licenses, development proposals, affect real people on real blocks, and I believe those people should have a direct hand in shaping the outcome, not just a commissioner assuming they know best.  So my plan is simple and direct. I intend to go to every household in my SMD, in person, and give people a real chance to talk to me or leave their concerns behind, whether that's a conversation on their porch or a QR code they can use on their own time to reach me directly. I won't hear from all 2,000 people, and I won't pretend that whoever I do hear from speaks for everyone. But that outreach becomes the foundation I build from. It tells me what people are actually worried about, not what I assume they're worried about.  Beyond that first round of outreach, my job doesn't stop at listening once. I plan to actively work to get more people engaged with our meetings themselves, whether that means letting neighbors know when something on the agenda will actually affect them, or simply making meetings feel worth showing up to. A commissioner can't represent people who don't know a decision is being made. Part of representing this community well is making sure more of it knows what's happening and has a chance to weigh in before decisions get made, not after.  I won't have perfect information from every constituent. No commissioner does. But I'd rather build my decisions on direct, ongoing conversations with my neighbors than on my own convictions about what's best for a community I was elected to serve, not lead from the front of.
column37: I think I'm the right person for this because I'm not running on my own agenda, I'm running to actually listen and act on what my neighbors need. This is a neighborhood position, and I believe the decisions that come out of it should be shaped by the neighborhood, not by whatever platform I walked in with.  I'm personally affected by the same things most of my neighbors are: the cost of living in this city, the feeling that homeownership here is out of reach, and yes, sometimes that uneasy feeling walking home alone at night past a block that's been dark and empty for years. I'm not approaching these issues from a distance. I live them too.  What I bring to this role is a real plan to hear from people, not just the ones who already show up to meetings, but as many of my 2,000 neighbors as I can reach, and to use that input as the actual foundation for what I push for. I want to help build a neighborhood that feels safer to walk through, that people are proud to call home, and that actually has room for the people who want to live here.  I'm not looking to lead from the front. I'm looking to represent this community as it actually is, and fight for what it actually needs.

When people have a real stake in their community, not just a lease renewal, they invest in it. Homeownership access isn't just an economic issue for me. It's how we build a city people actually feel is theirs.

column26: There are TEN post-pandemic office conversions in SMD 2C02: three hotel projects and seven residential. From 2024 to 2030, there are already planned to be 1,466 new residential units created in 2C02. More conversions are being considered, and I expect the list to grow during the 2027-2028 ANC term.  I have “One Big Idea” for SMD 2C02. I want to add a distinctly new kind of conversion of a former downtown office or commercial building to use as Workforce Housing for Downtown Service Workers. I am committed to the work of the learning curve and coalition building necessary to execute the One Big Idea.  My premise is that if you work Downtown and make Downtown possible for all of us, you should have a chance of living downtown. If you are a housekeeper in a hotel, a service worker back-of-house in a restaurant, a worker for a custodial, concierge, or security company serving a downtown building, a retail clerk, an entry-level medical, geriatric, or home-health aide, a gig worker making deliveries, you should not have to face a lengthy, expensive commute to affordable entry-level housing.  I want to provide adult co-housing with adult amenities. ‘Co-housing’ means a private room and bathroom, with shared facilities for cooking, eating, gathering, remote working, video gaming, and other amenities. ‘Co-housing’ is not necessarily a forever home, not family housing, not permanent supportive housing. I want the One Big Idea to serve residents at 30% AMI, costing no more than 30% of their income for rent and utilities.  I want to explore alternative funding models and sources without the automatic assumption of reliance on DC budget funding. Federal tax credits, investment by corporate, philanthropic, and corporate sources for the conversion construction costs. Ongoing support by the spectrum of private, not-for-profit, and other Downtown stakeholders should be the foundation for total costs not covered by residents’ monthly contributions.

column38: As I end my first ANC term, I would like to post an update on the situation that gave me the call to enter public service in 2024. In 2021, DC bought the property at 1339 Green Court, NW for use by the Department of Human Services (DHS) as a 150-bed, low-barrier, men's shelter. The site itself seemed to me to be wildly unsuitable for the purpose, and I persistently asked functional questions framed by the future safety of 150 of our most vulnerable neighbors:  1) contamination of the structure by 70 years as an industrial building;  2) alley-landlocked site with no sidewalks or pedestrian access;  3) limited access to firetrucks and emergency equipment;  4) alley lot zoning restrictions requiring challengeable variances; and 5) construction challenges with no space for a crane or construction material.  In early 2025,  my persistence led DHS to task the Department of General Services (DGS) to conduct a feasibility study of the property for use as a men's shelter. No funding has been allocated for a DGS study in the FY2025, FY2026, or FY2027 Budgets, effectively shelving the project indefinitely. In May 2026, DGS confirmed that 1339 Green Court has been removed from the DHS inventory and returned to DGS.  During the entire process, I pledged to find other sites in my own SMD 2C02 for use to address the needs of our unhoused neighbors. I am thrilled that Metropolitan AME Church, on the exterior surface of their historic church, is undertaking to build 27 units of Permanent Supportive Housing for Black veterans, and I have enthusiastically supported the initial stages of zoning variances which have been approved.

column12: As an ANC for over 10 years, I've witnessed Black and brown neighbors being systematically displaced by rising costs and weakened protections, and how much harder it is for seniors to age in place. But the need for affordable housing impacts everyone, across income levels, ages, and ethnicities.  To me, affordable housing means income-restricted, subsidized homes where families pay no more than 30% of their income and can live with dignity alongside market-rate residents and not warehoused in concentrated sites. Market-rate housing is unsubsidized and priced by the private market, with no income-eligibility requirements. The distinction matters most in how we deploy it.  At Bruce Monroe and Park Morton, we fought for a deliberate mix: replacement units for displaced Park Morton families, additional deeply affordable units, and market-rate housing alongside them. Mixed-income development helps keep a corridor economically diverse rather than gentrifying wholesale.  Affordable housing shouldn't mean "cheap." It should mean high-quality, dignified housing reachable for teachers, service workers, seniors, and long-term residents whose incomes haven't kept pace with rising costs. Market-rate development also plays a role, generating the density and revenue that can make projects like Bruce Monroe financially possible. ANCs play a critical role, and I look forward to continuing this work for Park Morton, Bruce Monroe, and beyond.

Getting the Park Morton/Bruce Monroe redevelopment to the finish line. This effort is more than a decade old, has been among ANC 1E's highest priorities the entire time I've served, and is critically important to every resident in the lower Georgia Avenue community. I'm running for re-election to this seat specifically to see it through. I'm deeply concerned about the gentrification and displacement pressure facing our Black and Brown neighbors along the corridor, and I believe the District owes it to Park Morton families to finish what we started.

If elected, I would: If elected, I would work hard to push for a coordinated effort in bringing the selected developers and architects for Bruce Monroe’s redevelopment project, the Department of Parks and Recreation, and Deputy Mayor for Planning and Economic Development on the community engagement and construction process forward, hold the District to the one-for-one affordable replacement commitment and the right-to-return for Park Morton residents, and ensure the community design process for the permanent one-acre park alongside the housing is successful. I'll keep working with the Deputy Mayor for Planning and Economic Development, Office of Planning, Howard University, and DC Council to keep the corridor's other pipeline projects and the comprehensive plan revisions shaping them moving in the same direction.
column36: I rely on a mix of tools, because no single one reaches everyone: resident surveys, direct business, non-profit/community stakeholder, civic association and social media engagement, door to door education and promotion,community walks, regular SMD meetings, and one-on-one time with neighbors who request it. I've used these approaches for almost 12 years on ANC 1E from documenting resident priorities for WMATA's Better Bus Network redesign to working with District Government, developments, residents and community stakeholders to organize a strong community process on Park Morton and Bruce Monroe’s redevelopment to gathering comments to inform my resolutions on the Crosstown Project and community safety investments and strategies. I know I won't hear from every one of the roughly 2,000 people I represent, and that the loudest voices at a given meeting don't automatically reflect the majority view. So I try to actively go find the residents who aren't already in the room, especially seniors, people with disabilities, renters, younger neighbors, and people who can't make an evening meeting rather than waiting for consensus to arrive on its own, while still being transparent in my decision-making. You can’t please everyone but you have to get the job done and my constituents know the tenacity and positive spirit I bring to this work and that I have everyone’s best interest in mind.
column37: I've proudly served and represented Park View and Pleasant Plains for almost 12 years, and lived here for 20. And I've stayed in the fight for Park Morton and Bruce Monroe longer than almost anyone else at the table, testifying before the DC Council, advocating for funding, engaging the community whenever possible and helping secure ANC 1E's unanimous resolution of support. I ran for the Ward 1 DC Council seat this year because I believe deeply in this community's future, and while that race didn't go my way in the primary, it didn't change what I'm accountable for right now: making sure Bruce Monroe's 273 units — and the families waiting on them — actually get built. We experienced a major milestone in getting the support from the DC Council, ANC1E and the Zoning Commission to the finish line, however, there is more work that needs to be done. We still need to rally the community and engage them in the design process and support the Park Morton resident’s right to return. That unfinished work, and the relationships and institutional knowledge built over a decade of doing it, are exactly why I'm asking to continue as ANC1E commissioner.

column12: While both market-rate and affordable housing are vital to a complete neighborhood ecosystem, they serve distinct functions driven by entirely different mechanisms.  Market-rate housing relies on private development and supply-demand cycles to house people at prevailing costs. It is essential because failing to build enough market-rate units only intensifies competition, bidding up prices on older housing stock and squeezing out middle-income households.  Affordable housing is deliberately structured through tools like Inclusionary Zoning, subsidies, or public intervention to decouple housing costs from speculative market pressures. It ensures that public servants, service workers, seniors, and healthcare professionals are not priced out of the communities they serve.  Ultimately, market-rate housing drives overall production and supply absorption, while affordable housing is an active equity tool that prevents displacement and keeps our neighborhoods economically diverse.

column12: Affordable housing carries an income restriction — a covenant, subsidy, or inclusionary set-aside tying rent to a share of area median income. Market-rate housing carries no such restriction. It’s not a difference in quality or in who deserves to live there, and "market-rate" does not inherently mean “expensive.” But market-rate rents are expensive here in DC, and that is a consequence of a choice we've made. When a region adds jobs and households faster than it adds homes, the existing stock gets auctioned off to whoever can bid highest. Scarcity doesn't ration housing by need; it rations by income. The result is that older buildings, which used to house teachers, service workers, and young families without any subsidy at all, get renovated and repriced — and the households they used to serve are pushed out or pushed further away. So the two categories are linked. Restricting supply doesn't preserve affordability; it destroys the unsubsidized affordability we already have and dumps the entire burden onto subsidy programs that can never be funded at the scale required. Every unit we don't build becomes a household competing for one that already exists. Dedicated affordable housing is essential — it's the only tool that reaches the lowest incomes, and I support expanding it. But it can't do the job alone. If we want market-rate housing to be affordable to anyone but the wealthiest, we have to build enough of it.

column36: I approach decision-making as a mix of active outreach, transparency, and honesty about uncertainty rather than assuming silence means consent or that the loudest voices in the room represent the whole SMD. First, I try to widen who I actually hear from, rather than relying only on those who show up to ANC meetings, which tend to skew toward retirees, homeowners, and people with fewer scheduling constraints. That means using tools like community surveys, as I did with the Pennsylvania Avenue/Minnesota Avenue intersection redesign, canvassing directly on specific issues, and using social media and listservs to reach residents who will never attend a meeting but will respond to a direct, low-effort ask. Second, when I do hear from constituents, I try to distinguish between a genuine cross-section of opinion and an organized or vocal minority. A dozen passionate emails on one side of an issue isn't the same as a representative sample, and I try to be honest with myself and with residents about which one I'm looking at before I treat it as a mandate. Third, on issues where I can't get meaningful direct input, because perhaps they're too technical, too fast-moving, or too under-the-radar for most residents to weigh in, I rely on established public policy principles, and my own professional background in advocacy and compliance work to make a judgment call, and I try to explain that reasoning publicly rather than hiding behind "constituent feedback" I don't actually have. Finally, I believe part of the job is proactively surfacing issues before they become emergencies, rather than only reacting to what constituents happen to bring to me. The snow removal and vacant property issues in 7B03 are good examples: most residents don't think to email their Commissioner about unplowed streets or a rotting rowhouse next door, but part of representing them well is noticing these problems myself, investigating, and acting without waiting for a critical mass of complaints. Ultimately, I try to make decisions I can defend publicly and explain clearly, not just decisions that reflect whoever emailed me last, because being a good representative means using your judgment responsibly when you don't and can't have a full picture of every constituent's view.

column38: A few additional notes to round out my answers above. On Q10, I checked all four combinations because I consider public ownership of the land and the housing itself to be the defining feature of social housing, not who performs construction or day-to-day management. As long as the District retains ownership and control of the underlying asset, it can guarantee the unit stays permanently off the speculative market and set the terms such as rent levels, tenant protections, and eligibility regardless of who was contracted to build or manage it. This mirrors systems like Vienna's Gemeindebau and Singapore's HDB, which routinely use private contractors while remaining unambiguously public housing. Contracting out can be a practical necessity given the District's limited in-house capacity, and I don't think that should disqualify a unit from being considered social housing as long as public ownership remains the anchor, though I'd support strong contractual and oversight requirements on any private management company to ensure accountability isn't lost in the handoff.  I answered "enough" on Q12 regarding historic districts, but I want to be clear about what that reflects. ANC 7B doesn't currently have any historic districts, so "enough" is accurate to my SMD today, but it also reflects my broader view. I don't support expanding historic district designations. There's a meaningful difference between a building or landmark having historic significance worth preserving, and designating entire zones or neighborhoods as historic, which can be used to broadly restrict housing development and density. I'd rather see preservation tools used narrowly, for individual structures that genuinely warrant it, than applied at the neighborhood scale. My answer to Q15 also doesn't fully capture my view on car ownership. The realistic number of vehicles a family needs varies depending on where in the District they live and what transit is available; a family in 7B03 is in a different position than one steps from a Metro station. Rather than assume a single "right" number citywide, I'd rather see the District focus on making zero or one vehicle a realistic choice everywhere, through better bus frequency, protected bike infrastructure, and safer pedestrian access. On Q27 and Q28, I selected the options indicating I would introduce a resolution in support of dedicated bus lanes and protected bike lanes, and want to be clear that isn't hypothetical, I've already written and passed resolutions on these issues. Looking ahead, two priorities for the next two years: working with DDOT and NPS to finally implement resolution 7B-23-05, which calls for pedestrian and cyclist improvements on 27th Street between Naylor Road and Texas Avenue and has passed but seen no real movement; and pushing for real action on the vacant and blighted houses in 7B03 I've raised repeatedly. I'm proud of the work I've done on these issues, and I look forward to continuing it if reelected.

column12: To me, affordable housing is housing that is realistically attainable for residents and does not leave them financially overburdened just to remain housed. It may be income-restricted or subsidized, but affordability should ultimately reflect what a household can reasonably afford. Market-rate housing, by contrast, is generally priced according to current market conditions without income restrictions or subsidies. That does not automatically mean it is unaffordable or expensive; affordability depends on a household's income. In Ward 7, I believe the distinction is especially important. We need quality housing at a range of price points while also protecting opportunities for longtime residents, seniors, working families, and first-time homebuyers to remain in and invest in their communities. I also believe vacant and blighted properties should be returned to productive use rather than allowed to sit deteriorating while residents continue to face housing challenges.

column14: A family-sized home provides enough rooms, living space, storage, and basic amenities for families to live comfortably. Generally, I think of this as homes with two or more bedrooms, with a meaningful supply of three- and four-bedroom homes for larger and multigenerational families. Family-sized housing should also be attainable at different income levels. A three-bedroom unit does little to address a family's housing needs if the family cannot realistically afford to live there. In Ward 7, I believe we should preserve and expand opportunities for families to put down roots, raise children, care for aging relatives, and remain in the community as their needs change. That means supporting a healthy mix of apartments, townhomes, and single-family homes, including accessible housing for families that include seniors or residents with disabilities. Ultimately, family-sized housing should be measured not just by bedroom count, but by whether a home is safe, functional, affordable, and appropriate for the people who will live there.

column23: I support adding housing and expanding housing choices throughout the District, but I do not believe a single housing type, such as six-unit apartment buildings, should automatically be permitted on every residential lot in every neighborhood. Land-use decisions should consider a neighborhood's existing character, available infrastructure, transit access, parking, environmental impacts, and the needs of current residents. In communities like mine in Ward 7, increased housing density should also be accompanied by equitable investment in grocery stores, restaurants, retail, transportation, and other neighborhood amenities. I support thoughtful growth, including rehabilitating vacant and blighted properties and creating appropriate opportunities for new and varied housing types. My “no” is not opposition to housing or apartments; it reflects my belief that responsible development should be community-informed and appropriate to the location rather than applied uniformly across every neighborhood in the District.

column26: I would be open to approximately 210 additional homes in my SMD or ANC, but I would not approach that goal by simply distributing additional density uniformly throughout established residential blocks. In ANC 7E and SMD 7E02, I believe new housing opportunities can begin by activating underutilized commercial parcels, vacant lots, infill opportunities, boarded-up apartment buildings, and vacant or blighted properties that can be responsibly rehabilitated and returned to productive use. Major corridors such as Pennsylvania Avenue SE and East Capitol Street may also provide opportunities for additional housing where existing and improved infrastructure can support growth. I am also open to thoughtfully planned missing-middle housing, such as accessory dwelling units, duplexes, and appropriate small multi-unit development. These options can provide additional housing choices and allow for gradual, contextual growth without applying the same density or housing type to every residential block. New housing should include a meaningful range of affordability levels, family-sized homes, and accessible housing. Equitable citywide housing goals also mean that every part of the District should contribute to meeting our housing needs rather than disproportionately concentrating affordable housing or new development in particular wards. In Ward 7, however, housing production must be accompanied by equitable neighborhood investment. Our community has limited access to full-service grocery stores, restaurants, retail, and Metrorail. Adding hundreds of residents without addressing the services and infrastructure that they—and current residents—need would not create a complete community. I support pairing new housing with improved transit frequency, streetscape and pedestrian improvements, infrastructure, and neighborhood-serving retail. As an ANC commissioner, I would advocate for thoughtful, community-informed development that addresses vacant and neglected properties, respects established residential areas, expands housing opportunities, and ensures that growth benefits longtime residents while welcoming new neighbors.

In my community in Ward 7, we do not have a Metrorail station within the neighborhood, and residents have limited nearby access to full-service grocery stores, restaurants, retail, and other everyday destinations. I am willing to walk, bike, and use Metrobus more often, and participating in the National Week Without Driving would also give me an opportunity to experience firsthand where our transportation network works and where gaps remain. Our long-term goal should be to make alternatives to driving so safe, reliable, convenient, and accessible that residents choose them—not simply to make driving more difficult for communities that do not yet have comparable transportation options or neighborhood amenities.

I feel the biggest issue in my neighborhood is the lack of equitable neighborhood investment and access to basic amenities and services. Residents of 7E02 should not have to routinely leave our community for things that residents in other parts of the District can access close to home. We have limited access to full-service grocery stores, restaurants, and neighborhood-serving retail, no Metrorail station within our neighborhood, and vacant or blighted properties that remain underutilized while our community needs both housing and economic investment. These issues are interconnected. When residents must drive outside the neighborhood for groceries, dining, shopping, and other everyday needs, transportation becomes an equity issue. Likewise, adding housing without bringing the services, infrastructure, and economic opportunities needed to support residents does not create a complete community. My position is that Ward 7 deserves thoughtful growth and the same quality of neighborhood investment, amenities, and opportunities available throughout the District

If elected, I would: If elected, I would focus on the issues within my authority while being transparent with residents about those that are not. When an issue falls outside the ANC's authority, my responsibility would not end there. I would identify the agency, elected official, developer, property owner, or other party responsible and work to connect residents with them while advocating for accountability and follow-through.  I would listen to residents and document our priorities so that I am advocating from a clear community mandate. I would work with fellow commissioners, the Ward 7 Council office, District agencies, developers, property owners, and community organizations to pursue neighborhood-serving retail, responsible development, improved transportation, and the productive reuse of vacant and blighted properties.  I would use the ANC's advisory role and “great weight,” introduce or support resolutions when appropriate, submit testimony and formal comments, and bring responsible parties to the table when community concerns require action.  Most importantly, I would keep 7E02 residents informed about what I can and cannot do as their commissioner, who is responsible for addressing an issue, what actions have been taken, and where matters stand. I cannot promise that every problem will be resolved, but I can promise accessibility, transparency, persistent follow-through, and accountability
column36: I believe good representation requires actively seeking community input rather than assuming that the residents who attend ANC meetings or contact me most frequently speak for everyone in 7E02. Traditional public engagement can have structural limitations: residents who have the time and flexibility to attend weeknight meetings or testify at hearings may not reflect the full diversity of a single-member district. Renters, homeowners, seniors, shift workers, transit-dependent residents, young families, people with disabilities, and others may experience the same issues but have fewer opportunities to participate.  Rather than expecting every constituent to come to me, I would meet residents where they are. I would use ANC meetings, neighborhood walks, community events, outdoor office hours, email, phone, social media, surveys, newsletters, and conversations with civic, faith-based, senior, tenant, homeowner, and other community groups. I would also look for opportunities to engage residents at transit stops and community gathering spaces and use accessible or multilingual materials when needed.  When making decisions, I would weigh community input alongside objective information, including relevant agency data, traffic and pedestrian safety information, housing needs, transit reliability, District policies, and the short- and long-term effects on 7E02. I would also consider residents who may be affected by a decision but are not represented in the room, including younger and future generations who will inherit the community we shape today.  There will be times when residents disagree. My responsibility is to listen respectfully, seek additional input when appropriate, evaluate the evidence and trade-offs, and make the decision I believe best serves 7E02 while considering our community's role within the broader District.  Most importantly, I will be transparent. Residents deserve to know what I support or oppose, why I reached a decision, what information I considered, and what trade-offs were involved—even when my decision differs from the position of the most vocal participants.  To me, representation means being accessible enough to listen, proactive enough to seek out unheard voices, responsible enough to do the homework, independent enough to make difficult decisions, and accountable enough to explain them.
column37: I believe I am the right person to serve 7E02 because service, accountability, and follow-through are values I have practiced throughout my life—not qualities I discovered because I decided to run for office. As a U.S. Army veteran and retired federal employee, I understand public service, responsibility, and the importance of working within systems while also knowing when to ask questions, elevate concerns, and persist until residents receive answers. Long before considering a run for ANC, I was advocating for issues affecting my neighborhood and Ward 7—contacting District agencies and elected officials, asking questions, following up when concerns went unanswered, and speaking up when I believed our community deserved better. I also understand the limits of an ANC commissioner's authority. I will address matters within my role and be transparent when something falls outside it. In those cases, I will identify who is responsible, connect residents to the appropriate resources, advocate on their behalf, and follow up. I am not running because I believe I have all the answers. I am running because I am willing to listen, learn, do the homework, communicate honestly, and consistently show up for my neighbors. 7E02 deserves representation that is accessible, responsive, transparent, and persistent. That is the standard of service I would bring to the position
column38: My positions are guided by a simple principle: equity should mean that every part of the District has access not only to housing, but also to the transportation, amenities, services, and economic investment necessary for a community to thrive. I support increasing our housing supply, expanding affordable and family-sized housing, rehabilitating vacant and blighted properties, and creating thoughtful opportunities for additional housing types. I also support the District's goal of ensuring affordable housing is distributed throughout every planning area. Ward 7 has long contributed significantly to the District's affordable housing supply, and I believe every part of the city should share that responsibility and opportunity. At the same time, housing production should not be considered in isolation. In 7E02, residents have limited access to full-service grocery stores, restaurants, neighborhood-serving retail, and Metrorail. Asking communities to accommodate additional density while basic amenities and infrastructure lag behind does not, by itself, create an equitable or complete community. The same principle informs my transportation positions. I support safe walking and biking infrastructure, improved and more reliable bus service, and transportation investments that give residents meaningful alternatives to driving. However, policies designed to discourage driving must recognize that residents do not begin with equal access to transit or nearby destinations. We should make alternatives to driving more practical and attractive, not disproportionately burden residents whose neighborhoods have fewer options. I also value the character and history of Ward 7's established communities. Our neighborhoods and their longstanding Black history deserve recognition and preservation, while still allowing responsible rehabilitation, appropriate development, and opportunities for new neighbors to call Ward 7 home. I am not opposed to growth or change. I support thoughtful, equitable growth that is informed by residents, supported by infrastructure, and accompanied by investment. My goal is a Ward 7 where longtime residents can remain and thrive, new residents are welcomed, and people do not have to leave their neighborhood to access the basic opportunities and amenities available elsewhere in Washington.

column12: I believe affordable housing and market-rate housing serve different but equally important purposes in a healthy community.  I know what it's like to reside in unhealthy conditions, work and save to change that.  Affordable housing is intended to ensure that lower- and moderate-income individuals and families are not priced out of the neighborhoods where they live and work. Its cost is generally tied to household income or established affordability standards rather than simply what the private market will bear.  Market-rate housing, by contrast, is generally priced according to supply, demand, location, and overall market conditions without an affordability requirement or subsidy.  I do not believe these two forms of housing should be viewed as being in competition with one another. Washington needs housing at different income levels. Responsible growth should provide opportunities for new residents while protecting longtime residents from displacement and respecting the character of established neighborhoods.  My goal is a diverse, mixed-income community where working families, seniors, young professionals, and people at different income levels have an opportunity to call the neighborhood home.

column14: To me, family-sized housing means housing that gives families enough space, stability, and affordability to put down roots and remain part of their community as their needs change.  It generally means homes with two, three, or more bedrooms, but bedroom count alone does not make housing family-friendly. Families also need adequate living and storage space, safe buildings, and reasonable access to transportation, schools, childcare, parks, recreation, groceries, and other everyday necessities.  In a growing neighborhood like Ivy City, I believe new residential development should include a meaningful number of units designed for families. If most new housing consists only of studios and one-bedroom apartments, it becomes difficult for households to remain in the neighborhood as their families grow.  Family-sized housing should also exist at different price points, including affordable and market-rate options. A strong neighborhood should provide opportunities for families of different incomes and at different stages of life.  Ultimately, family-sized housing means creating homes where people can establish roots, raise children, build relationships with their neighbors, and become long-term members of the community.

column23: I support building more housing in the District, including apartments, but I do not believe that every type of housing is appropriate on every block of every neighborhood.  Washington is a city of very different neighborhoods, each with its own character, infrastructure, transportation access, street configuration, historic resources, and existing housing patterns. A zoning policy that automatically allows six-unit apartment buildings everywhere does not adequately recognize those differences.  I support greater density and multifamily housing in appropriate locations, particularly along major corridors, near public transportation, and in areas where infrastructure can accommodate additional residents. I also support creating more affordable and family-sized housing.  At the same time, residents should have a meaningful voice when significant zoning changes are proposed for established residential neighborhoods. New development should consider parking, traffic, pedestrian safety, schools, utilities, public transportation, and the existing character of the surrounding community.  We can increase Washington's housing supply without adopting a one-size-fits-all approach. I favor thoughtful growth that creates more homes while respecting the characteristics and needs of individual neighborhoods.

Rather than dramatically increasing density on established residential blocks, I would prioritize underutilized commercial and industrial properties, vacant or redevelopment-ready parcels, and locations along major transportation corridors where additional density can be accommodated responsibly.  Ivy City has historically contained a mixture of residential, commercial and industrial uses. As some properties transition away from older industrial uses, we have an opportunity to consider mixed-use redevelopment that can provide new housing while also bringing neighborhood-serving retail, services and public improvements.  Any significant residential development should take infrastructure into consideration, including public transportation, parking, traffic, pedestrian safety, utilities, schools and other services. I would also want new development to include a meaningful mix of housing, including affordable and family-sized units, rather than concentrating exclusively on studios and small apartments.  I do not believe meeting a citywide housing target should mean simply assigning an arbitrary number of units to every neighborhood regardless of local conditions. However, I believe Ivy City can contribute to Washington's housing needs through thoughtful development in appropriate locations.  My goal would be to add housing while preserving Ivy City's identity, protecting existing residents and businesses, and ensuring that new development contributes positively to the community.

Public safety and quality of life are the biggest issues facing Ivy City. We need effective law enforcement, but enforcement alone will not solve every problem. We also need greater access to mental-health and substance-use professionals, stronger educational opportunities, and better coordination among District agencies.  One example is the alley adjacent to the shelter in Ivy City. Poor management of this area has contributed to persistent drug activity, violence, public health and sanitation concerns, and other dangerous behavior that affects shelter residents, neighborhood residents, employees, and businesses. We must address these conditions while treating people experiencing homelessness, addiction, or mental-health crises with dignity and connecting them with appropriate services.  Parking and transportation decisions are also significant quality-of-life concerns for residents and businesses. At the same time, I want Ivy City to have more positive community activities, including arts, music, cultural events, youth programs, and neighborhood festivals.  I believe public safety means creating a neighborhood that is safe, clean, welcoming, and active for everyone.

If elected, I would: If elected, I would use the ANC's influence and my relationships with District agencies to aggressively advocate for solutions while recognizing that an ANC commissioner cannot directly command MPD or other agencies.  I would document recurring problems, bring them formally before the ANC, request agency action and written follow-up, introduce or support ANC resolutions when appropriate, and maintain regular communication with MPD, DDOT, DPW, DBH, DHS and other agencies responsible for the issues affecting Ivy City.  For the shelter and surrounding area, I would push for coordinated action involving law enforcement, homeless-services providers, mental-health and substance-use professionals, sanitation services, shelter management, residents, and businesses. My goal would be both accountability and getting people who need help connected with appropriate services.  I would also advocate for practical solutions to parking and pedestrian-safety problems and work to bring more arts, educational programs, community events, and family-friendly activities to Ivy City.  Most importantly, I would follow up. Referring a constituent to an agency is not enough. I would track problems, communicate progress publicly, and continue pressing for action until residents receive an answer.
column36: An ANC commissioner represents the entire community, not simply the residents who attend meetings or speak the loudest. If elected, I will make a deliberate effort to hear from people throughout my district before making important decisions.  I believe representation requires going to the community rather than expecting the community to always come to you. I will regularly walk the neighborhood, speak directly with residents and local businesses, attend community events, and use meetings, social media, email, surveys, and direct outreach to seek input. I will make a particular effort to reach people who may never attend an ANC meeting.  When an important issue arises, I will seek information from multiple sources. I will listen to those who support a proposal and those who oppose it, review the facts, consult District agencies and subject-matter experts when appropriate, and consider both the immediate and long-term consequences for Ivy City.  I will not assume that the loudest voices necessarily represent the majority. At the same time, leadership sometimes requires making a difficult decision after listening to everyone and carefully examining the facts.  Transparency will be fundamental to how I serve. Residents should know what issues are before the ANC, what position I take, why I take it, and what actions I am pursuing on their behalf.  My commitment is simple: **Your voice will always be heard.** That does not mean everyone will always agree with every decision I make. It means every constituent will be treated with respect, given an opportunity to be heard, and represented fairly—whether they voted for me or not.
column37: I believe I am the right person to serve as ANC Commissioner because Ivy City is not simply where I am running for office—it is my home and a community I have been deeply involved with for years.  I've lived in Ivy City since 2016 and worked in the neighborhood for more than a decade. As a Director of Operations, I've experienced solving problems, managing people and budgets, working with government agencies, and bringing people with different interests together.  My commitment to public safety is demonstrated through years of cooperation with Ward 5 MPD, including providing video analysis and digital evidence that has assisted investigations. In 2025, MPD recognized me as a Ward 5 Outstanding Citizen for those efforts.  My connection to Ward 5 also goes back generations. My ancestors settled here, my father grew up in Ward 5, and members of my family are buried at Mount Olivet Cemetery in Ivy City. Serving this community is personal to me.  Most importantly, I am accessible. I walk these streets, speak with residents and businesses, see our challenges firsthand, and believe constituent concerns deserve follow-through, not just promises.  I will bring experience, energy, transparency, accountability, and a unique, left-handed, right brain burst of creativity bundled in an ANC. Whether someone agrees with me or not, **their voice will always be heard.**
column38: My answers reflect a belief that Washington can grow without losing sight of the people and neighborhoods that make the city successful. I support creating more housing, including affordable and family-sized housing, and I welcome responsible development. At the same time, I do not believe every housing or land-use policy should be applied identically to every neighborhood.  Ivy City has a unique mixture of residential, commercial and industrial uses. New development can bring housing, jobs, neighborhood-serving businesses and investment, but residents and existing businesses should have a meaningful voice in how that growth occurs. I support greater density where appropriate while also respecting neighborhood character, infrastructure limitations and historic resources.  My transportation positions follow a similar principle of balance. I strongly support reliable public transportation, safer streets, walking and bicycle infrastructure. However, I do not believe improving one form of transportation should automatically require making another form unnecessarily difficult. Residents, seniors, families, employees and businesses have different transportation needs. In Ivy City, parking is already a significant concern, and eliminating additional parking without considering the consequences can create new problems rather than solve existing ones.  I believe government should provide people with better transportation choices rather than dictate one choice for everyone.  As an ANC Commissioner, I would approach housing, transportation and land-use decisions individually, listen to residents and businesses, examine the facts, and work toward practical compromises. I am pro-growth, but I believe growth should be responsible, inclusive and beneficial to the community that is being asked to accommodate it.  My goal is an Ivy City that welcomes new neighbors and investment while remaining a place where existing residents, families and businesses can continue to thrive.

column12: My point of view is that market-rate housing is priced at what the market will bear. It is an important component in increasing the city’s tax base and in creating an affordable city. For example, when Austin added roughly 120,000 homes over about ten years, the rents in Class C buildings fell 11.4% and Class A rents fell 2.6%. In contrast, affordable housing is priced below that through subsidy, regulation, or building age. There are a variety of policy handles to create affordability and they need to be used correctly. Inclusionary zoning can reach roughly 50–80% of AMI before new housing development does not pencil out and nothing gets built. Deeply affordable units – which are also needed – require direct public investment rather than a requirement added onto private development. In my opinion, this is why the Office of Planning correctly proposed exempting projects with a one-third deep-affordability set-aside from design review in ZC 25-13.

If elected, I would: A commissioner's formal authority is advisory, but it’s real and can be effective. In ZC 25-13, I worked with colleagues to shape the ANC's resolution and filed my own comment with the Zoning Commission arguing that design-review criteria should be objective and measurable, so large corridor projects aren't tied up for years by standards no architect can design to. I'd apply the same approach to gentle density: bring my colleagues along where I can, and make the record myself where I can't.
column36: I hear from constituents through ANC meetings, neighborhood events, and organizations like the Cleveland Park Community Association. I have found being active and introducing resolutions helps get people involved and wanting to share their opinions.  But I try to weigh this input carefully. The people who come to a Tuesday evening ANC meeting are not a random sample of my 2,000 constituents. They skew toward homeowners, longer-tenured residents, and people with the time and flexibility to attend. Renters, younger residents, people working evening shifts, and people with small children are often underrepresented but they also have a lot at stake. Also not present are the future residents who could live here if there was more housing. So I treat what I hear as important evidence, not as a vote count. Where the input I receive conflicts with what I think serves the ANC and the district as a whole, I say so and explain why. On ZC 25-13, several of the loudest voices wanted more discretionary design review. I concluded that vague, unmeasurable review criteria would delay or block housing development on Wisconsin Avenue and raise costs for people who aren't at our meetings — including people who don't live here yet because they can't afford to – and the comments I filed individually said that. I also try to weigh input I can check against evidence — Office of Planning capacity analysis, zoning case records, election data — rather than relying only on impressions from the people who reach me.
column37: I served a previous term as commissioner so I think there is a track record I can point to of doing the homework, making arguments on the merits, listening to my colleagues respectfully and bringing them along where possible, being willing to say what I think, and introducing substantive resolutions. I'd rather be persuasive than loud. For example, on ZC 25-13, I read the Office of Planning's supplemental report closely enough to notice that its exemption for deeply affordable projects conceded the argument about discretionary review's cost — and I used that to make the case to my colleagues. I proposed amendments to our resolution rather than introducing a competing one, worked through several drafts with the commissioner who authored it, and we ended up passing something 5-0 that asked the Zoning Commission for clear standards and a defined timetable. Where the ANC chose not to take a substantive position, I filed my own comment so the argument was in the record. I think this is what being an effect ANC Commissioner requires.
column38: I would like to go into more detail on a couple of questions. Re the National Week Without Driving. I declined not because I disagree with the goal but because I try not to commit to things I'm not confident I'll do. We have two young children and most weeks a car trip isn't optional. What I will commit to is the policy work, which I think matters more: I'd introduce resolutions supporting dedicated bus lanes, protected bike lanes, and road pricing, and shifting more of my own grocery trips to foot. Re the affordable housing question. I checked rent control because it does produce below market rents, but I'd distinguish it from the other mechanisms listed because it isn’t be targeted by need. It may also not be that effective at producing below market rents: the Office of Revenue Analysis found rent control only delivers about a 4.6% discount against comparable Class B market-rate stock. I'd rather deliver deep affordability through direct public investment in order to reach the households that need it.

column12: In theory, housing could be both market-rate and affordable. But when housing is market-rate, it’s functioning primarily as a commodity, which I consider unethical and unlikely to produce sufficient and timely affordability. Interventions like rent control, housing vouchers, or the Tenant Opportunity to Purchase Act (TOPA) help blunt market-rate impacts, but are constantly eroded by market pressures and landlord lobbying. I believe long-lasting affordability and quality will only come from treating housing as a public good (like libraries or air quality) rather than as a commodity. That would mean publicly directed and/or financed construction, limiting the ability to use residences as investment vehicles, tenant control of property management, and more. In the meantime, I support building as much housing as possible under the Inclusionary Zoning (IZ) Affordable Housing Program, since that’s the best tool on the books that I know of. I’m eager to negotiate in Board of Zoning Adjustment (BZA) cases for voluntary inclusionary units and/or for additional units on new developments in order to trigger the IZ thresholds.

I think “family-sized housing” ought to include configurations that support those dynamics as well. And that goes beyond bedrooms; it can mean multiple kitchens, or common space shared among dormitory units, or accessory dwelling units. I also want us to think outside the lot; family housing includes good parks, schools, and other amenities nearby, because it truly does take a village and we should design our environments accordingly. So, overall, I think family-sized housing should mean housing that fits people’s varied needs, rather than housing that forces people to contort or compress their lives.

My target issue is the stiflingly high rent, both commercial and residential, that keeps our storefronts empty and our residents over-burdened. For example, a current proposal in 4C seeks to redevelop two properties on Upshur St and charge $45/sqft for the new commercial space. I think this high rent will limit the possible businesses, especially small, new, and local businesses, at that location in a way that is detrimental to the neighborhood.  I want rents to come down dramatically.

If elected, I would: I would continue to use every opportunity to advocate for density, Inclusionary Zoning (IZ), and other mechanisms to keep rents low. This would include negotiations in Board of Zoning Adjustment (BZA) and Alcoholic Beverage and Cannabis Administration (ABCA) cases, ANC resolutions, and testimony to the DC Council. In my Upshur St example above, so long as concerns around trash, etc were addressed, I would support additional residences on upper floors in order to bring down the rent per unit. More generally, I support almost all of the DC YIMBY platform, particularly on the issues of setbacks, floor area ratio, car parking, and lot coverage. column36: First, I want my constituents to know that outreach and communication is a top priority for me in the near future. As a first-term Commissioner taking on the duties of Chair for an ANC that was in financial reporting non-compliance, I’ve focused heavily on internal concerns and on educating myself as to the powers and duties of a Commissioner. Now, I am turning to external concerns, like avenues of communication. I hope that consistent communication from me will prompt more people to share their thoughts and sentiments. I will provide this communication through our website, an email newsletter, and in-person community engagement. When it comes time to make decisions, I will draw upon these interactions as background and I will solicit opinions directly when I can. But as the question notes, that won’t be perfect. I will draw upon expertise of District agencies, other Commissioners, and DC-focused research; I will consult with trusted members of my social circle who are active and informed on areas like climate, urbanism, and race; I will continue reading books on political theory, policy, and history (I just finished The Rise and Decline of Patriarchal Systems by Nancy Folbre); and, ultimately, I will rely on my sense of ethics to find outcomes that are equitable, just, and supportive of an accessible, inclusive, sustainable DC.
column37: I don’t know if I’m the best person to be Commissioner. But last election, as in so many SMDs, I was the only one who volunteered. My reason for volunteering again is the same: I want to serve my neighborhood and my city. Over my first term, I’ve been energized by the chance to help folks. In an atomized and alienated society like ours, I see the hyperlocal structure of ANCs as a seed for community restoration. In my 11 years of political organizing, the most effective leaders bring a combination of bureaucratic skill and social cohesion. I’ve always had an analytical mind, which has served me well in my physics major, software engineering career, and (most importantly) board game night. I think it has aided me greatly in my research and application of ANC duties, zoning regulations, governmental structures, and policy matters. But I left software because I’m disgusted by the industry’s ethics. Flock cameras, generative AI, “educational” tech, pervasive social media, invasive advertising, and Palantir mercenaries are driving us into a societal pit of despair. With 4C back in financial compliance and with a firm sense of the ANC role, I want to move beyond the bureaucratic and into the community. I’ll draw upon the same skills I used as a leader of Sunrise Movement DC, where I applied consensus-based decision making, hosted social events, fostered relationships with other organizations, and met people with warmth and an open mind. Let’s build a community, not just houses.

column38: On Question #29 on congestion pricing, I'm more undecided with a tinge of cautious support, so I took the least committed "yes" answer on that one. I fully accept that congestion pricing has been great for New York City, and I agree with the theory behind congestion pricing. However, the 2021 DC study was outdated by the time Mayor Bowser released it 5 years later. I think a new study is warranted that can take into account post-COVID traffic and commuting patterns and also look to NYC's experience, and I'm not saying "a new study is needed" in a NIMBY-like way just to delay, delay, delay. Even if economically valid, I'm also very cautious about moving forward with congestion pricing due to Congressional interference. Politically, it would require buy-in from the Representatives and Senators of our neighbors in Virginia and Maryland. Many Congresspeople would love to use their unethical power to overturn our local laws too, so congestion pricing would have to be passed at a favorable time and implemented rapidly. Overall, I'm not as anti-car as many pro-housing urbanists are though. I'm a car owner. I love having my car. I'm not going to give it up. I travel to the outer suburbs a few times a month on average. What takes me an hour in my car would take 2 transfers and 2 hours by public transportation or $60 by rideshare each way. I think residents should be able to have cars if they want them. However, I think we should make DC a city where cars aren't as necessary so that most people can live comfortably without them. I support dedicated bus lanes and protected bike lanes even though I don't often ride the bus and don't own a bike. I don't think it's a contradiction to support bike-friendly and public transportation-friendly policies while also continuing to make owning and using a car an option that one can choose, even if it's a bit more of a hassle or having to pay a bit of a premium. Along those same lines, I'm in favor of robotaxis. There are certainly questions on how to best implement them, but I'd rather they be permitted sooner rather than later. On Question #5, I said my ANC has "enough homes". As elaborated in some of my other answers, ANC 1A is the densest in DC. If anybody wants to develop a property to make it denser, I'll of course be supportive, but DC's focus should be on making most other neighborhoods denser. Lastly, on Question #12 on historic districts, ANC 1A only slightly overlaps with the Meridian Hill Historic District. It affects only about 3.5 blocks in ANC 1A, some of which are owned by embassies, so it's not a significant issue in this ANC. I would probably be supportive of at least reducing the part labeled "historic" in ANC 1A though.
