As I talk to my neighbors it is clear that the biggest issues in our neighborhood are public safety, general trash and cleanliness of our alleys and streets, and receiving equitable treatment and responsiveness from city agencies like DPW, DOB, and DGS. In 2026 alone, there have been multiple fatal shootings in our neighborhood involving teenagers. Our neighborhood is a hotspot for illegal dumping and neighbors often reach out to me about DPW missing their entire alley’s trash during collection days. When neighbors reach out to their city agencies, we deserve to be heard and responded to - just as much as every other ward in D.C.

If elected, I would: Since I’ve been serving as my neighborhood’s Commissioner, I’ve made it my number one priority to build strong relationships with district agencies and Councilmember Felder’s Office to bring long-over due attention to Rosedale. I’ve organized multiple community cleanups alongside Councilmember Felder and DPW, I’ve worked with district agencies to lead a Public Safety Walk throughout our SMD, and I’ve helped advocate for new pilot programs, like the Roving Clean Team, which gives Rosedale dedicated attention from street sweepers. We’ve worked together to address multiple scofflaw vehicles, removing dangerous and abandoned vehicles from the streets. And we’ve worked with DOB to enforce that property owners do their part in securing abandoned properties that make it a safe haven for illegal activity.  As Commissioner, I will continue to bridge the gap between residents and their government, while consistently advocating for our neighborhood’s fair share of attention and resources from the District. I won’t stop until these needs are met.
column36: I’m not sure I accept the notion that our representative can’t connect with all residents in an SMD. I am proactively engaging with neighbors on every block - especially those who are leaders and advocates with a goal to improve our district. To me, everyone in Rosedale is advocating for cleaner streets, alleys, equitable city services, safety, better housing policy, and overall improved quality of life. I have yet to meet a neighbor who opposes those values, and I lead every discussion or position I have with that starting point. While some issues like bike lanes or parking become more debated topics, I always intend to find common ground solutions that meet the needs of everyone, not just those that are the loudest. My goal will always be to make sound decisions that echo the voices of the neighbors I represent.
column37: Rosedale is my home. The people who share this home with me have become more than just neighbors, they have become my community - even like family to me. When I purchased my home in this neighborhood nearly 4 years ago, I quickly recognized the almost-intentional lack of dedicated resources, services, and care for our neighborhood from District agencies. When I’d pick up litter along my street, I’d hear long-time neighbors say “good luck, the city will never help us.” And often they were right, we were missing leadership to advocate for these issues on our behalf.  Since becoming Commissioner in January of 2026, our neighborhood has made so much progress in addressing chronic issues related to trash collection, alley conditions, traffic safety, abandoned vehicles and homes - all symptoms of an unhealthy neighborhood. We still have a lot of work to do, especially in the scope of public safety, but I believe the investments I’ve made with Councilmember Felder and agency leaders at DPW, DOB, and DGS are the unlock to finding real solutions that better the lives of every Rosedale resident in SMD 7D06.
column38: I think often our conversation on housing, transportation, and land use ignores incorporating the experiences and points of view of the residents who actually live in the SMD being discussed. A desirable community is one where people can comfortably live, feel safe in their homes, and afford to stay long-term to build stability for themselves.  On housing, I do believe we should build more if we want to be a neighborhood where people of all income levels, life stages, and family sizes can afford to live. It’s how we create healthy neighborhoods. That means it is critical to build both affordable and market-rate homes. At the same time, I don't think responsible growth means dismissing concerns of current residents and home-owners who have the best pulse check on their neighborhood. We shouldn’t ignore their concerns for the sake of anyone’s unchecked bias for development. Good planning should take seriously our neighbor’s questions about public safety, traffic, infrastructure, neighborhood character, tree canopies and green space, construction impacts, and the cumulative effect of development on a block or neighborhood. Residents should have a meaningful voice, and that process should be about improving proposals rather than simply deciding whether change happens at all. On transportation, I come at this from a somewhat different perspective because I don't own a car. I value having safe, convenient alternatives to driving, and I want to see continued investment in transit, sidewalks, crosswalks, and safer streets. But I don't think the people who drive should be treated as the problem. Many neighbors depend on cars for work, caregiving, disability, errands, or other parts of their lives. A good transportation policy should give people more choices without making everyday life harder for those who need or choose to drive. More broadly, I want to approach these issues with curiosity rather than a predetermined ideological answer. The best outcome won't always be the one that most neatly fits into a particular policy category. As an ANC commissioner, I want to understand the evidence, listen to residents with different experiences, and weigh neighborhood impacts alongside the larger need for safety and growth in our neighborhood. For me, a win is when a neighborhood can keep existing residents in place, change and grow in a well thought out and careful way, and can welcome new residents without making current residents feel like their concerns no longer matter. I think we can do both and I approach the ANC with that balance in mind.

In my opinion, the biggest issue in our neighborhood is pedestrian safety. North Capitol Street is functionally a highway that cuts through the middle of a residential neighborhood. The road encourages dangerous, high-speed driving, and the sidewalks and pedestrian infrastructure are terrible. First Street NW is better, but by no means ideal—drivers routinely ignore stop signs, and there is minimal traffic calming infrastructure. The result is an environment that is hostile to pedestrians and the neighborhood, and that serves no one except for out-of-state drivers speeding through our community.

If elected, I would: I have passed resolutions and advocated with the DC government for several changes, and will continue to do so if reelected. Those include permanent traffic calming infrastructure on First ST NW, including speed bumps, raised crosswalks, stop-sign cameras, and permanent sidewalk bump-outs; and a full overhaul of North Capitol St NW, including sidewalk expansions, protected bus lanes, increased mixed-use zoning, and (once federal funding is once again a realistic possibility) a deck-over or full “community boulevard” conversion.
column36: Resident input is invaluable for knowing where safety improvements are most needed, and I often seek (and will continue to seek) resident input to know where to target my advocacy for pedestrian safety improvements. But when it comes to issues like increasing density, expanding transit access, or permitting businesses to operate, I think Commissioners often hear from a very small group of residents who are opposed to improvements that would benefit the community as a whole. If I believe a zoning or transit change would benefit the community and I hear opposition from a small group of opponents, I will still support the change. However, if I were to hear widespread opposition from a very large cross-section of the community, then I would more seriously reconsider my support for the proposal.
column37: I am a passionate advocate for pedestrian safety, transit access, and economic opportunity. Although I have only been a commissioner for a few months (following a special election), I have relentlessly advocated for pedestrian safety improvements on First Street and North Capitol Street and for WMATA to acknowledge and correct its failure to provide reliable bus service in Bloomingdale. I also understand how deeply unaffordable our city has become—in my day job, I am a union lawyer, and I know that working people are being increasingly priced out of DC. As a lawyer, I fight to make sure they are paid fairly for their labor. And as a Commissioner, I fight (and will continue to fight) to make sure our city builds enough housing to ensure that working people are not forced to spend most of that fair pay just to afford a place to live.

My SMD is fortunate to be in a relatively strong position overall, but one recurring issue is that many streets don't feel safe, particularly if you're not in a car. I support expanding bike lanes throughout the ANC, particularly on corridors where residents already report near-misses or avoid biking altogether. I think well-implemented bike lanes not only add space for cyclists but also slow down traffic, making streets safer for everyone. I do also think, though, that it has to be done thoughtfully: in the right locations and in ways that don't cut off access for drivers, delivery vehicles, or residents who depend on cars.

If elected, I would: I'd work to establish a strong, consistent line of communication with fellow 4C02 residents. A key part of the job is hearing the most pressing concerns and using the authority of the office to elevate them — I'd like to start a monthly newsletter, and maybe even hold "office hours" at local businesses for residents who'd like to meet face-to-face. Commissioners don't control city agencies or set citywide policy, but we have real leverage through formal input and by virtue of just being a visible elected official. My biggest overarching goal would be to use that position to make sure residents' concerns are actually heard by the people who can act on them.

Lastly, neighborhood-level systems for disseminating and collecting information already exist — listservs, group chats, and so on — and as a commissioner I'd want to plug into those to aid the flow of information. I believe this is directly connected to the continued concentration of poverty in Ward 7. Decisions by the Council and mayoral administrations have allowed a disproportionate amount of deeply affordable housing to be concentrated east of the river without enough mixed-income development, jobs, retail, and amenities to support these communities. I would also push for balanced development that brings a mix of affordable, market-rate, family-sized, and homeownership opportunities. The biggest issue in my neighborhood is ensuring that every resident can safely and fully access the public resources our city provides. My SMD includes the Petworth and Upshur recreation centers, McFarland, Roosevelt, Dorothy Height, and Powell schools, the Petworth Library, and the Upshur Street commercial corridor. Because of this, the needs throughout my SMD are varied, but all tether to the fact that these spaces should be community anchors—safe, welcoming, well-maintained, and accessible to residents of every age, income, background, and ability. Access means more than having a facility nearby; it means that the space is functioning, residents know what is available, programs reflect community needs, and safety concerns do not prevent people from using it.

If elected, I would: I would continue serving as a connector, advocate, and accountability partner between residents and District agencies. I would proactively seek input from people who may not regularly attend ANC meetings, identify barriers to accessing neighborhood facilities and services, and help residents navigate the agencies responsible for addressing them. I would use ANC resolutions, budget testimony, agency relationships, public meetings, and persistent follow-up to advocate for safe facilities, timely repairs, inclusive programming, accessible information, and responsible investment in our neighborhood. Because commissioners do not directly operate schools, libraries, recreation centers, or commercial corridors, I would be honest about the limits of the role while using its visibility and convening power to bring residents, agencies, schools, businesses, and community organizations together around practical solutions.
column36: I do not assume that the people who attend an ANC meeting or email me most frequently necessarily represent the full community. When an issue has broad implications, I try to create accessible ways for more residents to weigh in. For example, I collected more than 500 survey responses to inform a resolution I introduced and passed in support of funding for PKEEP. I also seek perspectives less formally through conversations with neighbors, parents, local organizations, businesses, and people using our public spaces.  I approach decisions by listening, educating myself about the issue, and trying not to enter with a predetermined answer. I consider resident input alongside available data, similar experiences and issues in other ANCs, agency expertise, and the broader impact on the District. Ultimately, I see my role as making informed decisions in the public interest, not tallying the loudest opinions or leaning on my perspective alone. I will explain how I reached a decision, be transparent about the factors I considered, and remain open to new information.
column37: I am the right person to continue serving 4C01 because I combine a deep personal investment in this neighborhood with a practical understanding of how to turn community concerns into action. That gives me direct knowledge of many of the systems I am working to improve—but I also know my experience is only one perspective. I have a responsibility to seek out and understand residents whose circumstances and relationships with the city differ from mine.  During my first term, I have built relationships with residents, schools, businesses, community organizations, fellow commissioners, and District agencies. I have learned when an issue calls for a formal resolution, when residents need a convener, and when progress depends on persistent behind-the-scenes follow-up.  I am responsive, curious, and willing to do the often unglamorous work of navigating city systems until residents get an answer. I would bring the knowledge and relationships I developed during my first term—along with the same openness, persistence, and commitment to making 4C01 work for everyone—to a second term.

column38: Yes. I believe our city should have a debate about using tax policy, in addition to zoning policy, to spur housing creation. Specifically, I support exploring a land value tax (LVT) or a split-rate tax. The idea is to tax property based on the highest and best use of the land, rather than what is built on it. For example, if an investor owns a parking lot on land zoned for high-density residential, they should be taxed as if they had built a high-density apartment building. column12: I see affordable housing and market-rate housing as different primarily in how the price is determined and whether there are affordability restrictions. In the United States, the Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD) defines affordable housing as housing on which the occupant is paying no more than 30 percent of gross income for housing costs, including utilities. The term is also often used as shorthand for income-restricted affordable housing for low- and moderate-income households.  Market-rate housing is generally not income-restricted or subsidized, and its price is determined by the housing market. I do not think “affordable” simply means “cheap,” or that market-rate necessarily means “expensive.” A market-rate home can be affordable to a particular household depending on that household’s income, while an income-restricted unit can still be unaffordable to some households.  I think we need more housing across the spectrum, including both income-restricted affordable housing and market-rate housing. The proposed RFK development, which would add substantial new housing including affordable housing, is an important opportunity for the District and for Ward 7. Expanding our housing supply, while ensuring that new development includes meaningful affordable housing, is important to me.

I would help residents push for the things that would actually benefit our neighborhood, especially better transit access, and I would speak up for those priorities myself. column36: I don't think an ANC commissioner can assume that the people who email them or show up at meetings represent all 2,000 constituents. I want to make a real effort to hear from people who don't normally participate in ANC meetings or reach out to their commissioner.  I am already working on building those connections. I attend River Terrace Community Organization (RTCO) meetings, send a neighborhood newsletter that reaches more than 300 residents, and participate in two neighborhood group chats - a general neighborhood chat and a gardening group. I also want to do more to get information and opportunities for community input posted through RTCO's Facebook page and other neighborhood channels.  For bigger issues, I want to bring the issue to residents rather than waiting for people to find me. For example, when the possibility of the National Guard coming to our neighborhood came up, I discussed it with residents at a meeting and also asked for feedback by email. I listened to the feedback I received and opposed it.  I also think an ANC commissioner has to consider the people who aren't directly involved in a particular dispute. If there is a dispute about parking, for example, I want to consider not just the needs of people who park on the street, but also the needs of bus riders, pedestrians, cyclists, and people with mobility needs. If there is a question about new development, I want to consider both the concerns of current residents and the needs of people who need or want to live in the neighborhood. If there is a traffic issue, I want to think about drivers as well as people walking, biking, and taking transit.  I don't think my job is simply to count emails and follow whichever side sends the most. I would consider the range of feedback I receive, the people who may not be participating, the facts and potential impacts of an issue, and my own judgment about what is best for the neighborhood. I would also try to be transparent about how I reached a decision especially when there is disagreement.  My goal is to make it easier for residents to know what is happening, make their voices heard, and understand how decisions are being made. I don't expect to hear from every resident, but I do want to make sure that the people I hear from are not the only people I'm representing.

column37: I believe I am the right person to serve as an ANC commissioner because I have a genuine commitment to serving my community and making sure residents have a voice in decisions that affect their everyday lives. I understand that being an ANC commissioner is not about having all the answers. It is about being accessible, willing to learn, willing to listen, and willing to advocate for the people you represent. I would bring that approach to the position.  I care deeply about issues that affect families, seniors, young people, renters, homeowners, and residents who may not always feel heard by government. I believe our community deserves someone who will communicate openly, work with different perspectives, and make decisions based on what is best for the entire SMD not just a particular group.  My leadership is also grounded in service and faith. I believe the work I do is bigger than me, and that my ability to serve others is a responsibility and an opportunity. If elected, I would bring that same spirit of service, accountability, and community advocacy to the ANC. column38: I want GGWash to know that my positions on housing, transportation, and land use are rooted in one basic belief: our communities should work for the people who live in them. I believe we can add housing without losing the character and history that make our neighborhoods special. We should also make it easier for residents to get around without having to depend on a car by investing in reliable public transportation, safe sidewalks, crosswalks, and other transportation options. column12: As an ANC 1E02 commissioner, I view affordable housing and market-rate housing as complementary parts of a healthy and inclusive neighborhood. Affordable housing is housing that is accessible to households with lower or moderate incomes, often through income-based requirements, public financing, or other affordability mechanisms. Market-rate housing, by contrast, is generally priced according to local market conditions, without income restrictions. The distinction is especially important in a neighborhood like ours, where rising housing costs can make it difficult for longtime residents, working families, seniors, and younger residents to remain in the community. While market-rate development can increase the overall housing supply and bring investment to the neighborhood, it does not necessarily create housing that is affordable to residents at every income level. I believe housing policy should support a range of housing types and price points while preserving the diversity and stability of our community. Increasing the supply of affordable housing alongside responsible market-rate development can help ensure that neighborhood growth benefits both current residents and future residents, rather than contributing to displacement or making the community accessible only to higher-income households.

Family-sized housing should also be genuinely attainable for working families—not limited to large units that are priced beyond the reach of most residents. In ANC 1E02, I believe we should encourage a range of housing options that allow families to remain in the neighborhood as they grow, while also supporting seniors, caregivers, and multigenerational households. A diverse housing stock strengthens a community. Families should have the opportunity to put down roots, children should be able to grow up near friends and schools, and residents should not have to leave the neighborhood simply because their household has grown. To me, creating and preserving family-sized housing is therefore both a housing issue and a community-stability issue.

One of the biggest issues facing our neighborhood is rising housing costs and the risk of displacement. As prices increase, longtime residents, working families, seniors, and younger people may struggle to stay. At the same time, we need more housing to meet demand and ease pressure on supply.  My position is that ANC 1E02 should support responsible housing growth while prioritizing affordability, family-sized housing, and neighborhood stability. Development and affordability should go together. We can welcome new homes while advocating for affordable units, preserving existing affordable housing, and supporting housing for a range of households.

If elected, I would: An ANC cannot set rents or directly control most housing policy, but commissioners can advocate and convene. If elected, I would engage residents early, communicate clearly about developments, and use the ANC to push for affordability, family-sized units, tenant protections, and community benefits.  I would also work with residents, housing groups, developers, and District agencies to support both new housing and preservation. Most importantly, I would ensure community concerns are consistently raised with decision-makers. My goal is to use the ANC’s voice to help shape growth so more residents can afford to stay in our neighborhood.
column36: I approach decision-making as an ANC commissioner by recognizing that I will never hear from every constituent directly, and that the voices I do hear may not reflect the full diversity of the neighborhood. Because of that, I would treat constituent input as one important source of information, not the only one.  To make balanced decisions, I would actively seek out a wide range of perspectives through office hours, community meetings, walking the neighborhood, surveys, and outreach to groups that are often less heard, including renters, seniors, young people, and non-English-speaking residents. I would also rely on data from District agencies, planning documents, and housing and demographic trends to understand the broader impact of issues affecting the community. My goal would be to combine lived experience with evidence, and to be transparent about how I reach conclusions.  I also recognize that ANC commissioners serve in an advisory role, which means part of my responsibility is to weigh competing interests and think about long-term neighborhood outcomes, not just immediate preferences. I would aim to make decisions that are fair, consistent, and grounded in equity, especially when different groups in the community have different needs or priorities.  Housing is a clear example of this. Rising housing costs and the risk of displacement affect many residents, but I would not assume there is a single community position on how to respond. Instead, I would listen to tenants concerned about affordability, homeowners concerned about neighborhood change, housing advocates focused on supply, and developers working within zoning constraints. I would then evaluate proposals based on how well they balance affordability, stability, and responsible growth.  In practice, I would use the ANC’s role to elevate community concerns to District agencies, encourage early and transparent engagement on development projects, and advocate for outcomes that expand housing options while protecting long-term residents. My decisions would be guided by a commitment to represent the whole community as fairly as possible, even when not every voice can be heard equally or agree.
column37: I believe I am the right person to serve as an ANC commissioner because I would bring a thoughtful, inclusive, and practical approach to representing my SMD. I understand that the role is not simply to represent the loudest voices, but to listen to residents with different experiences and priorities and work toward solutions that serve the broader community.  I would make myself accessible through community meetings, office hours, neighborhood walks, and direct outreach, while making a deliberate effort to hear from renters, homeowners, seniors, families, young people, and residents who may not typically participate in ANC meetings.  I also believe good representation requires more than listening. I would review the facts, understand District policies and data, seek out different perspectives, and be transparent about how I reach decisions. On issues such as housing, development, transportation, public safety, and neighborhood services, I would balance immediate concerns with the long-term interests of the community.  I recognize the ANC's authority is limited, but I believe commissioners can be effective advocates. I would elevate constituent concerns to the appropriate agencies, engage early on important proposals, build constructive relationships, and follow through.  Most importantly, I would work to represent the entire SMD fairly and consistently. My goal is to be accessible, prepared, respectful, and accountable to the community I serve.
column38: I would like GGWash to understand that my positions on housing, affordable housing, transportation, and land use are fundamentally connected. I believe ANC 1E02 should be a neighborhood where people at different income levels and stages of life can afford to live, where families can find appropriately sized homes, and where residents can access jobs, schools, businesses, parks, and services without being dependent on a car. I support adding housing, particularly along major corridors such as Georgia Avenue and on vacant or underutilized commercial properties, surface parking lots, and other sites where additional density can be accommodated responsibly. I believe increasing the housing supply is important, but I do not view housing as simply a numbers exercise. New development should include affordable and family-sized housing and should be planned with the needs of existing residents in mind. Affordable housing should also mean preserving affordability that already exists. I would support efforts to prevent displacement and preserve existing affordable homes, while recognizing that the District needs to build substantially more housing to meet current and future demand. We should be able to pursue both goals at the same time. Transportation and land use should be planned together. I support making it easier and safer to walk, bike, and use public transportation, particularly along corridors where we are encouraging additional housing. New development should be accompanied by attention to pedestrian safety, sidewalks, transit access, traffic impacts, and public infrastructure. Finally, I recognize the limits of the ANC's authority. I would not promise residents that an ANC can solve the District's housing or transportation challenges by itself. Instead, I would focus on using the Commission's voice effectively: engaging residents early, reviewing proposals carefully, advocating with District agencies, and building constructive relationships with community organizations, planners, developers, and other stakeholders. My goal is a neighborhood that grows without losing its diversity—a place where new residents are welcomed, longtime residents can stay, and public investment and development work together to create a more affordable, connected, and resilient community.

column26: Although ANC 2B is already the fifth most densely populated ANC, there are still opportunities to add hundreds more housing units. The Safeway, the McDonalds and the CVS on 17th St are low density commercial sites on prime corner lots in a major corridor. Furthermore, with the election of Janeese Lewis-George as Mayor, there is an opportunity for this site to be used for social housing rather than the usual private sector mix of market rate and affordable units. Also just outside ANC 2B is the Sunoco station currently being demolished at 15th and U which would be a prime location to build hundreds of units of new housing. There is no information available about what the owner’s plans are for that site, but ensuring that as much new housing as possible is built on that site should be a priority. The biggest issue for my SMD is traffic safety. The future of 17th St between R and P is a key piece: the protected bike lanes north of R and south of P have slowed traffic and made the street safer. But between R and P, compromises made to preserve streateries left a bike lane going north with none going south, while the pre-existing delivery truck problem was never addressed. I support pedestrianizing 17th St between R and P provided alley access for residents and trash/recycling collection is preserved. But even if that’s only possible in the longer term, more can be done now: with the streateries on the west side gone, a two-way protected bike lane there should be revisited. The ANC should also work with Safeway, True Value, CVS and other businesses to end 53-ft trailer deliveries and restrict delivery hours — at peak times, trucks routinely block crosswalks, a problem that predates the bike lanes. All flex posts should become permanent curb extensions; trucks and cars currently drive over them, endangering pedestrians and cyclists. I support protected bike lanes on Q and R Streets even if it costs a lane of parking, though a two-way lane on R St alone (rather than one-way lanes on both streets) may better preserve parking. Finally, as the protected bike network expands, I support extending the downtown prohibition on riding bicycles and personal mobility devices on sidewalks to ANC 2B. Our often-narrow sidewalks should primarily be for pedestrians.

If elected, I would: If elected, I would introduce a resolution asking the DC Council and DDOT to extend to ANC 2B the existing prohibition on riding bicycles and personal mobility devices on sidewalks in the Central Business District. As the protected bike network expands, I believe sidewalks in ANC 2B should primarily be for pedestrians. Many are narrow and already heavily used, and pedestrians should not have to compete with bikes and scooters for limited space. The ANC should also work with DDOT to identify locations where better bike infrastructure can make this restriction practical while preserving safe routes for cyclists.
column36: First, ANC members have to follow established law and procedures as they currently stand, not as they wish them to be. For example, if 60% of the property owners on a block follow the established procedure and petition to replace a female gingko tree with a male tree, the ANC should consider that petition on its merits. Blocking it or, worse, refusing even to consider it without a specific reason, simply because the ANC members oppose ever replacing a healthy mature tree, is an abuse of their discretionary power. Second, although it won't be possible to hear from all constituents, it's important for ANC members to solicit feedback from their constituents and keep their constituents informed of important matters that directly affect their SMDs. I intend to do both. I will try to listen respectfully to constituents who wish to make their views known to me. And even if I have a strongly held view on a matter, that doesn't mean that concerns expressed by individual constituents should just be dismissed out of hand. For example, I strongly support the bike lanes and road diet that have transformed 17th Street between Massachusetts Avenue and T St. But I know there are residents of my SMD who have serious concerns, particularly about pedestrian safety. To the extent those concerns can be reasonably addressed, they should be. At the same time, I would not give undue weight to the views of various civic associations that are unlikely to represent the views of the majority of residents in my SMD. Finally, it's important to recognize that, although ANCs are hyperlocal bodies, the vast majority of ANC members run unopposed and, even in those cases where there is more than one candidate, most voters are not well informed about the views of the candidates. For this reason, a little humility is in order. I think that ANCs should largely stick to weighing in on local matters that directly affect their constituents rather than treating every citywide policy debate as an occasion for a resolution — whether the topic is land use, historic preservation or something else entirely. There's a difference between taking the job seriously and taking yourself seriously. If elected to ANC 2B, I intend to do the former and try to avoid too much of the latter.

I understand that an ANC commissioner cannot stop or approve development alone, but we can bring residents to the table, hold developers and District agencies accountable, pass ANC resolutions, provide testimony, and advocate before agencies such as the Zoning Commission and Board of Zoning Adjustment. I would push for affordable and family-sized housing, responsible development, infrastructure improvements, and meaningful community benefits when appropriate. Most importantly, I would communicate with residents early, not after decisions have already been made, and make sure all voices in the neighborhood have an opportunity to be heard.

If elected, I would: I feel one of the biggest issues in my neighborhood is how we manage growth and development while making sure the people who already live here are not pushed out or forgotten. I support more affordable and family-sized housing, but I also believe development must make sense for the neighborhood and the infrastructure that supports it. We need to consider traffic, parking, public transportation, schools, public safety, and the character and history of our community. I want growth that creates opportunities for working families, seniors, and longtime residents to remain in the neighborhood, not development that is only focused on adding market-rate units.
column36: As an ANC commissioner, I would remember that I represent every resident in my single-member district, not just the people who attend meetings or are the loudest in the room. I would make an effort to hear from residents in different ways—community meetings, walking the neighborhood, email, phone calls, social media, surveys, and conversations with people who may not normally participate.  When making decisions, I would listen to the community, review the facts, consider who will be affected, and pay special attention to residents whose voices are often left out. I also understand that leadership sometimes means making a decision when there is no clear majority. In those situations, I would make the decision I believe best serves the overall community and be transparent about why I made it. I may not always make the decision everyone wants, but residents will always know that I listened, did my homework, and made the decision with the community’s best interest in mind.

column12: Affordable housing in ANC 4B06 generally refers to units that are means-tested, income‑restricted, subsidized, or rent‑controlled, ensuring residents pay no more than 30% of their household income on housing costs, aligning with federal definitions and local interpretations. These units are often created through programs like Inclusionary Zoning, which requires developers of larger residential projects to set aside a percentage of units as affordable, tying the number of units to building size so that increased density can produce more affordable homes. Market‑rate housing, by contrast, is built by private developers without subsidies or rent controls and is typically more expensive, often costing more than 30% of a household’s income and reflecting prevailing real‑estate market conditions rather than an affordability standard. In ANC 4B06, the distinction matters because the community’s housing strategy emphasizes adding density near transit corridors to expand supply while ensuring affordability is preserved through income‑restricted units. Affordable housing supports lower‑income residents by capping costs and providing long‑term stability, while market‑rate housing expands overall inventory but does not inherently meet affordability needs unless paired with policy tools requiring set‑asides or deeper affordability levels.

Our streets were not designed for the level of vehicle speed and volume they experience today, and the result is an environment where near‑misses, unsafe crossings, and resident complaints have become routine. Too many intersections lack all‑way stop control and too many pedestrian crossings rely on faded paint or insufficient signage to keep people safe. I believe that safe, walkable streets are a fundamental neighborhood right, not an amenity, and that building this environment starts with strong advocacy, thoughtful data collection, and persistent follow‑through with District agencies. I would push for targeted DDOT evaluations at the most hazardous intersections and request the installation of four‑way stop signs, speed humps, raised crosswalks, and upgraded pedestrian signageBy combining constituent input with agency partnership and evidence‑based solutions, I would work to create calmer, safer streets that support walking, biking, and everyday neighborhood life.

If elected, I would: If elected, I would focus on addressing what I believe is the neighborhood’s biggest issue: traffic safety. Unsafe intersections, frequent speeding, and inadequate pedestrian protections continue to put residents—especially children, seniors, and people with disabilities—at risk, and improving street safety is both urgent and achievable within an ANC commissioner’s authority. My strategy would begin with systematically identifying the most dangerous intersections and corridors through community feedback, walk audits, and data shared by DDOT. I would then file formal ANC resolutions requesting all‑way stop conversions, speed humps, raised crosswalks, clearer signage, and curb extensions, prioritizing locations where residents report near‑misses or where previous incident data shows heightened risk. Because the ANC’s power is advisory, I would maintain regular communication with DDOT to ensure requests are not only logged but advanced through the evaluation and installation process. By combining evidence‑based advocacy, structured community engagement, and consistent agency coordination, I would work to create safer, calmer, and more walkable streets for everyone in our neighborhood.
column36: As an elected ANC commissioner representing roughly 2,000 constituents, I would make decisions through a structured, transparent, and community‑centered process designed to balance individual input, data‑driven analysis, and the broader needs of the entire District. Because of this, my decision‑making approach must actively seek out multiple forms of input while also relying on consistent principles of equity, safety, accessibility, and long‑term community stability. My first step would be to maintain regular and open communication channels, including monthly SMD meetings, issue‑specific listening sessions, and accessible digital tools like surveys and newsletters. These platforms ensure that a wide range of voices—including those who cannot attend meetings—can share their experiences and concerns. I would supplement resident feedback with available data from District agencies, including DDOT, DCRA, MPD, and the Office of Planning, using evidence‑based information to understand trends, identify needs, and evaluate potential outcomes. When constituent perspectives differ, I would examine not just the number of people expressing a view but the equity implications of the issue, the potential benefits or harms to vulnerable groups, and whether the proposed action aligns with adopted District‑wide goals such as housing production, safe streets, environmental sustainability, and accessibility. As a commissioner, my decisions would center on fairness and transparency. I would clearly explain the rationale for each position I take, referencing data, community feedback, and District policy so residents understand how and why decisions were made—even when they may disagree. Character should evolve in ways that welcome more people, support small businesses, and improve public spaces. I want GGWash to understand that my approach is holistic, informed by community voices, and grounded in a commitment to making our neighborhood—and our city—more inclusive, more sustainable, and more connected.

column12: At its core, the distinction between affordable housing and market-rate housing lies in how rents are set, who the homes serve, and the funding mechanisms behind them.  Market-Rate Housing  Market-rate housing operates on private market supply and demand dynamics. Rents and sale prices are set by property owners to maximize revenue based on location, amenities, and market competition. While market-rate supply is essential for absorbing overall demand and reducing broad regional price pressures, market forces alone do not set prices low enough to accommodate lower-income households without consuming an unsustainable portion of their earnings.  Affordable Housing  Affordable housing is structurally protected so that housing costs do not exceed 30% of a household's gross income. It encompasses two primary forms:  Income-Restricted / Subsidized Affordable Housing: Capped by government regulations, tax credits (like LIHTC), local subsidies (like DC's Housing Production Trust Fund), or Inclusionary Zoning (IZ). Eligibility is tied to specific Area Median Income (AMI) bands—such as 30%, 50%, or 80% AMI—ensuring homes remain accessible to low- and moderate-income working families, seniors, and service workers.  Naturally Occurring Affordable Housing (NOAH): Older, un-subsidized private market properties that remain affordable due to age or location.  Both market-rate and affordable housing are necessary components of a balanced, equitable city housing ecosystem.

Safe, walkable streets and active, well-maintained housing blocks are the baseline every District neighborhood deserves.

column36: As an ANC Commissioner representing Single Member District 8A01, making fair, effective decisions requires balancing constituent feedback with rigorous policy analysis, proactive outreach, and data-driven equity. Relying solely on inbox messages or evening meetings risks favoring a vocal minority over working families, renters, seniors, and youth who lack time to attend multi-hour public forums.  To serve the entire community, I guide my leadership through a four-part framework:  1. Proactive Community Engagement  Instead of waiting for residents to reach out, I meet them where they gather. I conduct regular neighborhood walkthroughs, hold pop-up office hours at parks and bus stops, maintain an active digital presence, and collaborate with local schools, churches, and tenant associations to gather broad, representative input.  2. Grounding Decisions in Data & Policy  I weigh constituent feedback against land-use data, traffic safety metrics, housing production numbers, and long-range city plans. Decisions shouldn't stem from loud pushback alone; they must be grounded in evidence showing long-term benefits for affordability, safety, and neighborhood quality of life.  3. Applying an Equity & Anti-Displacement Lens  Land-use and transit decisions in Ward 8 carry high stakes for affordability and equity. I evaluate every proposal by asking: Who benefits, and who bears the cost? I prioritize keeping long-term residents housed, attracting essential commercial services, protecting vulnerable road users, and expanding housing choices.  4. Transparent Communication  On contentious issues, I clearly explain the rationale behind my votes. Through published meeting summaries and updates, I detail the data, statutory context, and public input that shaped each decision.  Ultimately, my role is to act as an accessible, accountable trustee—using proactive outreach, data analysis, and equity-focused policy to build a safer, more vibrant neighborhood for all 2,000 constituents.

column38: In Ward 8 and across Single Member District 8A01, housing, land use, and transportation are not isolated policy silos—they are deeply interconnected drivers of equity, displacement prevention, and community health. When considering my positions, I encourage Greater Greater Washington (GGWash) to keep three core principles at the center:  1. Equity Means Proactive Investment East of the River  For too long, policy debates in the District have treated housing production and infrastructure investments as one-size-fits-all across every Ward. While Ward 3 needs aggressive upzoning to unlock high-opportunity areas, Ward 8 requires a balanced strategy that pairs density and missing-middle housing with strict anti-displacement protections, tenant support, and capital investments in long-neglected commercial corridors. We must legalize rowhomes, triplexes, and sixplexes while ensuring that public land disposition, Inclusionary Zoning, and Housing Production Trust Fund resources deliver deeply affordable, family-sized units directly where working families are at risk of being priced out.  2. Complete Streets and Transit Reliability Are Civil Rights Issues  In Historic Anacostia and Fairlawn, a significant portion of our residents rely on Metrobus and walking to reach jobs, healthcare, and schools. Yet, our corridors continue to suffer from speed-heavy vehicle traffic, delayed buses, and unsafe pedestrian crossings. Transportation policy must explicitly prioritize vulnerable road users over private automobile throughput. Dedicated bus lanes, protected micro-mobility infrastructure, and automated traffic enforcement along corridors like Good Hope Road SE and Marion Barry Avenue SE are essential tools to save lives, improve bus transit speeds, and connect East of the River residents to regional economic opportunities.  3. Activating Blighted and Vacant Land First  Before expanding development into established residential green spaces, our immediate land-use focus should be turning tax-delinquent, vacant, and blighted structures into active housing and community assets. Neglected parcels drag down local safety, encourage illegal dumping, and hold back neighborhood vitality. By streamlining District agency oversight—pushing DOB, OAG, and DMPED to utilize judicial receivership, tax auctions, and public land transfers—we can rapidly convert neighborhood eyesores into vibrant market-rate and income-restricted housing.  Ultimately, my goal as an ANC Commissioner is to bring a forward-thinking, multimodal, and supply-positive urbanism to Ward 8—one that embraces density, insists on transit equity, and protects the long-term culture and residents of our community.

column12: Affordable housing and market-rate housing serve different purposes within the overall housing market, but both are essential to creating healthy, economically diverse communities. Affordable housing is designed to ensure that households can obtain safe, decent housing without spending more than approximately 30 percent of their income on housing costs. It may be income-restricted, subsidized, or developed through public-private partnerships, although not all affordable housing receives direct government subsidies.  Market-rate housing is priced according to current market conditions and is generally not income-restricted or subsidized. Rental rates and home prices are determined by supply and demand rather than affordability requirements. Depending on a household's income, market-rate housing may be affordable for some residents but unaffordable for others.  A balanced housing strategy should include a range of housing options—including affordable, workforce, and market-rate housing—to meet the needs of individuals and families at different income levels. Expanding the housing supply, encouraging mixed-income developments, streamlining development processes, and fostering public-private partnerships can help improve housing affordability while supporting economic growth, neighborhood stability, and a high quality of life for all residents.

Family-sized housing can exist at a variety of price points, and households should seek housing that aligns with their financial means. If a particular home is beyond a family's budget, they should consider other housing options that better fit their financial situation.

However, I would use the office to be a strong advocate and liaison for residents. I would regularly engage with MPD district leadership, the Mayor's Office, and relevant agencies to communicate neighborhood concerns and advocate for targeted enforcement and public safety resources.  I would organize regular community meetings with public safety officials, encourage residents to report crimes and suspicious activity, promote Neighborhood Watch and other community-based initiatives, and work with agencies to address environmental factors that contribute to crime, such as poor lighting, abandoned properties, illegal dumping, and overgrown lots. I would also advocate for traffic calming measures, improved pedestrian safety, and investments in youth and community programs that help prevent crime before it occurs.  My goal would be to build trust between residents and government, ensure community concerns are heard, and pursue practical, collaborative solutions that make the neighborhood safer for everyone.

Residents deserve to feel safe in their homes, while walking their streets, using public transportation, and enjoying neighborhood parks and businesses. Concerns such as violent crime, property crime, illegal dumping, traffic safety, reckless driving, and quality-of-life issues can erode residents' confidence and negatively affect neighborhood stability and economic vitality.  I believe public safety is a shared responsibility that requires collaboration among law enforcement, government agencies, neighborhood organizations, businesses, and residents. While effective policing is important, long-term public safety also depends on community engagement, youth opportunities, environmental design, code enforcement, and timely responses to resident concerns. My position is that the District should continue investing in proactive crime prevention strategies while strengthening partnerships between residents and public safety agencies.

My vision for 5D01 focuses on three core pillars:  Smart Infrastructure: Tackling Traffic and Parking The most pressing issues in our district are traffic congestion and parking shortages. I will work directly with city agencies to evaluate and implement traffic flow improvements, including converting select streets to one-way systems to reduce gridlock and improve safety. My goal is to make our streets manageable for residents while maintaining access for visitors.  Preserving Our Heritage and Green Space Union Market’s history defines our character, but we need room to breathe. I am committed to securing a dedicated community park and more green space. We must ensure that as we grow, we create places where neighbors connect and families thrive, honoring our roots while building a sustainable future.  Collaborative Development Growth should serve the people. I will work constructively with developers to ensure our neighborhood's evolution is transparent and resident-driven. I am your bridge to the planning process, ensuring your voice is at the center of every decision.  I am running because I believe the best version of Union Market is one where development and community thrive together. I look forward to earning your vote and working for you to ensure our district remains a place we are all proud to call home.

If elected, I would: As a candidate for ANC 5D01, I am committed to ensuring our neighborhood’s rapid growth benefits everyone. My platform centers on five key areas:  Housing: A thriving neighborhood must be inclusive. I support diverse housing options that allow residents at all income levels to live and work here, ensuring 5D01 remains a home for both long-term residents and new neighbors.  Transportation: Our biggest challenge is the strain on our streets. I will prioritize practical, data-driven solutions to manage traffic congestion and parking. This includes advocating for traffic studies to explore one-way street conversions and improved infrastructure that prioritizes pedestrian safety.  Land Use: Development must be intentional and community-focused. I advocate for mixed-use spaces that integrate residential and commercial needs with essential public amenities, like green space and community facilities.  Small Businesses: Local shops are our heartbeat. I am committed to a business-friendly environment that helps our entrepreneurs operate and thrive.  I am running to ensure that as 5D01 continues to become a world-class destination, it never loses sight of the people who make it a neighborhood.
column36: As an ANC Commissioner, my role is to balance individual constituent concerns with the broader, long-term health of our entire 5D01 community. Representing roughly 2,000 neighbors means acknowledging that our district is diverse in its needs, backgrounds, and priorities. To make informed, fair decisions, I will rely on a multi-layered approach:  Proactive Engagement and Data-Driven Outreach I cannot wait for feedback to come to me. I will actively seek out the "silent majority" by utilizing digital platforms, community forums, and consistent office hours to ensure that voices from different corners of our district—renters, homeowners, long-term residents, and new arrivals—are heard. By intentionally reaching out to those who may not typically engage with the ANC, I can ensure my decisions are informed by a broader cross-section of our community rather than just the most vocal few.  Focusing on Core Community Values When faced with conflicting viewpoints, I will ground my decisions in the fundamental pillars of our district’s success: safety, sustainability, and community identity. If a proposal aligns with our collective goals—such as reducing traffic congestion, creating accessible green space, or ensuring responsible development—it will receive my support. I will weigh individual requests against these shared objectives to ensure that my actions benefit the neighborhood as a whole, rather than serving narrow interests.  Transparency and Accessibility Transparency is the best antidote to the fear that a representative is only listening to a select group. I will clearly articulate the "why" behind my votes. When I take a position, I will share the data, the community feedback, and the reasoning that led to that conclusion. By keeping our process open, I allow constituents to understand the trade-offs involved in complex decisions, which builds trust even among those who may initially disagree with a specific outcome.  Collaboration with Stakeholders As a Real Estate Professional, I understand how to navigate complex project stakeholders and city agencies. I will use this experience to facilitate productive conversations between residents, developers, and city officials. My goal is not to force a decision, but to find common ground. By fostering a collaborative environment, we can often find solutions that address the primary concerns of multiple groups simultaneously.  Ultimately, my responsibility is to be a steward of the Union Market District. I will listen deeply, analyze the facts, and prioritize the long-term vitality of our neighborhood, ensuring that 5D01 remains a place where everyone has the opportunity to thrive. My door will always be open, and I will remain accountable to all 2,000 of my constituents by consistently working toward the common good.

column12: Affordable housing should mean more than simply labeling a unit “affordable.” It should mean that working people and families can pay their rent without having to choose between housing, groceries, health care, or transportation. That often requires income restrictions, public investment, rent limits, or other protections that keep homes within reach over time. Market-rate housing is different because its price is largely driven by the market and is not required to serve people at a particular income level. We need more housing overall, including market-rate housing, but increasing supply alone will not meet every need. Public investment and long-term affordability protections are still necessary to make sure lower-income residents are not priced out. The real distinction is whether there is a meaningful and enforceable commitment to keeping the housing affordable for the people who need it most.
